docs.text: Creating Distributable Python Packages So far you've shared code by copying .py files around. In this notebook we turn a small text-utility module into a real package that anyone can install with pip install , run from the terminal, and upgrade cleanly. Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Explain the difference between a script, a module and a distributable package Lay out a package using the modern src/ layout Write a complete pyproject.toml with metadata, dependencies and build settings Install your package locally in editable mode with pip install -e . Create CLI entry points so users can run your package from the terminal Build a wheel ( .whl ) and a source distribution ( .tar.gz ) Publish a package to TestPyPI Pick the right version number using semantic versioning Prerequisites Python 3.9 or newer Comfortable with functions, modules and import Basic terminal use (running commands, changing directories) pip available (the notebook installs build , pytest and twine for you when needed) How to Use This Notebook Run the cells from top to bottom . We build one package, texttools , step by step, and later cells depend on files written by earlier ones. The package is created in a folder called texttools_project/ next to this notebook. You can open it in your editor at any point to see the real files. Try the practice tasks and the challenge yourself first, then open Show solution to compare. Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read only the recaps when revising. 1. Why Not Just Share a .py File? Say you've written a handy Python utility and a teammate wants to use it. The first thing most people do is email them the file. Here's what tends to go wrong: Problem What happens They save the file in the wrong folder ImportError : Python can't find it Your code needs requests Nobody told them to install it You fix a bug They're still running the old copy They want to run it as a command They have to work out how to call the script You release v2 Nobody knows which version they have A distributable package fixes all of these. It's a bundle that: installs with one command: pip install texttools declares its own dependencies, so pip installs them too carries a version number can add commands to the terminal can be upgraded cleanly with pip install --upgrade The Packaging Pipeline at a Glance You write code | v [ pyproject.toml ] <- describes your package (name, version, dependencies...) | v [ python -m build ] <- bundles your code into distributable files | v [ .whl + .tar.gz files ] <- the "wheel" is what pip actually installs | v [ twine upload ] <- publishes the files to PyPI | v [ pip install texttools ] <- your users install it We'll go through every step of this pipeline in this notebook. Quick recap Copying .py files breaks as soon as there are dependencies, bug fixes or new versions. A package has a name, a version, its dependencies and (optionally) terminal commands. The pipeline is: pyproject.toml -> python -m build -> twine upload -> pip install . 2. Anatomy of a Modern Python Package The src/ Layout There are two common ways to lay out a package. We'll use the src/ layout , which is what the Python Packaging Guide recommends: texttools_project/ <- project root (usually your git repo) | +-- src/ | +-- texttools/ <- the actual Python package | +-- __init__.py <- marks it as a package, defines the public API | +-- core.py <- the utility functions | +-- cli.py <- the command-line interface | +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py <- unit tests | +-- pyproject.toml <- package metadata and build settings +-- README.md Why put the package inside src/ ? If the package folder sits right next to your tests, Python can import the local folder instead of the installed package . Your tests then pass on your machine even when the installed version is broken. With src/ , the only way to import texttools is to install it, so your tests check what users actually get. Layout What can go wrong Flat (no src/ ) The local folder shadows the installed package during tests src/ layout Tests always run against the installed package What __init__.py Does __init__.py has two jobs: It tells Python that this folder is a package , not just a folder. It defines the public API : what users get when they write import texttools . Here's the __init__.py we're going to write. Don't run anything yet; we create the real file in Step 1 below. # src/texttools/__init__.py __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count , reverse_words , title_case_smart __all__ = [ "word_count" , "reverse_words" , "title_case_smart" ] __version__ is the usual way to expose your package's version in code. __all__ controls what from texttools import * brings in. Listing names here makes your public API explicit. Step 1: Create the Folder Structure Now let's build texttools for real. Run the cells below in order. Each one writes a file into texttools_project/ . import os import pathlib # Everything goes inside texttools_project/, next to this notebook. BASE = pathlib . Path ( "texttools_project" ) dirs = [ BASE / "src" / "texttools" , BASE / "tests" , ] for d in dirs : d . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) print ( "Directories created:" ) for d in dirs : print ( f " { d } " ) Directories created: texttools_project/src/texttools texttools_project/tests Step 2: Write the Package Code core.py holds the three functions our package offers. We store the file's contents in a string and write it to disk, so you can read the whole file right here in the notebook. # src/texttools/core.py - the actual utility functions core_code = '''"""Core text utility functions for texttools.""" def word_count(text: str) -> dict: """Count the frequency of each word in a string. Args: text: The input string to analyse. Returns: A dictionary mapping each word (lowercased) to its count. Example: >>> word_count("the cat sat on the mat") {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} """ words = text.lower().split() counts: dict = {} for word in words: # Strip basic punctuation word = word.strip(".,!?;:'") if word: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 return counts def reverse_words(text: str) -> str: """Reverse the order of words in a string. Args: text: The input string. Returns: A new string with word order reversed. Example: >>> reverse_words("Hello World") 'World Hello' """ return " ".join(reversed(text.split())) def title_case_smart(text: str) -> str: """Convert a string to title case, skipping common short words. Short connector words (a, an, the, and, but, or, for, nor, on, at, to, by, in, of, up) remain lowercase unless they are the first or last word. Args: text: The input string. Returns: A title-cased string respecting common style guidelines. Example: >>> title_case_smart("the lord of the rings") 'The Lord of the Rings' """ SKIP = {"a", "an", "the", "and", "but", "or", "for", "nor", "on", "at", "to", "by", "in", "of", "up"} words = text.lower().split() result = [] for i, word in enumerate(words): if i == 0 or i == len(words) - 1 or word not in SKIP: result.append(word.capitalize()) else: result.append(word) return " ".join(result) ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "core.py" ) . write_text ( core_code ) print ( "core.py written." ) core.py written. # src/texttools/__init__.py - the public API init_code = '''"""texttools - a small text utility library.""" __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart __all__ = ["word_count", "reverse_words", "title_case_smart"] ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( init_code ) print ( "__init__.py written." ) __init__.py written. What just happened? We now have src/texttools/core.py and src/texttools/__init__.py on disk. You can't import texttools yet, because Python doesn't know about the src/ folder. Installing the package (Section 4) is what fixes that. Quick recap Use the src/ layout: src/<package>/ for code, tests/ beside it, pyproject.toml at the root. src/ stops your tests from accidentally importing the local folder instead of the installed package. __init__.py marks a package and defines its public API ( __version__ , __all__ ). 3. pyproject.toml Deep Dive pyproject.toml is the one file that describes your package. It replaced the older setup.py and setup.cfg files, which you'll still see in older projects. It has a few tables (sections). Let's go through them one at a time. [build-system] : how to build the package This tells pip which build tool to use. We use setuptools : [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=77" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" We ask for setuptools 77 or newer because that's the version that understands the modern license = "MIT" field below. [project] : what the package is [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3" , "Operating System :: OS Independent" , ] A few notes: dependencies lists other packages yours needs, e.g. ["requests>=2.31"] . Ours needs none. license is a short SPDX code like "MIT" or "Apache-2.0" . Older tutorials write license = {text = "MIT"} and add a License :: ... classifier; current setuptools warns about both, so don't copy that style. classifiers are tags that help people find your package on PyPI. [project.scripts] : terminal commands This creates CLI commands (more on this in Section 5): [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # ^command ^module ^function [tool.setuptools.packages.find] : where the code lives This tells setuptools to look inside src/ for packages. You need it for the src/ layout: [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] Step 3: Write pyproject.toml and README.md Now we put all of those tables together into one file. # Write the pyproject.toml for texttools pyproject = """[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=77"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting" authors = [{name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com"}] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3", "Operating System :: OS Independent", ] [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] """ ( BASE / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( pyproject ) print ( "pyproject.toml written." ) pyproject.toml written. pyproject.toml says readme = "README.md" , so that file has to exist too. PyPI shows it as your package's front page. # Write a minimal README.md (referenced by pyproject.toml) readme = '''# texttools A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting. ## Installation ~~~bash pip install texttools ~~~ ## Usage ~~~python from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart print(word_count("the cat sat on the mat")) # {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} print(reverse_words("Hello World")) # 'World Hello' print(title_case_smart("the lord of the rings")) # 'The Lord of the Rings' ~~~ ## CLI ~~~bash texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" texttools reverse "Hello World" texttools titlecase "the lord of the rings" ~~~ ''' ( BASE / "README.md" ) . write_text ( readme ) print ( "README.md written." ) README.md written. Quick recap [build-system] says how to build (setuptools); [project] says what the package is. Use license = "MIT" (an SPDX string), not the old {text = ...} table or license classifiers. [project.scripts] maps a terminal command to a Python function. With the src/ layout you need [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] . 4. Installing Locally with pip install -e . Before publishing anything, you want to use and test the package on your own machine. The -e flag means editable install . Editable Install vs Regular Install Mode Command How it works Regular pip install . Copies your files into site-packages . Every change needs a reinstall. Editable pip install -e . Points Python at your source folder. Changes show up straight away. During development you'll almost always use editable mode. What Happens Under the Hood pip install -e texttools_project/ | v reads pyproject.toml | v writes a small .pth file into site-packages that points to src/ | v Python can now find 'import texttools' Step 4: Install the Package In a terminal you'd run pip install -e texttools_project/ . Here we run the same command from Python so it installs into this notebook's environment. import subprocess , sys result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) if result . returncode == 0 : print ( "Package installed successfully." ) else : print ( "Error:" ) print ( result . stderr ) # Make the package importable in the current kernel session # (pip editable installs use .pth files, loaded at startup, not dynamically) src_path = str ( BASE / "src" ) if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) print ( f "Added { src_path } to sys.path" ) Package installed successfully. Added texttools_project/src to sys.path What just happened? pip installed texttools in editable mode. The .pth file it wrote is only read when Python starts, so this already-running notebook wouldn't see it. That's why the cell also adds src/ to sys.path by hand. In a fresh terminal or a restarted kernel you wouldn't need that line. Let's check that the import works. # Verify the install # Force a fresh import in case texttools was already loaded for key in list ( sys . modules . keys ()): if key . startswith ( "texttools" ): del sys . modules [ key ] import texttools print ( f "texttools version: { texttools . __version__ } " ) print () sample = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" print ( "word_count():" ) print ( texttools . word_count ( sample )) print () print ( "reverse_words():" ) print ( texttools . reverse_words ( sample )) print () print ( "title_case_smart():" ) print ( texttools . title_case_smart ( "the lord of the rings: the return of the king" )) texttools version: 0.1.0 word_count(): {'the': 2, 'quick': 1, 'brown': 1, 'fox': 1, 'jumps': 1, 'over': 1, 'lazy': 1, 'dog': 1} reverse_words(): dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the title_case_smart(): The Lord of the Rings: the Return of the King Checkpoint: you should see texttools version: 0.1.0 followed by the results of the three functions. If you get ModuleNotFoundError , re-run the install cell above. Notice the title-case result: the stays lowercase after Rings: because our function only looks at word position, not punctuation. Good enough for a teaching example. Quick recap pip install -e . installs your package in editable mode: edit the code, re-run, no reinstall. A regular pip install . copies the files, so you'd need to reinstall after every change. Editable installs work through a .pth file that Python reads at start-up. 5. Entry Points: Creating CLI Commands Entry points let users run your package as a normal terminal command: $ texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 How It Works When pip installs your package, it reads [project.scripts] from pyproject.toml : [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # ^command ^module ^function pip then creates a tiny launcher program called texttools in your environment's bin/ folder ( Scripts\ on Windows). Running it simply calls texttools.cli.main() . Step 5: Write the CLI Module cli.py uses argparse from the standard library to read the command-line arguments. It has three sub-commands: count , reverse and titlecase . # src/texttools/cli.py - command-line interface cli_code = '''"""Command-line interface for texttools.""" import argparse import sys from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart def main() -> None: """Entry point for the texttools CLI.""" parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( prog="texttools", description="Text utility commands", ) subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True) # count command count_parser = subparsers.add_parser("count", help="Count word frequencies") count_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to analyse") # reverse command reverse_parser = subparsers.add_parser("reverse", help="Reverse word order") reverse_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to reverse") # titlecase command title_parser = subparsers.add_parser("titlecase", help="Smart title case") title_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to convert") args = parser.parse_args() if args.command == "count": counts = word_count(args.text) for word, n in sorted(counts.items()): print(f" {word} : {n} ") elif args.command == "reverse": print(reverse_words(args.text)) elif args.command == "titlecase": print(title_case_smart(args.text)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( cli_code ) print ( "cli.py written." ) # Reinstall so pip registers the new entry point result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "Package reinstalled." if result . returncode == 0 else result . stderr ) # Make sure src/ is still on the path if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) cli.py written. Package reinstalled. We reinstalled because entry points are created at install time. Adding cli.py alone doesn't create the texttools command. Now let's try the CLI. In a terminal you would type texttools count "..." . Here we call the same code with python -m texttools.cli , which works no matter where the launcher was installed. # Test the CLI programmatically result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "count" , "the cat sat on the mat" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat':" ) print ( result . stdout ) result2 = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "titlecase" , "the lord of the rings" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings':" ) print ( result2 . stdout ) texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat': cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings': The Lord of the Rings Checkpoint: the word counts should be sorted alphabetically, and the title should read The Lord of the Rings . Why if __name__ == "__main__": ? That guard at the bottom of cli.py is what makes python -m texttools.cli work. The installed texttools command doesn't need it, because it calls main() directly. The guard is just handy while you're developing. Quick recap [project.scripts] turns command = "module:function" into a real terminal command. The command is created when the package is installed, so reinstall after adding an entry point. argparse sub-parsers give you git -style sub-commands like texttools count . 6. Testing the Installed Package Tests should run against the installed package, not loose source files. The src/ layout guarantees that: the tests can only import texttools because it's installed. Test Structure tests/ +-- test_core.py Note there's no __init__.py in tests/ . pytest doesn't need one, and leaving it out avoids confusing import problems. Step 6: Write and Run the Tests # Write the test file test_code = '''"""Tests for texttools.core""" import pytest from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart class TestWordCount: def test_basic_count(self): result = word_count("the cat sat on the mat") assert result["the"] == 2 assert result["cat"] == 1 def test_case_insensitive(self): result = word_count("Python python PYTHON") assert result["python"] == 3 def test_strips_punctuation(self): result = word_count("hello, world!") assert "hello" in result assert "world" in result def test_empty_string(self): assert word_count("") == {} class TestReverseWords: def test_basic_reverse(self): assert reverse_words("Hello World") == "World Hello" def test_single_word(self): assert reverse_words("Python") == "Python" def test_multiple_words(self): assert reverse_words("one two three") == "three two one" class TestTitleCaseSmart: def test_short_words_lowercase(self): result = title_case_smart("the lord of the rings") assert result == "The Lord of the Rings" def test_first_word_always_capitalised(self): result = title_case_smart("of mice and men") assert result.startswith("Of") def test_last_word_always_capitalised(self): result = title_case_smart("the cat in the hat") assert result.endswith("Hat") def test_single_word(self): assert title_case_smart("python") == "Python" ''' ( BASE / "tests" / "test_core.py" ) . write_text ( test_code ) print ( "test_core.py written." ) test_core.py written. # Install pytest if needed subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "pytest" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) # Run the tests result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pytest" , str ( BASE / "tests" ), "-v" , "--color=no" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( result . stdout ) if result . stderr : print ( result . stderr ) ============================= test session starts ============================== platform darwin -- Python 3.12.14, pytest-9.2.0, pluggy-1.7.0 -- .venv/bin/python cachedir: .pytest_cache rootdir: texttools_project configfile: pyproject.toml plugins: platformdirs-4.14.0, anyio-4.15.1 collecting ... collected 11 items texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_basic_count PASSED [ 9%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_case_insensitive PASSED [ 18%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_strips_punctuation PASSED [ 27%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_empty_string PASSED [ 36%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_basic_reverse PASSED [ 45%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_single_word PASSED [ 54%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_multiple_words PASSED [ 63%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_short_words_lowercase PASSED [ 72%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_first_word_always_capitalised PASSED [ 81%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_last_word_always_capitalised PASSED [ 90%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_single_word PASSED [100%] ============================== 11 passed in 0.01s ============================== Checkpoint: you should see 11 passed . If a test fails, read the assertion message, fix core.py , and run the test cell again. Thanks to the editable install there's no need to reinstall. Quick recap Put tests in tests/ next to src/ , with no __init__.py . Run them with python -m pytest tests/ . Because of the src/ layout, a passing test means the installed package works. 7. Building a Distribution When you're ready to share the package, you build it into files that pip can install: Format Extension Description Wheel .whl Ready-to-install archive. Fast to install and the most common format. Source distribution (sdist) .tar.gz Archive of your source code. pip builds it on the user's machine. Always publish both . pip prefers the wheel and falls back to the sdist. The build Tool python -m build reads pyproject.toml and creates both files in a dist/ folder: dist/ +-- texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl +-- texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz Reading a Wheel's Filename texttools - 0.1.0 - py3 - none - any .whl ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ package version python abi platform py3 = works with Python 3 none = no compiled code, so no ABI requirement (pure Python) any = works on any operating system Step 7: Build the Package This is the same as running python -m build texttools_project/ in a terminal. It can take a little while the first time because it sets up a clean build environment. # Install the build tool if not already present subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "build" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) # Build the package result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "build" , str ( BASE )], capture_output = True , text = True , env = { ** os . environ , "NO_COLOR" : "1" }, # plain text output, no colour codes ) # The full log is long; the last line tells us whether it worked print ( result . stdout . strip () . splitlines ()[ - 1 ] if result . stdout . strip () else "(no output)" ) if result . returncode != 0 : print ( "STDERR:" , result . stderr [ - 1000 :]) Successfully built texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz and texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl A wheel is just a zip file, so we can look inside it with the zipfile module: import zipfile dist_dir = BASE / "dist" print ( "Contents of dist/:" ) for f in sorted ( dist_dir . iterdir ()): size_kb = f . stat () . st_size / 1024 print ( f " { f . name : 45s } { size_kb : .1f } KB" ) print () # Peek inside the wheel (it is just a zip file) whl = next ( dist_dir . glob ( "*.whl" )) print ( f "Contents of { whl . name } :" ) with zipfile . ZipFile ( whl ) as z : for name in sorted ( z . namelist ()): print ( f " { name } " ) Contents of dist/: texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl 3.4 KB texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz 3.1 KB Contents of texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl: texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/entry_points.txt texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/top_level.txt texttools/__init__.py texttools/cli.py texttools/core.py Checkpoint: dist/ should contain one .whl and one .tar.gz . Inside the wheel you should see your three .py files plus a dist-info/ folder. METADATA holds what you wrote in pyproject.toml , and entry_points.txt holds the texttools command. Quick recap python -m build creates a wheel ( .whl ) and an sdist ( .tar.gz ) in dist/ . A wheel name reads name-version-python-abi-platform.whl ; py3-none-any means pure Python. A wheel is a zip file of your package plus a dist-info/ metadata folder. 8. Publishing to TestPyPI PyPI (the Python Package Index, pypi.org ) is the official registry. pip install downloads from there. TestPyPI ( test.pypi.org ) is a separate practice server. Always try an upload there before using the real PyPI. Before You Publish Create an account at test.pypi.org . Create an API token: Account settings -> API tokens . Install twine : pip install twine . Pick a unique name . Package names on PyPI and TestPyPI are first come, first served, and texttools is almost certainly taken. Change name in pyproject.toml to something like texttools-yourname , then rebuild. Users still write import texttools , because the import name comes from the src/texttools/ folder, not from name . The Workflow Build -> Check -> Upload python -m build twine check dist/* twine upload dist/* Step 8: Check the Files Before Uploading twine check makes sure your metadata is valid and that your README will display properly on PyPI. # Install twine subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "twine" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) import glob as glob_module dist_files = glob_module . glob ( str ( BASE / "dist" / "*" )) result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "twine" , "--no-color" , "check" ] + dist_files , capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( result . stdout ) if result . stderr : print ( result . stderr ) Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl: PASSED Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz: PASSED Checkpoint: both files should say PASSED . Step 9: Upload to TestPyPI (in your terminal) This step isn't run in the notebook because it needs your own TestPyPI account and token. In a terminal, from the texttools_project/ folder: twine upload --repository testpypi dist/* When twine asks for credentials: Username: __token__ (type exactly that) Password: your API token, which starts with pypi- To avoid typing the token every time, save it in a ~/.pypirc file in your home folder: # ~/.pypirc [testpypi] username = __token__ password = pypi-your-token-here Keep this file private and never commit it to git. Step 10: Install From TestPyPI pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ texttools-yourname If your package has dependencies, add --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ so pip can find them on the real PyPI (TestPyPI doesn't host most packages). Step 11: Publish to the Real PyPI Once everything works on TestPyPI, create an account and token on pypi.org and run: twine upload dist/* pip install texttools-yourname Quick recap Practise on TestPyPI first; real PyPI uploads can't be undone. twine check dist/* validates the files; twine upload publishes them. Log in with username __token__ and an API token as the password. The distribution name ( name in pyproject.toml ) must be unique; the import name can stay the same. 9. Versioning Best Practices Semantic Versioning (SemVer) Most Python packages use semantic versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . 1 . 4 . 2 ^ ^ ^ MAJOR MINOR PATCH Part Bump it when... Example MAJOR you break backwards compatibility 1.4.2 -> 2.0.0 MINOR you add a feature that doesn't break existing code 1.4.2 -> 1.5.0 PATCH you fix a bug without changing the API 1.4.2 -> 1.4.3 When you bump one part, reset the parts to its right to zero. Versions starting with 0. (like 0.1.0 ) tell users the API isn't stable yet. Keeping the Version in One Place Right now the version lives in two places: pyproject.toml -> version = "0.1.0" src/texttools/__init__.py -> __version__ = "0.1.0" Update one, forget the other, and they drift apart. There are two clean fixes. Option A: read the version from the installed metadata. pyproject.toml becomes the only place you write the version, and your code asks for it at run time: # Option A: importlib.metadata reads version from the installed package metadata. # pyproject.toml is the ONLY place you define the version. from importlib.metadata import version , PackageNotFoundError try : pkg_version = version ( "texttools" ) except PackageNotFoundError : pkg_version = "unknown" print ( f "Version from metadata: { pkg_version } " ) Version from metadata: 0.1.0 Option B: keep __version__ in __init__.py and let pyproject.toml read it. Remove the version = ... line from [project] and add: [project] dynamic = [ "version" ] [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = "texttools.__version__" } Now __init__.py is the one place to change the version. (You must delete the fixed version line; setuptools refuses a version that's both fixed and dynamic .) Releasing a New Version 1. Update the version (pyproject.toml, or __init__.py with Option B) 2. git commit -m "Bump version to 0.2.0" 3. git tag v0.2.0 4. Delete the old dist/ folder, then: python -m build 5. twine upload dist/* PyPI never lets you upload the same version twice, even if you delete it. If you made a mistake, release a new patch version. Quick recap SemVer: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for bug fixes. Keep the version in one place: read it with importlib.metadata.version() or use dynamic = ["version"] . Every upload needs a new version number; PyPI won't accept the same one twice. 10. Full Package Checklist Use this list before every release: Structure [ ] src/<package>/ layout with __init__.py [ ] __version__ defined (or using importlib.metadata) [ ] tests/ folder with no __init__.py [ ] README.md with installation and usage examples pyproject.toml [ ] name is unique (search PyPI first) [ ] version follows SemVer [ ] description is one informative sentence [ ] requires-python set correctly [ ] dependencies listed (even if empty) [ ] license set as an SPDX string, e.g. "MIT" [ ] classifiers added [ ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] Quality [ ] All public functions have docstrings [ ] Tests cover the normal cases and the edge cases [ ] twine check passes with no warnings Publishing [ ] Tested on TestPyPI first [ ] Git tag created for this version [ ] No secrets or passwords in the code 11. Practice A few quick tasks to check your understanding before the bigger challenge. Answer each one before opening the solution. Task 1: Which number do you bump? texttools is at version 1.4.2 . What is the next version for each change? You fix a bug where word_count("") crashed. You add a new function char_count() . You rename reverse_words() to reverse() and delete the old name. Show solution 1.4.3 : a bug fix is a PATCH. 1.5.0 : a new feature that doesn't break anything is a MINOR bump (PATCH resets to 0). 2.0.0 : removing a name breaks existing code, so it's a MAJOR bump. Task 2: Add a second command Add a terminal command called tt-count that runs a function count_main() in texttools/cli.py . What do you add to pyproject.toml , and what must you do afterwards? Show solution [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" tt-count = "texttools.cli:count_main" Then write count_main() in cli.py and reinstall ( pip install -e . ), because commands are only created at install time. Task 3: Read a wheel filename What does requests-2.32.3-py3-none-any.whl tell you? And what would you guess numpy-2.1.0-cp312-cp312-macosx_14_0_arm64.whl means? Show solution requests version 2.32.3 , for any Python 3 ( py3 ), with no compiled code ( none ), on any operating system ( any ). numpy version 2.1.0 , compiled for CPython 3.12 ( cp312 ), using the CPython 3.12 ABI, and only for macOS 14 on Apple Silicon ( arm64 ). numpy contains C code, so it needs a separate wheel per platform. Challenge: Build Your Own Package Build a distributable package called numtools (or pick your own name) from scratch. Requirements Use the src/ layout. Write a proper pyproject.toml with all the fields we used. Expose at least 3 functions in the public API through __init__.py . Add a CLI entry point with at least 2 sub-commands. Include tests that cover each function. Pass twine check after building. Ideas for Functions Theme Possible functions Numbers is_prime(n) , fibonacci(n) , factorial(n) Dates days_until(date) , is_weekend(date) , format_date(date, style) Files count_lines(path) , find_duplicates(dir) , largest_files(dir, n) Colours hex_to_rgb(hex) , rgb_to_hex(r, g, b) , contrast_ratio(c1, c2) Starter Structure numtools/ +-- src/ | +-- numtools/ | +-- __init__.py | +-- core.py | +-- cli.py +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py +-- pyproject.toml +-- README.md Work in the cell below. You can copy the patterns from the texttools cells above, or create the files in your editor and run the commands in a terminal. # Your workspace - build numtools here challenge_base = pathlib . Path ( "numtools" ) # TODO: Create the src/numtools/ and tests/ directories # TODO: Write core.py with at least 3 functions # TODO: Write __init__.py exposing the public API # TODO: Write cli.py with a main() entry point # TODO: Write pyproject.toml # TODO: Write test_core.py # TODO: pip install -e numtools/ # TODO: pytest numtools/tests/ # TODO: python -m build numtools/ # TODO: twine check numtools/dist/* print ( "Good luck!" ) Good luck! Stuck? Open a hint before you look at the full solution. Hint 1: pyproject.toml skeleton [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=77" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "numtools" version = "0.1.0" description = "YOUR DESCRIPTION HERE" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] numtools = "numtools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] Hint 2: is_prime() implementation def is_prime ( n : int ) -> bool : if n < 2 : return False for i in range ( 2 , int ( n ** 0.5 ) + 1 ): if n % i == 0 : return False return True Show solution import pathlib , subprocess , sys root = pathlib . Path ( "numtools" ) pkg = root / "src" / "numtools" pkg . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) ( root / "tests" ) . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) ( pkg / "core.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""Small number utilities.""" def is_prime(n: int) -> bool: """Return True if n is a prime number.""" if n < 2: return False for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1): if n % i == 0: return False return True def fibonacci(n: int) -> list: """Return the first n Fibonacci numbers.""" seq = [] a, b = 0, 1 for _ in range(n): seq.append(a) a, b = b, a + b return seq def factorial(n: int) -> int: """Return n! for n >= 0.""" if n < 0: raise ValueError("n must be >= 0") result = 1 for i in range(2, n + 1): result *= i return result ''' ) ( pkg / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""numtools - small number utilities.""" __version__ = "0.1.0" from numtools.core import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial __all__ = ["is_prime", "fibonacci", "factorial"] ''' ) ( pkg / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""Command-line interface for numtools.""" import argparse from numtools.core import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="numtools") sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True) for name in ("prime", "fib", "fact"): sub.add_parser(name).add_argument("n", type=int) args = parser.parse_args() if args.command == "prime": print(is_prime(args.n)) elif args.command == "fib": print(fibonacci(args.n)) elif args.command == "fact": print(factorial(args.n)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ''' ) ( root / "tests" / "test_core.py" ) . write_text ( '''import pytest from numtools import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial def test_is_prime(): assert is_prime(7) assert not is_prime(1) assert not is_prime(9) def test_fibonacci(): assert fibonacci(6) == [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5] assert fibonacci(0) == [] def test_factorial(): assert factorial(0) == 1 assert factorial(5) == 120 with pytest.raises(ValueError): factorial(-1) ''' ) ( root / "README.md" ) . write_text ( "# numtools \n\n Small number utilities: is_prime, fibonacci, factorial. \n " ) ( root / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( '''[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=77"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "numtools" version = "0.1.0" description = "Small number utilities" authors = [{name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com"}] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] numtools = "numtools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] ''' ) def run ( * args ): out = subprocess . run ([ sys . executable , "-m" , * args ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( " " . join ( args [: 2 ]), "->" , "OK" if out . returncode == 0 else out . stdout + out . stderr ) run ( "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( root ), "--quiet" ) run ( "pytest" , str ( root / "tests" ), "-q" ) run ( "build" , str ( root )) run ( "twine" , "check" , * map ( str , ( root / "dist" ) . glob ( "*" ))) In a terminal, the last four lines are simply: pip install -e numtools/ pytest numtools/tests/ python -m build numtools/ twine check numtools/dist/* Summary & Cheat Sheet Concept Remember this src/ layout Keeps local source from shadowing the installed package during tests __init__.py Marks the package, defines the public API, holds __version__ pyproject.toml One file for metadata, dependencies and build settings Editable install pip install -e . : changes show up without reinstalling Entry points [project.scripts] maps a terminal command to a Python function python -m build Creates .whl and .tar.gz in dist/ twine twine check validates, twine upload publishes to PyPI/TestPyPI SemVer MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH : think about which number your change deserves Commands You'll Use Most pip install -e . # editable install while developing python -m pytest tests/ # run the tests python -m build # create dist/*.whl and dist/*.tar.gz twine check dist/* # validate before uploading twine upload --repository testpypi dist/* # practice upload twine upload dist/* # real upload to PyPI Further Reading Python Packaging User Guide Writing your pyproject.toml TestPyPI setuptools documentation What's Next The next notebook, FastAPI , moves from libraries to web services. The same ideas carry over: a pyproject.toml or requirements.txt to pin dependencies, a clear project layout, and tests that run against what you actually ship.
docs.title: Creating Distributable Packages

docs.text: So far you've shared code by copying .py files around. In this notebook we turn a small text-utility module into a real package that anyone can install with pip install , run from the terminal, and upgrade cleanly.
docs.title: Creating Distributable Python Packages

docs.text: By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Explain the difference between a script, a module and a distributable package Lay out a package using the modern src/ layout Write a complete pyproject.toml with metadata, dependencies and build settings Install your package locally in editable mode with pip install -e . Create CLI entry points so users can run your package from the terminal Build a wheel ( .whl ) and a source distribution ( .tar.gz ) Publish a package to TestPyPI Pick the right version number using semantic versioning
docs.title: Learning Objectives

docs.text: Python 3.9 or newer Comfortable with functions, modules and import Basic terminal use (running commands, changing directories) pip available (the notebook installs build , pytest and twine for you when needed)
docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.text: Run the cells from top to bottom . We build one package, texttools , step by step, and later cells depend on files written by earlier ones. The package is created in a folder called texttools_project/ next to this notebook. You can open it in your editor at any point to see the real files. Try the practice tasks and the challenge yourself first, then open Show solution to compare. Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read only the recaps when revising.
docs.title: How to Use This Notebook

docs.text: Say you've written a handy Python utility and a teammate wants to use it. The first thing most people do is email them the file. Here's what tends to go wrong: Problem What happens They save the file in the wrong folder ImportError : Python can't find it Your code needs requests Nobody told them to install it You fix a bug They're still running the old copy They want to run it as a command They have to work out how to call the script You release v2 Nobody knows which version they have A distributable package fixes all of these. It's a bundle that: installs with one command: pip install texttools declares its own dependencies, so pip installs them too carries a version number can add commands to the terminal can be upgraded cleanly with pip install --upgrade
docs.title: 1. Why Not Just Share a .py File?

docs.text: You write code | v [ pyproject.toml ] <- describes your package (name, version, dependencies...) | v [ python -m build ] <- bundles your code into distributable files | v [ .whl + .tar.gz files ] <- the "wheel" is what pip actually installs | v [ twine upload ] <- publishes the files to PyPI | v [ pip install texttools ] <- your users install it We'll go through every step of this pipeline in this notebook. Quick recap Copying .py files breaks as soon as there are dependencies, bug fixes or new versions. A package has a name, a version, its dependencies and (optionally) terminal commands. The pipeline is: pyproject.toml -> python -m build -> twine upload -> pip install .
docs.title: The Packaging Pipeline at a Glance
2. Anatomy of a Modern Python Package

docs.text: There are two common ways to lay out a package. We'll use the src/ layout , which is what the Python Packaging Guide recommends: texttools_project/ <- project root (usually your git repo) | +-- src/ | +-- texttools/ <- the actual Python package | +-- __init__.py <- marks it as a package, defines the public API | +-- core.py <- the utility functions | +-- cli.py <- the command-line interface | +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py <- unit tests | +-- pyproject.toml <- package metadata and build settings +-- README.md Why put the package inside src/ ? If the package folder sits right next to your tests, Python can import the local folder instead of the installed package . Your tests then pass on your machine even when the installed version is broken. With src/ , the only way to import texttools is to install it, so your tests check what users actually get. Layout What can go wrong Flat (no src/ ) The local folder shadows the installed package during tests src/ layout Tests always run against the installed package
docs.title: The src/ Layout

docs.text: __init__.py has two jobs: It tells Python that this folder is a package , not just a folder. It defines the public API : what users get when they write import texttools . Here's the __init__.py we're going to write. Don't run anything yet; we create the real file in Step 1 below. # src/texttools/__init__.py __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count , reverse_words , title_case_smart __all__ = [ "word_count" , "reverse_words" , "title_case_smart" ] __version__ is the usual way to expose your package's version in code. __all__ controls what from texttools import * brings in. Listing names here makes your public API explicit.
docs.title: What __init__.py Does

docs.text: Now let's build texttools for real. Run the cells below in order. Each one writes a file into texttools_project/ . import os import pathlib # Everything goes inside texttools_project/, next to this notebook. BASE = pathlib . Path ( "texttools_project" ) dirs = [ BASE / "src" / "texttools" , BASE / "tests" , ] for d in dirs : d . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) print ( "Directories created:" ) for d in dirs : print ( f " { d } " ) Directories created: texttools_project/src/texttools texttools_project/tests
docs.title: Step 1: Create the Folder Structure

docs.text: core.py holds the three functions our package offers. We store the file's contents in a string and write it to disk, so you can read the whole file right here in the notebook. # src/texttools/core.py - the actual utility functions core_code = '''"""Core text utility functions for texttools.""" def word_count(text: str) -> dict: """Count the frequency of each word in a string. Args: text: The input string to analyse. Returns: A dictionary mapping each word (lowercased) to its count. Example: >>> word_count("the cat sat on the mat") {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} """ words = text.lower().split() counts: dict = {} for word in words: # Strip basic punctuation word = word.strip(".,!?;:'") if word: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 return counts def reverse_words(text: str) -> str: """Reverse the order of words in a string. Args: text: The input string. Returns: A new string with word order reversed. Example: >>> reverse_words("Hello World") 'World Hello' """ return " ".join(reversed(text.split())) def title_case_smart(text: str) -> str: """Convert a string to title case, skipping common short words. Short connector words (a, an, the, and, but, or, for, nor, on, at, to, by, in, of, up) remain lowercase unless they are the first or last word. Args: text: The input string. Returns: A title-cased string respecting common style guidelines. Example: >>> title_case_smart("the lord of the rings") 'The Lord of the Rings' """ SKIP = {"a", "an", "the", "and", "but", "or", "for", "nor", "on", "at", "to", "by", "in", "of", "up"} words = text.lower().split() result = [] for i, word in enumerate(words): if i == 0 or i == len(words) - 1 or word not in SKIP: result.append(word.capitalize()) else: result.append(word) return " ".join(result) ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "core.py" ) . write_text ( core_code ) print ( "core.py written." ) core.py written. # src/texttools/__init__.py - the public API init_code = '''"""texttools - a small text utility library.""" __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart __all__ = ["word_count", "reverse_words", "title_case_smart"] ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( init_code ) print ( "__init__.py written." ) __init__.py written. What just happened? We now have src/texttools/core.py and src/texttools/__init__.py on disk. You can't import texttools yet, because Python doesn't know about the src/ folder. Installing the package (Section 4) is what fixes that. Quick recap Use the src/ layout: src/<package>/ for code, tests/ beside it, pyproject.toml at the root. src/ stops your tests from accidentally importing the local folder instead of the installed package. __init__.py marks a package and defines its public API ( __version__ , __all__ ).
docs.title: Step 2: Write the Package Code

docs.text: pyproject.toml is the one file that describes your package. It replaced the older setup.py and setup.cfg files, which you'll still see in older projects. It has a few tables (sections). Let's go through them one at a time.
docs.title: 3. pyproject.toml Deep Dive

docs.text: This tells pip which build tool to use. We use setuptools : [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=77" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" We ask for setuptools 77 or newer because that's the version that understands the modern license = "MIT" field below.
docs.title: [build-system]: how to build the package

docs.text: [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3" , "Operating System :: OS Independent" , ] A few notes: dependencies lists other packages yours needs, e.g. ["requests>=2.31"] . Ours needs none. license is a short SPDX code like "MIT" or "Apache-2.0" . Older tutorials write license = {text = "MIT"} and add a License :: ... classifier; current setuptools warns about both, so don't copy that style. classifiers are tags that help people find your package on PyPI.
docs.title: [project]: what the package is

docs.text: This creates CLI commands (more on this in Section 5): [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # ^command ^module ^function
docs.title: [project.scripts]: terminal commands

docs.text: This tells setuptools to look inside src/ for packages. You need it for the src/ layout: [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ]
docs.title: [tool.setuptools.packages.find]: where the code lives

docs.text: Now we put all of those tables together into one file. # Write the pyproject.toml for texttools pyproject = """[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=77"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting" authors = [{name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com"}] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3", "Operating System :: OS Independent", ] [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] """ ( BASE / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( pyproject ) print ( "pyproject.toml written." ) pyproject.toml written. pyproject.toml says readme = "README.md" , so that file has to exist too. PyPI shows it as your package's front page. # Write a minimal README.md (referenced by pyproject.toml) readme = '''# texttools A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting. ## Installation ~~~bash pip install texttools ~~~ ## Usage ~~~python from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart print(word_count("the cat sat on the mat")) # {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} print(reverse_words("Hello World")) # 'World Hello' print(title_case_smart("the lord of the rings")) # 'The Lord of the Rings' ~~~ ## CLI ~~~bash texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" texttools reverse "Hello World" texttools titlecase "the lord of the rings" ~~~ ''' ( BASE / "README.md" ) . write_text ( readme ) print ( "README.md written." ) README.md written. Quick recap [build-system] says how to build (setuptools); [project] says what the package is. Use license = "MIT" (an SPDX string), not the old {text = ...} table or license classifiers. [project.scripts] maps a terminal command to a Python function. With the src/ layout you need [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] .
docs.title: Step 3: Write pyproject.toml and README.md

docs.text: Before publishing anything, you want to use and test the package on your own machine. The -e flag means editable install .
docs.title: 4. Installing Locally with pip install -e .

docs.text: Mode Command How it works Regular pip install . Copies your files into site-packages . Every change needs a reinstall. Editable pip install -e . Points Python at your source folder. Changes show up straight away. During development you'll almost always use editable mode.
docs.title: Editable Install vs Regular Install

docs.text: pip install -e texttools_project/ | v reads pyproject.toml | v writes a small .pth file into site-packages that points to src/ | v Python can now find 'import texttools'
docs.title: What Happens Under the Hood

docs.text: In a terminal you'd run pip install -e texttools_project/ . Here we run the same command from Python so it installs into this notebook's environment. import subprocess , sys result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) if result . returncode == 0 : print ( "Package installed successfully." ) else : print ( "Error:" ) print ( result . stderr ) # Make the package importable in the current kernel session # (pip editable installs use .pth files, loaded at startup, not dynamically) src_path = str ( BASE / "src" ) if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) print ( f "Added { src_path } to sys.path" ) Package installed successfully. Added texttools_project/src to sys.path What just happened? pip installed texttools in editable mode. The .pth file it wrote is only read when Python starts, so this already-running notebook wouldn't see it. That's why the cell also adds src/ to sys.path by hand. In a fresh terminal or a restarted kernel you wouldn't need that line. Let's check that the import works. # Verify the install # Force a fresh import in case texttools was already loaded for key in list ( sys . modules . keys ()): if key . startswith ( "texttools" ): del sys . modules [ key ] import texttools print ( f "texttools version: { texttools . __version__ } " ) print () sample = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" print ( "word_count():" ) print ( texttools . word_count ( sample )) print () print ( "reverse_words():" ) print ( texttools . reverse_words ( sample )) print () print ( "title_case_smart():" ) print ( texttools . title_case_smart ( "the lord of the rings: the return of the king" )) texttools version: 0.1.0 word_count(): {'the': 2, 'quick': 1, 'brown': 1, 'fox': 1, 'jumps': 1, 'over': 1, 'lazy': 1, 'dog': 1} reverse_words(): dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the title_case_smart(): The Lord of the Rings: the Return of the King Checkpoint: you should see texttools version: 0.1.0 followed by the results of the three functions. If you get ModuleNotFoundError , re-run the install cell above. Notice the title-case result: the stays lowercase after Rings: because our function only looks at word position, not punctuation. Good enough for a teaching example. Quick recap pip install -e . installs your package in editable mode: edit the code, re-run, no reinstall. A regular pip install . copies the files, so you'd need to reinstall after every change. Editable installs work through a .pth file that Python reads at start-up.
docs.title: Step 4: Install the Package

docs.text: Entry points let users run your package as a normal terminal command: $ texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2
docs.title: 5. Entry Points: Creating CLI Commands

docs.text: When pip installs your package, it reads [project.scripts] from pyproject.toml : [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # ^command ^module ^function pip then creates a tiny launcher program called texttools in your environment's bin/ folder ( Scripts\ on Windows). Running it simply calls texttools.cli.main() .
docs.title: How It Works

docs.text: cli.py uses argparse from the standard library to read the command-line arguments. It has three sub-commands: count , reverse and titlecase . # src/texttools/cli.py - command-line interface cli_code = '''"""Command-line interface for texttools.""" import argparse import sys from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart def main() -> None: """Entry point for the texttools CLI.""" parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( prog="texttools", description="Text utility commands", ) subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True) # count command count_parser = subparsers.add_parser("count", help="Count word frequencies") count_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to analyse") # reverse command reverse_parser = subparsers.add_parser("reverse", help="Reverse word order") reverse_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to reverse") # titlecase command title_parser = subparsers.add_parser("titlecase", help="Smart title case") title_parser.add_argument("text", help="Text to convert") args = parser.parse_args() if args.command == "count": counts = word_count(args.text) for word, n in sorted(counts.items()): print(f" {word} : {n} ") elif args.command == "reverse": print(reverse_words(args.text)) elif args.command == "titlecase": print(title_case_smart(args.text)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ''' ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( cli_code ) print ( "cli.py written." ) # Reinstall so pip registers the new entry point result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "Package reinstalled." if result . returncode == 0 else result . stderr ) # Make sure src/ is still on the path if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) cli.py written. Package reinstalled. We reinstalled because entry points are created at install time. Adding cli.py alone doesn't create the texttools command. Now let's try the CLI. In a terminal you would type texttools count "..." . Here we call the same code with python -m texttools.cli , which works no matter where the launcher was installed. # Test the CLI programmatically result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "count" , "the cat sat on the mat" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat':" ) print ( result . stdout ) result2 = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "titlecase" , "the lord of the rings" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings':" ) print ( result2 . stdout ) texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat': cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings': The Lord of the Rings Checkpoint: the word counts should be sorted alphabetically, and the title should read The Lord of the Rings . Why if __name__ == "__main__": ? That guard at the bottom of cli.py is what makes python -m texttools.cli work. The installed texttools command doesn't need it, because it calls main() directly. The guard is just handy while you're developing. Quick recap [project.scripts] turns command = "module:function" into a real terminal command. The command is created when the package is installed, so reinstall after adding an entry point. argparse sub-parsers give you git -style sub-commands like texttools count .
docs.title: Step 5: Write the CLI Module

docs.text: Tests should run against the installed package, not loose source files. The src/ layout guarantees that: the tests can only import texttools because it's installed.
docs.title: 6. Testing the Installed Package

docs.text: tests/ +-- test_core.py Note there's no __init__.py in tests/ . pytest doesn't need one, and leaving it out avoids confusing import problems.
docs.title: Test Structure

docs.text: # Write the test file test_code = '''"""Tests for texttools.core""" import pytest from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart class TestWordCount: def test_basic_count(self): result = word_count("the cat sat on the mat") assert result["the"] == 2 assert result["cat"] == 1 def test_case_insensitive(self): result = word_count("Python python PYTHON") assert result["python"] == 3 def test_strips_punctuation(self): result = word_count("hello, world!") assert "hello" in result assert "world" in result def test_empty_string(self): assert word_count("") == {} class TestReverseWords: def test_basic_reverse(self): assert reverse_words("Hello World") == "World Hello" def test_single_word(self): assert reverse_words("Python") == "Python" def test_multiple_words(self): assert reverse_words("one two three") == "three two one" class TestTitleCaseSmart: def test_short_words_lowercase(self): result = title_case_smart("the lord of the rings") assert result == "The Lord of the Rings" def test_first_word_always_capitalised(self): result = title_case_smart("of mice and men") assert result.startswith("Of") def test_last_word_always_capitalised(self): result = title_case_smart("the cat in the hat") assert result.endswith("Hat") def test_single_word(self): assert title_case_smart("python") == "Python" ''' ( BASE / "tests" / "test_core.py" ) . write_text ( test_code ) print ( "test_core.py written." ) test_core.py written. # Install pytest if needed subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "pytest" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) # Run the tests result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pytest" , str ( BASE / "tests" ), "-v" , "--color=no" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( result . stdout ) if result . stderr : print ( result . stderr ) ============================= test session starts ============================== platform darwin -- Python 3.12.14, pytest-9.2.0, pluggy-1.7.0 -- .venv/bin/python cachedir: .pytest_cache rootdir: texttools_project configfile: pyproject.toml plugins: platformdirs-4.14.0, anyio-4.15.1 collecting ... collected 11 items texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_basic_count PASSED [ 9%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_case_insensitive PASSED [ 18%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_strips_punctuation PASSED [ 27%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestWordCount::test_empty_string PASSED [ 36%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_basic_reverse PASSED [ 45%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_single_word PASSED [ 54%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestReverseWords::test_multiple_words PASSED [ 63%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_short_words_lowercase PASSED [ 72%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_first_word_always_capitalised PASSED [ 81%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_last_word_always_capitalised PASSED [ 90%] texttools_project/tests/test_core.py::TestTitleCaseSmart::test_single_word PASSED [100%] ============================== 11 passed in 0.01s ============================== Checkpoint: you should see 11 passed . If a test fails, read the assertion message, fix core.py , and run the test cell again. Thanks to the editable install there's no need to reinstall. Quick recap Put tests in tests/ next to src/ , with no __init__.py . Run them with python -m pytest tests/ . Because of the src/ layout, a passing test means the installed package works.
docs.title: Step 6: Write and Run the Tests

docs.text: When you're ready to share the package, you build it into files that pip can install: Format Extension Description Wheel .whl Ready-to-install archive. Fast to install and the most common format. Source distribution (sdist) .tar.gz Archive of your source code. pip builds it on the user's machine. Always publish both . pip prefers the wheel and falls back to the sdist.
docs.title: 7. Building a Distribution

docs.text: python -m build reads pyproject.toml and creates both files in a dist/ folder: dist/ +-- texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl +-- texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz
docs.title: The build Tool

docs.text: texttools - 0.1.0 - py3 - none - any .whl ^ ^ ^ ^ ^ package version python abi platform py3 = works with Python 3 none = no compiled code, so no ABI requirement (pure Python) any = works on any operating system
docs.title: Reading a Wheel's Filename

docs.text: This is the same as running python -m build texttools_project/ in a terminal. It can take a little while the first time because it sets up a clean build environment. # Install the build tool if not already present subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "build" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) # Build the package result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "build" , str ( BASE )], capture_output = True , text = True , env = { ** os . environ , "NO_COLOR" : "1" }, # plain text output, no colour codes ) # The full log is long; the last line tells us whether it worked print ( result . stdout . strip () . splitlines ()[ - 1 ] if result . stdout . strip () else "(no output)" ) if result . returncode != 0 : print ( "STDERR:" , result . stderr [ - 1000 :]) Successfully built texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz and texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl A wheel is just a zip file, so we can look inside it with the zipfile module: import zipfile dist_dir = BASE / "dist" print ( "Contents of dist/:" ) for f in sorted ( dist_dir . iterdir ()): size_kb = f . stat () . st_size / 1024 print ( f " { f . name : 45s } { size_kb : .1f } KB" ) print () # Peek inside the wheel (it is just a zip file) whl = next ( dist_dir . glob ( "*.whl" )) print ( f "Contents of { whl . name } :" ) with zipfile . ZipFile ( whl ) as z : for name in sorted ( z . namelist ()): print ( f " { name } " ) Contents of dist/: texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl 3.4 KB texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz 3.1 KB Contents of texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl: texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/METADATA texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/RECORD texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/WHEEL texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/entry_points.txt texttools-0.1.0.dist-info/top_level.txt texttools/__init__.py texttools/cli.py texttools/core.py Checkpoint: dist/ should contain one .whl and one .tar.gz . Inside the wheel you should see your three .py files plus a dist-info/ folder. METADATA holds what you wrote in pyproject.toml , and entry_points.txt holds the texttools command. Quick recap python -m build creates a wheel ( .whl ) and an sdist ( .tar.gz ) in dist/ . A wheel name reads name-version-python-abi-platform.whl ; py3-none-any means pure Python. A wheel is a zip file of your package plus a dist-info/ metadata folder.
docs.title: Step 7: Build the Package

docs.text: PyPI (the Python Package Index, pypi.org ) is the official registry. pip install downloads from there. TestPyPI ( test.pypi.org ) is a separate practice server. Always try an upload there before using the real PyPI.
docs.title: 8. Publishing to TestPyPI

docs.text: Create an account at test.pypi.org . Create an API token: Account settings -> API tokens . Install twine : pip install twine . Pick a unique name . Package names on PyPI and TestPyPI are first come, first served, and texttools is almost certainly taken. Change name in pyproject.toml to something like texttools-yourname , then rebuild. Users still write import texttools , because the import name comes from the src/texttools/ folder, not from name .
docs.title: Before You Publish

docs.text: Build -> Check -> Upload python -m build twine check dist/* twine upload dist/*
docs.title: The Workflow

docs.text: twine check makes sure your metadata is valid and that your README will display properly on PyPI. # Install twine subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "twine" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) import glob as glob_module dist_files = glob_module . glob ( str ( BASE / "dist" / "*" )) result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "twine" , "--no-color" , "check" ] + dist_files , capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( result . stdout ) if result . stderr : print ( result . stderr ) Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl: PASSED Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz: PASSED Checkpoint: both files should say PASSED .
docs.title: Step 8: Check the Files Before Uploading

docs.text: This step isn't run in the notebook because it needs your own TestPyPI account and token. In a terminal, from the texttools_project/ folder: twine upload --repository testpypi dist/* When twine asks for credentials: Username: __token__ (type exactly that) Password: your API token, which starts with pypi- To avoid typing the token every time, save it in a ~/.pypirc file in your home folder: # ~/.pypirc [testpypi] username = __token__ password = pypi-your-token-here Keep this file private and never commit it to git.
docs.title: Step 9: Upload to TestPyPI (in your terminal)

docs.text: pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ texttools-yourname If your package has dependencies, add --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple/ so pip can find them on the real PyPI (TestPyPI doesn't host most packages).
docs.title: Step 10: Install From TestPyPI

docs.text: Once everything works on TestPyPI, create an account and token on pypi.org and run: twine upload dist/* pip install texttools-yourname Quick recap Practise on TestPyPI first; real PyPI uploads can't be undone. twine check dist/* validates the files; twine upload publishes them. Log in with username __token__ and an API token as the password. The distribution name ( name in pyproject.toml ) must be unique; the import name can stay the same.
docs.title: Step 11: Publish to the Real PyPI

docs.text: Most Python packages use semantic versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . 1 . 4 . 2 ^ ^ ^ MAJOR MINOR PATCH Part Bump it when... Example MAJOR you break backwards compatibility 1.4.2 -> 2.0.0 MINOR you add a feature that doesn't break existing code 1.4.2 -> 1.5.0 PATCH you fix a bug without changing the API 1.4.2 -> 1.4.3 When you bump one part, reset the parts to its right to zero. Versions starting with 0. (like 0.1.0 ) tell users the API isn't stable yet.
docs.title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer)

docs.text: Right now the version lives in two places: pyproject.toml -> version = "0.1.0" src/texttools/__init__.py -> __version__ = "0.1.0" Update one, forget the other, and they drift apart. There are two clean fixes. Option A: read the version from the installed metadata. pyproject.toml becomes the only place you write the version, and your code asks for it at run time: # Option A: importlib.metadata reads version from the installed package metadata. # pyproject.toml is the ONLY place you define the version. from importlib.metadata import version , PackageNotFoundError try : pkg_version = version ( "texttools" ) except PackageNotFoundError : pkg_version = "unknown" print ( f "Version from metadata: { pkg_version } " ) Version from metadata: 0.1.0 Option B: keep __version__ in __init__.py and let pyproject.toml read it. Remove the version = ... line from [project] and add: [project] dynamic = [ "version" ] [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = "texttools.__version__" } Now __init__.py is the one place to change the version. (You must delete the fixed version line; setuptools refuses a version that's both fixed and dynamic .)
docs.title: Keeping the Version in One Place

docs.text: 1. Update the version (pyproject.toml, or __init__.py with Option B) 2. git commit -m "Bump version to 0.2.0" 3. git tag v0.2.0 4. Delete the old dist/ folder, then: python -m build 5. twine upload dist/* PyPI never lets you upload the same version twice, even if you delete it. If you made a mistake, release a new patch version. Quick recap SemVer: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new features, PATCH for bug fixes. Keep the version in one place: read it with importlib.metadata.version() or use dynamic = ["version"] . Every upload needs a new version number; PyPI won't accept the same one twice.
docs.title: Releasing a New Version

docs.text: Use this list before every release: Structure [ ] src/<package>/ layout with __init__.py [ ] __version__ defined (or using importlib.metadata) [ ] tests/ folder with no __init__.py [ ] README.md with installation and usage examples pyproject.toml [ ] name is unique (search PyPI first) [ ] version follows SemVer [ ] description is one informative sentence [ ] requires-python set correctly [ ] dependencies listed (even if empty) [ ] license set as an SPDX string, e.g. "MIT" [ ] classifiers added [ ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] Quality [ ] All public functions have docstrings [ ] Tests cover the normal cases and the edge cases [ ] twine check passes with no warnings Publishing [ ] Tested on TestPyPI first [ ] Git tag created for this version [ ] No secrets or passwords in the code
docs.title: 10. Full Package Checklist

docs.text: A few quick tasks to check your understanding before the bigger challenge. Answer each one before opening the solution.
docs.title: 11. Practice

docs.text: texttools is at version 1.4.2 . What is the next version for each change? You fix a bug where word_count("") crashed. You add a new function char_count() . You rename reverse_words() to reverse() and delete the old name. Show solution 1.4.3 : a bug fix is a PATCH. 1.5.0 : a new feature that doesn't break anything is a MINOR bump (PATCH resets to 0). 2.0.0 : removing a name breaks existing code, so it's a MAJOR bump.
docs.title: Task 1: Which number do you bump?

docs.text: Add a terminal command called tt-count that runs a function count_main() in texttools/cli.py . What do you add to pyproject.toml , and what must you do afterwards? Show solution [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" tt-count = "texttools.cli:count_main" Then write count_main() in cli.py and reinstall ( pip install -e . ), because commands are only created at install time.
docs.title: Task 2: Add a second command

docs.text: What does requests-2.32.3-py3-none-any.whl tell you? And what would you guess numpy-2.1.0-cp312-cp312-macosx_14_0_arm64.whl means? Show solution requests version 2.32.3 , for any Python 3 ( py3 ), with no compiled code ( none ), on any operating system ( any ). numpy version 2.1.0 , compiled for CPython 3.12 ( cp312 ), using the CPython 3.12 ABI, and only for macOS 14 on Apple Silicon ( arm64 ). numpy contains C code, so it needs a separate wheel per platform.

Stuck? Open a hint before you look at the full solution. Hint 1: pyproject.toml skeleton [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=77" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "numtools" version = "0.1.0" description = "YOUR DESCRIPTION HERE" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] numtools = "numtools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] Hint 2: is_prime() implementation def is_prime ( n : int ) -> bool : if n < 2 : return False for i in range ( 2 , int ( n ** 0.5 ) + 1 ): if n % i == 0 : return False return True Show solution import pathlib , subprocess , sys root = pathlib . Path ( "numtools" ) pkg = root / "src" / "numtools" pkg . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) ( root / "tests" ) . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) ( pkg / "core.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""Small number utilities.""" def is_prime(n: int) -> bool: """Return True if n is a prime number.""" if n < 2: return False for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1): if n % i == 0: return False return True def fibonacci(n: int) -> list: """Return the first n Fibonacci numbers.""" seq = [] a, b = 0, 1 for _ in range(n): seq.append(a) a, b = b, a + b return seq def factorial(n: int) -> int: """Return n! for n >= 0.""" if n < 0: raise ValueError("n must be >= 0") result = 1 for i in range(2, n + 1): result *= i return result ''' ) ( pkg / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""numtools - small number utilities.""" __version__ = "0.1.0" from numtools.core import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial __all__ = ["is_prime", "fibonacci", "factorial"] ''' ) ( pkg / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( '''"""Command-line interface for numtools.""" import argparse from numtools.core import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial def main() -> None: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="numtools") sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True) for name in ("prime", "fib", "fact"): sub.add_parser(name).add_argument("n", type=int) args = parser.parse_args() if args.command == "prime": print(is_prime(args.n)) elif args.command == "fib": print(fibonacci(args.n)) elif args.command == "fact": print(factorial(args.n)) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ''' ) ( root / "tests" / "test_core.py" ) . write_text ( '''import pytest from numtools import is_prime, fibonacci, factorial def test_is_prime(): assert is_prime(7) assert not is_prime(1) assert not is_prime(9) def test_fibonacci(): assert fibonacci(6) == [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5] assert fibonacci(0) == [] def test_factorial(): assert factorial(0) == 1 assert factorial(5) == 120 with pytest.raises(ValueError): factorial(-1) ''' ) ( root / "README.md" ) . write_text ( "# numtools 

 Small number utilities: is_prime, fibonacci, factorial. 
 " ) ( root / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( '''[build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=77"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "numtools" version = "0.1.0" description = "Small number utilities" authors = [{name = "Your Name", email = "you@example.com"}] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.9" license = "MIT" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] numtools = "numtools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] ''' ) def run ( * args ): out = subprocess . run ([ sys . executable , "-m" , * args ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( " " . join ( args [: 2 ]), "->" , "OK" if out . returncode == 0 else out . stdout + out . stderr ) run ( "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( root ), "--quiet" ) run ( "pytest" , str ( root / "tests" ), "-q" ) run ( "build" , str ( root )) run ( "twine" , "check" , * map ( str , ( root / "dist" ) . glob ( "*" ))) In a terminal, the last four lines are simply: pip install -e numtools/ pytest numtools/tests/ python -m build numtools/ twine check numtools/dist/*
