docs.text: Django In this notebook we build a blog platform with Django and Django REST Framework (DRF). We start with one plain JSON view and end with a token-protected REST API, nested comment URLs and a customised admin site. Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Create a Django project and app from scratch Define models and run database migrations Query the database with the Django ORM Write function-based and class-based views and connect them to URLs Build a REST API with DRF serializers, ViewSets and routers Protect endpoints with token authentication and permissions Manage your data with the Django admin site Prerequisites Python 3.10 or newer The OOP notebook (classes, inheritance, decorators) and some HTTP basics The FastAPI notebook is helpful but not required. We compare the two frameworks a few times. Install everything used in this notebook: pip install django djangorestframework drf-nested-routers django-filter How to Use This Notebook Work through it top to bottom . Each section adds to the same project, called blogplatform . The code cells are not meant to be run inside Jupyter . Django code has to live inside a project. Each cell tells you where it goes: # file: blog/models.py means the cell is the full content of that file. Create (or replace) the file and paste it in. # add to: blogplatform/settings.py means paste the cell into the existing file. # run in: python manage.py shell means type or paste it into the Django shell. Cells marked Illustration are short pieces to read, not to copy. Run terminal commands ( python manage.py ... ) from the outer blogplatform/ folder, the one that contains manage.py . Try each Exercise yourself before opening Show solution . Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read just the recaps when revising. What We're Building We will build the Blog Platform : a web application with a REST API for blog posts, comments and authors. Browser / curl / Postman | | HTTP v [ Django + DRF ] <-- your Python code | | ORM v [ SQLite ] <-- db.sqlite3 Final Endpoint Table Method Path Auth Description GET /api/posts/ None List all posts POST /api/posts/ Token Create a post GET /api/posts/{id}/ None Get one post with comments PUT /api/posts/{id}/ Token + Owner Update a post DELETE /api/posts/{id}/ Token + Owner Delete a post POST /api/posts/{id}/publish/ Token + Owner Publish a post POST /api/posts/{id}/unpublish/ Token + Owner Unpublish a post GET /api/posts/{id}/comments/ None List comments on a post POST /api/posts/{id}/comments/ Token Add a comment POST /api/auth/register/ None Register a user POST /api/auth/token/ None Get an auth token DELETE /api/auth/token/revoke/ Token Log out (delete token) Project Structure blogplatform/ ├── manage.py ├── blogplatform/ <- project config │ ├── settings.py │ ├── urls.py │ └── wsgi.py └── blog/ <- our app ├── models.py ├── serializers.py ├── views.py ├── urls.py ├── permissions.py └── admin.py Quick recap One Django project ( blogplatform ) holds the settings; one app ( blog ) holds our code. Anyone can read posts and comments. Writing needs a token, and only the author may change their own post. 1. Setup & First View Django vs FastAPI Django FastAPI Philosophy Batteries included: ORM, admin, auth and templates built in Small core, add what you need Data validation Forms / DRF serializers Pydantic models Auto docs Not built in (DRF gives a browsable API) Swagger UI + ReDoc Async support Async views since 3.1; ORM mostly sync Native async/await Best for Full web apps, content sites, admin-heavy projects Fast APIs, microservices Creating a Project django-admin startproject blogplatform cd blogplatform python manage.py startapp blog startproject creates the configuration package (settings, root URLs). startapp creates one app : a self-contained folder with its own models, views and URLs. A Django project is made of one or more apps. Registering the App Open blogplatform/settings.py and add DRF and our app to the INSTALLED_APPS list that's already there: # add to: blogplatform/settings.py (edit the existing INSTALLED_APPS) INSTALLED_APPS = [ 'django.contrib.admin' , 'django.contrib.auth' , 'django.contrib.contenttypes' , 'django.contrib.sessions' , 'django.contrib.messages' , 'django.contrib.staticfiles' , 'rest_framework' , # <- Django REST Framework 'rest_framework.authtoken' , # <- Token authentication 'blog' , # <- our app ] Running the Development Server python manage.py migrate # apply the built-in migrations (creates db.sqlite3) python manage.py runserver # start the dev server at http://127.0.0.1:8000 Your First View A view is a Python function (or class) that receives an HttpRequest and returns an HttpResponse . JsonResponse is an HttpResponse that turns a dict into JSON for you. # file: blog/views.py (Section 1 checkpoint) from django.http import JsonResponse def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) Now connect it to a URL. The app gets its own urls.py , and the project's urls.py includes it under api/ : # file: blog/urls.py (Section 1 checkpoint; create this file) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health ), ] # file: blogplatform/urls.py (include the app URLs) from django.contrib import admin from django.urls import path , include urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), ] Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health/ and Django returns {"status": "ok", "version": "1.0.0"} . The full URL is the two pieces joined: api/ from the project's urls.py plus health/ from the app's urls.py . Exercise 1: Ping Add a GET /api/ping/ view that returns {"message": "pong", "timestamp": <current UTC time as a string>} . Use datetime from Python's standard library. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from datetime import datetime , timezone def ping ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "message" : "pong" , "timestamp" : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) . isoformat (), }) # add to: blog/urls.py (inside urlpatterns) # path('ping/', views.ping), Quick recap startproject makes the config package; startapp makes an app. Add the app to INSTALLED_APPS . A view takes a request and returns a response. JsonResponse(dict) returns JSON. URLs are split: the project's urls.py uses include() to hand a prefix over to the app's urls.py . 2. Models & Migrations What Is a Django Model? A model is a Python class that maps to a database table. Each class attribute is a column. Django's ORM turns Python code into SQL for you. # Illustration: the smallest possible model from django.db import models class Post ( models . Model ): title = models . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) body = models . TextField () Django names the table blog_post : app name plus model name, in lowercase. Common Field Types Field Python type SQL type CharField(max_length=N) str VARCHAR(N) TextField() str TEXT IntegerField() int INTEGER FloatField() float REAL BooleanField() bool BOOLEAN DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True) datetime DATETIME (set once, on create) DateTimeField(auto_now=True) datetime DATETIME (set on every save) ForeignKey(Model, on_delete=...) the related object INTEGER + foreign key constraint Relationships # Illustration (fields shortened) class Comment ( models . Model ): post = models . ForeignKey ( Post , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'comments' ) # CASCADE: deleting a Post also deletes all its Comments # related_name: lets you do post.comments.all() The Migration Workflow Edit models.py | v python manage.py makemigrations <- writes a migration file in blog/migrations/ | v python manage.py migrate <- runs it against the database Run both commands every time you change a model. Don't edit migration files by hand unless you really know what you're doing. Inspecting the Schema python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0001 # prints the SQL Django will run. Great for learning what the ORM does. Here is the full models.py for the project: # file: blog/models.py (Section 2 checkpoint) from django.db import models from django.contrib.auth.models import User class Post ( models . Model ): title = models . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) slug = models . SlugField ( unique = True ) body = models . TextField () published = models . BooleanField ( default = False ) author = models . ForeignKey ( User , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'posts' , ) created_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now_add = True ) updated_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now = True ) class Meta : ordering = [ '-created_at' ] # newest first by default def __str__ ( self ): return self . title class Comment ( models . Model ): post = models . ForeignKey ( Post , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'comments' ) author = models . ForeignKey ( User , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'comments' ) body = models . TextField () created_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now_add = True ) def __str__ ( self ): return f 'Comment by { self . author } on " { self . post } "' What just happened? author links each post to Django's built-in User model, so we get user accounts and passwords for free. related_name='posts' means you can write alice.posts.all() . Likewise post.comments.all() for comments. class Meta: ordering = ['-created_at'] makes every query return the newest posts first unless you ask otherwise. __str__ controls how a post is shown in the shell and the admin site. Now create the tables: python manage.py makemigrations blog python manage.py migrate Exercise 2: Slug and Published Flag Suppose your Post model started without slug and published . Add a slug field ( SlugField(unique=True) ) and a published boolean field (default False ), run makemigrations and migrate , and check the new columns with sqlmigrate . (The checkpoint above already includes both, so compare your answer with it.) Show solution # add to: blog/models.py (inside class Post) slug = models . SlugField ( unique = True ) published = models . BooleanField ( default = False ) # Then in the terminal: # python manage.py makemigrations blog # python manage.py migrate # python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0002 # the number of your new migration # # If the table already has rows, makemigrations asks for a default for `slug`. # A unique field can't share one default, so the easiest fix while learning is # to delete db.sqlite3 and the files in blog/migrations/ (keep __init__.py) # and start again. Quick recap A model is a class; each field is a column. Django adds an id primary key for you. ForeignKey(..., on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='...') links tables and gives you a reverse lookup. Changed a model? makemigrations , then migrate . Every time. 3. Django ORM All the code in this section runs in the Django shell , a Python prompt with your project already loaded: python manage.py shell Start with this session. It creates the user alice and a first post, which the later examples use. Run it only once: creating alice a second time fails because usernames are unique. Since Django 5.2 the shell imports your models automatically. The import lines in the cells are still there so the code also works in older versions and in plain scripts. # run in: python manage.py shell # Only needed if you run this as a plain script instead of in the shell: # import django, os # os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'blogplatform.settings') # django.setup() from django.contrib.auth.models import User from blog.models import Post , Comment # Create a user (only needed once) alice = User . objects . create_user ( username = 'alice' , password = 'secret123' ) # CREATE post = Post . objects . create ( title = 'Getting Started with Python' , slug = 'getting-started-python' , body = 'Python is a versatile language...' , author = alice , published = True , ) # READ all_posts = Post . objects . all () pub_posts = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) alice_posts = Post . objects . filter ( author__username = 'alice' ) . select_related ( 'author' ) # UPDATE post . title = 'Getting Started with Python (Revised)' post . save () The QuerySet Every ORM query returns a QuerySet : a lazy, chainable list of model objects. "Lazy" means Django doesn't run any SQL until you actually need the results, for example when you loop over it, slice it or call list() on it. # run in: python manage.py shell # Nothing hits the DB yet: qs = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) # DB query fires here: for post in qs : print ( post . title ) CRUD Operations Here are create, read, update and delete side by side. Note the last two lines delete data; that's fine on a practice database. # run in: python manage.py shell from blog.models import Post from django.contrib.auth.models import User author = User . objects . get ( username = 'alice' ) # CREATE post = Post . objects . create ( title = 'Hello Django' , slug = 'hello-django' , body = 'My first post.' , author = author , published = True , ) # READ: all Post . objects . all () # READ: filter Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) Post . objects . filter ( author__username = 'alice' ) # <- double-underscore traverses FK # READ: single record (raises DoesNotExist if missing) post = Post . objects . get ( slug = 'hello-django' ) # UPDATE post . title = 'Hello Django (Updated)' post . save () # Bulk UPDATE (no .save() needed) Post . objects . filter ( published = False ) . update ( published = True ) # DELETE post . delete () Post . objects . filter ( published = False ) . delete () Lookups (Filtering) Lookup Example Meaning exact (default) filter(title='Hello') title = 'Hello' icontains filter(title__icontains='django') case-insensitive LIKE gt / gte / lt / lte filter(id__gt=5) > , >= , < , <= in filter(id__in=[1, 2, 3]) id IN (1, 2, 3) isnull filter(slug__isnull=True) IS NULL Related field filter(author__username='alice') JOIN through the foreign key select_related and prefetch_related The N+1 problem : you load N posts with one query, then touching post.author runs one more query per post . These two methods fix it: # run in: python manage.py shell # BAD (the N+1 problem): one query per post to fetch the author for post in Post . objects . all (): print ( post . author . username ) # GOOD: single JOIN query for post in Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . all (): print ( post . author . username ) # For many-to-many or reverse FK (e.g., all comments per post) posts = Post . objects . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () Rule of thumb: select_related for a foreign key you follow forwards (post -> author, one object). prefetch_related for the reverse side or many-to-many (post -> comments, many objects). Exercise 3: Recent Python Posts Write one QuerySet that returns the 5 most recently created published posts whose title contains "python" (any case). Chain the methods together. Show solution # run in: python manage.py shell recent_python = ( Post . objects . filter ( published = True , title__icontains = 'python' ) . order_by ( '-created_at' )[: 5 ] ) print ( list ( recent_python )) Quick recap Model.objects gives you QuerySets: all() , filter() , exclude() , get() , order_by() . QuerySets are lazy and chainable. SQL runs only when you use the results. Double underscores do lookups ( title__icontains ) and follow relations ( author__username ). Use select_related / prefetch_related to avoid the N+1 query problem. 4. Views & URL Patterns Before we bring in DRF, let's see how far plain Django gets us. This helps you appreciate what DRF does for you in the next section. Function-Based Views (FBVs) A function-based view can handle several HTTP methods in one function. Check request.method to decide what to do. # Illustration (blog/views.py) from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt from django.http import JsonResponse from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods import json from .models import Post @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'POST' ]) def post_list ( request ): if request . method == 'GET' : posts = list ( Post . objects . values ( 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'published' )) return JsonResponse ( posts , safe = False ) elif request . method == 'POST' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post = Post . objects . create ( author = request . user , ** data ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id }, status = 201 ) Two things to notice: @csrf_exempt : Django protects every POST, PUT and DELETE against CSRF attacks by default. That check expects a token that only Django's own HTML forms send, so a JSON request from curl gets 403 Forbidden . We switch the check off for these demo views. DRF handles this properly for us later. author=request.user : every post needs an author. request.user is the logged-in user (or AnonymousUser if nobody is logged in, which is why the checkpoint below checks first). URL Patterns # Illustration (blog/urls.py) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'posts/' , views . post_list ), # /api/posts/ path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , views . post_detail ), # /api/posts/42/ ] URL converters: Converter Matches Example <int:pk> digits /posts/42/ gives pk=42 <str:slug> anything except / /posts/hello-world/ <slug:slug> letters, digits, - , _ /posts/hello-world/ <uuid:id> a UUID /items/550e8400-.../ get_object_or_404 # Illustration from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) # returns 404 if not found return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'body' : post . body }) Class-Based Views (CBVs) With a class-based view, each HTTP method is its own method on the class. Django calls get() for GET requests, delete() for DELETE, and so on: # Illustration from django.views import View from django.http import HttpResponse , JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 class PostDetailView ( View ): def get ( self , request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) def delete ( self , request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) post . delete () return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) # 204 means "no content", so no body # Illustration (blog/urls.py) path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , PostDetailView . as_view ()), Exercise 4: A Post Detail View Write a post_detail function-based view that handles: GET : return the post as JSON PUT : update title and body from the JSON request body DELETE : delete the post Use get_object_or_404 . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'PUT' , 'DELETE' ]) def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) if request . method == 'GET' : return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'body' : post . body }) if request . method == 'PUT' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post . title = data . get ( 'title' , post . title ) post . body = data . get ( 'body' , post . body ) post . save () return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) post . delete () # DELETE return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) Here is the full views.py and urls.py for this section. Compare how much code it takes; we'll replace all of it with a few lines of DRF in Section 6. # file: blog/views.py (Section 4 checkpoint: plain Django views) import json from django.http import HttpResponse , JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods from .models import Post def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'POST' ]) def post_list ( request ): if request . method == 'GET' : posts = list ( Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . values ( 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'author__username' , 'created_at' ) ) return JsonResponse ( posts , safe = False ) elif request . method == 'POST' : if not request . user . is_authenticated : return JsonResponse ({ 'error' : 'login required' }, status = 401 ) data = json . loads ( request . body ) post = Post . objects . create ( title = data [ 'title' ], slug = data [ 'slug' ], body = data [ 'body' ], author = request . user , ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }, status = 201 ) @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'PUT' , 'DELETE' ]) def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) if request . method == 'GET' : return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'slug' : post . slug , 'body' : post . body , 'author' : post . author . username , 'published' : post . published , }) elif request . method == 'PUT' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post . title = data . get ( 'title' , post . title ) post . body = data . get ( 'body' , post . body ) post . save () return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) elif request . method == 'DELETE' : post . delete () return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) # file: blog/urls.py (Section 4 checkpoint) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health ), path ( 'posts/' , views . post_list ), # /api/posts/ path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , views . post_detail ), # /api/posts/42/ ] What just happened? post_list only lists published posts, and it uses .values(...) to get plain dicts that JsonResponse can serialise. A model object can't be turned into JSON directly, which is why post_detail builds its dict by hand. safe=False is needed because we return a list rather than a dict. Quick recap Function-based views branch on request.method ; class-based views have one method per HTTP verb. path('posts/<int:pk>/', view) captures part of the URL and passes it to the view. get_object_or_404 saves you the try/except for missing objects. Plain Django views mean manual JSON, manual validation and dealing with CSRF yourself. DRF fixes all three. 5. Django REST Framework: Serializers Why DRF? Plain Django views work, but you write the JSON parsing, validation and serialisation by hand. Django REST Framework (DRF) gives you: Serializers : declare the fields once and get validation and JSON conversion Generic views / ViewSets : full CRUD in a few lines Browsable API : a clickable HTML page for every endpoint Authentication & permissions : ready-made classes you plug in ModelSerializer A ModelSerializer builds its fields from a model. It plays the same role as the Pydantic ...Create / ...Response models in FastAPI, in one class: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) from rest_framework import serializers from .models import Post , Comment class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author' ] The inner Meta class connects the serializer to a model. fields lists the columns to include; read_only_fields are sent back to the client but can't be set by it. Validation Add validate_<field> methods for checks on one field, and validate for checks that involve several fields: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): title = serializers . CharField ( min_length = 5 , max_length = 200 ) class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author' ] def validate_slug ( self , value ): """Field-level validator.""" if ' ' in value : raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'Slug must not contain spaces.' ) return value def validate ( self , data ): """Object-level validator (runs after all fields pass).""" if data . get ( 'published' ) and not data . get ( 'body' ): raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'A published post must have a body.' ) return data When a check fails, DRF answers 400 Bad Request with the error message under the field name, for example {"slug": ["Slug must not contain spaces."]} . Nested Serializers A serializer can be used as a field inside another one. Here each post includes its full list of comments: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) class CommentSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Comment fields = [ 'id' , 'body' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' ] class PostDetailSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): comments = CommentSerializer ( many = True , read_only = True ) # inline nested objects author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' , 'comments' ] source='author.username' reads a value through the relation, so the API shows "alice" instead of the author's id. Exercise 5: Comment Count Add a comment_count field to PostSerializer that returns how many comments each post has. Use serializers.SerializerMethodField and write a get_comment_count method. Show solution # add to: blog/serializers.py (inside PostSerializer) comment_count = serializers . SerializerMethodField () def get_comment_count ( self , obj ): return obj . comments . count () # and add 'comment_count' to Meta.fields Here is the full serializers.py , including the exercise. PostDetailSerializer inherits from PostSerializer and just adds the comments, so the two never get out of step. # file: blog/serializers.py (Section 5 checkpoint) from rest_framework import serializers from .models import Post , Comment class CommentSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Comment fields = [ 'id' , 'body' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' ] class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) comment_count = serializers . SerializerMethodField () class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' , 'comment_count' , ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' , 'comment_count' ] def get_comment_count ( self , obj ): return obj . comments . count () def validate_slug ( self , value ): if ' ' in value : raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'Slug must not contain spaces.' ) return value class PostDetailSerializer ( PostSerializer ): """Extends PostSerializer with full comment list for detail views.""" comments = CommentSerializer ( many = True , read_only = True ) class Meta ( PostSerializer . Meta ): fields = PostSerializer . Meta . fields + [ 'comments' ] Quick recap A ModelSerializer turns model objects into JSON and validates incoming JSON. Meta.fields picks the columns; read_only_fields are output-only. validate_<field>() for one field, validate() for several. Raise serializers.ValidationError . source='author.username' and SerializerMethodField add computed fields. 6. DRF Views & Routers APIView APIView is DRF's version of Django's View : one method per HTTP verb. On top of that, DRF parses JSON for you ( request.data ), turns Response objects into JSON, and runs authentication and permission checks. # Illustration (blog/views.py) from .models import Post from .serializers import PostSerializer from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework import status class PostListView ( APIView ): def get ( self , request ): posts = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) serializer = PostSerializer ( posts , many = True ) return Response ( serializer . data ) def post ( self , request ): serializer = PostSerializer ( data = request . data ) if serializer . is_valid (): serializer . save ( author = request . user ) return Response ( serializer . data , status = status . HTTP_201_CREATED ) return Response ( serializer . errors , status = status . HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST ) ModelViewSet A ViewSet puts all the operations for one resource in one class. A ModelViewSet gives you list , create , retrieve , update , partial_update and destroy without writing any of them: # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework import viewsets class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . all () serializer_class = PostSerializer DRF Router Give the ViewSet to a DefaultRouter and it creates all the URL patterns: # Illustration (blog/urls.py) from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter from . import views router = DefaultRouter () router . register ( 'posts' , views . PostViewSet , basename = 'post' ) urlpatterns = router . urls That one register call creates: URL Method Action /api/posts/ GET list /api/posts/ POST create /api/posts/{pk}/ GET retrieve /api/posts/{pk}/ PUT update /api/posts/{pk}/ PATCH partial_update /api/posts/{pk}/ DELETE destroy Custom Actions with @action For anything that isn't plain CRUD, add a method with @action . detail=True means it works on one object, so the URL includes the pk : # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework.decorators import action class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . all () serializer_class = PostSerializer @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): """POST /api/posts/{pk}/publish/ marks a post as published.""" post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' }) Exercise 6: Unpublish Add an @action called unpublish ( detail=True , methods=['post'] ) that sets post.published = False . Both /publish/ and /unpublish/ should work on the same ViewSet. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' }) Section 6 Checkpoint Replace blog/views.py and blog/urls.py with the two cells below. The comments live under each post ( /api/posts/1/comments/ ), which needs the drf-nested-routers package from the install command. Heads-up: until we add authentication in Section 7, you can read through the API but not create posts. perform_create saves self.request.user as the author, and an anonymous user can't be one, so a POST ends in a server error. That's exactly what the next section fixes. # file: blog/views.py (Section 6 checkpoint: DRF ViewSets) from django.http import JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from rest_framework import viewsets from rest_framework.decorators import action from rest_framework.response import Response from .models import Post , Comment from .serializers import PostSerializer , PostDetailSerializer , CommentSerializer def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () def get_serializer_class ( self ): # Use the detailed serializer (with comments) for single-object views if self . action == 'retrieve' : return PostDetailSerializer return PostSerializer def perform_create ( self , serializer ): # Automatically set the author to the authenticated user serializer . save ( author = self . request . user ) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' }) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' }) class CommentViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): serializer_class = CommentSerializer http_method_names = [ 'get' , 'post' , 'delete' , 'head' , 'options' ] def get_queryset ( self ): # Scope comments to the parent post return Comment . objects . filter ( post_id = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ] ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . order_by ( 'created_at' ) # oldest first def perform_create ( self , serializer ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ]) serializer . save ( author = self . request . user , post = post ) # file: blog/urls.py (Section 6 checkpoint: nested router) from django.urls import path from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter from rest_framework_nested import routers as nested_routers # pip install drf-nested-routers from . import views router = DefaultRouter () router . register ( 'posts' , views . PostViewSet , basename = 'post' ) # Nested: /api/posts/{post_pk}/comments/ posts_router = nested_routers . NestedDefaultRouter ( router , 'posts' , lookup = 'post' ) posts_router . register ( 'comments' , views . CommentViewSet , basename = 'post-comments' ) urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health )] + router . urls + posts_router . urls What just happened? get_serializer_class() picks the serializer per action: the detailed one (with comments) for a single post, the short one for lists. perform_create() is a hook DRF calls when saving a new object. We use it to fill in fields the client must not choose, like author . NestedDefaultRouter(router, 'posts', lookup='post') puts the comments URLs under a post, and passes the post's id to the view as self.kwargs['post_pk'] . CommentViewSet uses get_object_or_404 , so commenting on a post that doesn't exist gives 404 rather than a server error. It also sorts the comments ( order_by('created_at') ); Comment has no default ordering, and paginating an unsorted list makes DRF print a warning. Quick recap APIView : one method per verb, with request.data and Response doing the JSON work. ModelViewSet + DefaultRouter = full CRUD and all its URLs in a few lines. @action(detail=True, methods=['post']) adds extra endpoints like /publish/ . Override get_queryset , get_serializer_class and perform_create to customise a ViewSet. 7. Authentication & Permissions DRF Authentication Classes Class How the client proves who it is SessionAuthentication Django session cookie (logging in through a browser) BasicAuthentication HTTP Basic: username and password on every request. Testing only. TokenAuthentication Authorization: Token <token> header JWTAuthentication (from djangorestframework-simplejwt ) Authorization: Bearer <jwt> header We'll use TokenAuthentication . It's like the API key from the FastAPI notebook: a random string stored in the database, one per user. Setting Up Token Authentication Add this to the bottom of settings.py : # add to: blogplatform/settings.py REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication' , ], 'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly' , ], } Then run python manage.py migrate again. rest_framework.authtoken (which we added to INSTALLED_APPS in Section 1) brings its own table, authtoken_token . DRF also ships a ready-made view that swaps a username and password for a token. Add it to blogplatform/urls.py : # Illustration (blogplatform/urls.py; the final version is in Section 9) from rest_framework.authtoken import views as drf_auth_views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), path ( 'api/auth/token/' , drf_auth_views . obtain_auth_token ), # POST {username, password} ] Built-in Permission Classes Permission Effect AllowAny Everyone, logged in or not IsAuthenticated Must send a valid token / session IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly Anonymous users may only read (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) IsAdminUser request.user.is_staff must be True Custom Object-Level Permission Only a post's author should be able to edit or delete it. Built-in classes can't know that, so we write our own: # file: blog/permissions.py from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission , SAFE_METHODS class IsOwnerOrReadOnly ( BasePermission ): """Write access only to the object's owner; read access for everyone.""" def has_object_permission ( self , request , view , obj ): if request . method in SAFE_METHODS : return True return obj . author == request . user has_object_permission runs when the view loads one specific object (retrieve, update, delete and our publish action). SAFE_METHODS is the tuple ('GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS') , the methods that don't change anything. Apply it to the ViewSet. DRF checks every class in the list, and all of them must agree: # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly from .permissions import IsOwnerOrReadOnly class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] ... User Registration View DRF has no sign-up endpoint, so we write a small one. It creates the user and gives back a token straight away: # Illustration (blog/views.py; the full file is below) from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token from django.contrib.auth.models import User class RegisterView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [] # public endpoint def post ( self , request ): username = request . data . get ( 'username' ) password = request . data . get ( 'password' ) if not username or not password : return Response ({ 'error' : 'username and password required' }, status = 400 ) if User . objects . filter ( username = username ) . exists (): return Response ({ 'error' : 'username already taken' }, status = 400 ) user = User . objects . create_user ( username = username , password = password ) token = Token . objects . create ( user = user ) return Response ({ 'token' : token . key }, status = 201 ) permission_classes = [] overrides the default from settings.py , so anyone may call it. Otherwise nobody could register without already having a token. Exercise 7: Log Out Add a DELETE /api/auth/token/revoke/ endpoint that deletes the current user's token, so they have to log in again. It must require IsAuthenticated . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated class RevokeTokenView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ] def delete ( self , request ): request . user . auth_token . delete () return Response ( status = 204 ) # add to: blogplatform/urls.py (inside urlpatterns) # path('api/auth/token/revoke/', RevokeTokenView.as_view()), Here is the complete views.py with everything from Sections 6 and 7. Besides the new auth views, CommentViewSet now also uses IsOwnerOrReadOnly . Without it, any logged-in user could delete anyone else's comment. # file: blog/views.py (Section 7 checkpoint: full file) from django.http import JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from rest_framework import viewsets from rest_framework.decorators import action from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated , IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token from django.contrib.auth.models import User from .models import Post , Comment from .serializers import PostSerializer , PostDetailSerializer , CommentSerializer from .permissions import IsOwnerOrReadOnly def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] def get_serializer_class ( self ): if self . action == 'retrieve' : return PostDetailSerializer return PostSerializer def perform_create ( self , serializer ): serializer . save ( author = self . request . user ) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' }) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' }) class CommentViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): serializer_class = CommentSerializer permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] http_method_names = [ 'get' , 'post' , 'delete' , 'head' , 'options' ] def get_queryset ( self ): return Comment . objects . filter ( post_id = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ] ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . order_by ( 'created_at' ) # oldest first def perform_create ( self , serializer ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ]) serializer . save ( author = self . request . user , post = post ) class RegisterView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [] # public: anyone can register def post ( self , request ): username = request . data . get ( 'username' ) password = request . data . get ( 'password' ) if not username or not password : return Response ({ 'error' : 'username and password required' }, status = 400 ) if User . objects . filter ( username = username ) . exists (): return Response ({ 'error' : 'username already taken' }, status = 400 ) user = User . objects . create_user ( username = username , password = password ) token = Token . objects . create ( user = user ) return Response ({ 'token' : token . key }, status = 201 ) class RevokeTokenView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ] def delete ( self , request ): request . user . auth_token . delete () return Response ( status = 204 ) Quick recap Authentication answers "who are you?"; permissions answer "are you allowed?". Set defaults in REST_FRAMEWORK in settings.py ; override per view with permission_classes . Clients send Authorization: Token <key> . Get the key from /api/auth/token/ or /api/auth/register/ . Object-level rules ("only the author") go in has_object_permission . 8. Django Admin What Is the Admin? Django comes with a complete web admin site at /admin/ . You don't write any frontend code; you just register your models. python manage.py createsuperuser # creates an admin user python manage.py runserver # open http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ Basic Registration # Illustration (blog/admin.py, simplest version) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment admin . site . register ( Post ) admin . site . register ( Comment ) That's enough to get list, add, edit and delete pages for both models. Customising the Admin A ModelAdmin class controls the columns, filters, search box and more. An inline shows related objects (here, a post's comments) on the same page: # Illustration (blog/admin.py) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment class CommentInline ( admin . TabularInline ): model = Comment extra = 0 # don't show blank rows by default readonly_fields = [ 'author' , 'created_at' ] @admin . register ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'title' , 'author' , 'published' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'published' , 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' , 'author__username' ] prepopulated_fields = { 'slug' : ( 'title' ,)} # auto-fills slug from title inlines = [ CommentInline ] actions = [ 'make_published' ] @admin . action ( description = 'Mark selected posts as published' ) def make_published ( self , request , queryset ): queryset . update ( published = True ) @admin.action(description=...) is the current way to name a bulk action. Older code sets make_published.short_description = ... after the function, which still works. Common ModelAdmin Options Option Effect list_display Columns shown in the list of objects list_filter Filter panel in the sidebar search_fields Adds a search box (uses LIKE queries) ordering Default sort order prepopulated_fields Fills one field from another as you type inlines Shows related objects on the same page actions Bulk actions in the list view readonly_fields Fields shown but not editable Exercise 8: Comment Admin Register Comment with a CommentAdmin that shows post , author and created_at as columns, can be filtered by created_at , and can be searched by body and author__username . (Remove the plain admin.site.register(Comment) line, since a model can only be registered once.) Show solution # add to: blog/admin.py @admin . register ( Comment ) class CommentAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'post' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'body' , 'author__username' ] # file: blog/admin.py (Section 8 checkpoint) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment class CommentInline ( admin . TabularInline ): model = Comment extra = 0 readonly_fields = [ 'author' , 'created_at' ] @admin . register ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'title' , 'author' , 'published' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'published' , 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' , 'author__username' ] prepopulated_fields = { 'slug' : ( 'title' ,)} inlines = [ CommentInline ] actions = [ 'make_published' ] @admin . action ( description = 'Mark selected posts as published' ) def make_published ( self , request , queryset ): queryset . update ( published = True ) @admin . register ( Comment ) class CommentAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'post' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'body' , 'author__username' ] Quick recap python manage.py createsuperuser , then log in at /admin/ . @admin.register(Model) + a ModelAdmin class to customise the pages. list_display , list_filter , search_fields and inlines cover most needs. 9. Final settings.py & urls.py Time to put all the pieces together in the project's config files. blogplatform/settings.py These are only the parts we changed. Leave everything else that startproject generated as it is. Compared with Section 7 we've added SessionAuthentication (so you can log in to the browsable API) and pagination. # add to: blogplatform/settings.py (final version of the parts we changed) INSTALLED_APPS = [ 'django.contrib.admin' , 'django.contrib.auth' , 'django.contrib.contenttypes' , 'django.contrib.sessions' , 'django.contrib.messages' , 'django.contrib.staticfiles' , # third-party 'rest_framework' , 'rest_framework.authtoken' , # local 'blog' , ] REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication' , 'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication' , ], 'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly' , ], 'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS' : 'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination' , 'PAGE_SIZE' : 10 , } blogplatform/urls.py # file: blogplatform/urls.py (final) from django.contrib import admin from django.urls import path , include from rest_framework.authtoken import views as drf_auth_views from blog.views import RegisterView , RevokeTokenView urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), path ( 'api/auth/register/' , RegisterView . as_view ()), path ( 'api/auth/token/' , drf_auth_views . obtain_auth_token ), path ( 'api/auth/token/revoke/' , RevokeTokenView . as_view ()), path ( 'api-auth/' , include ( 'rest_framework.urls' )), ] Testing with curl # Register curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/auth/register/ \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username": "alice", "password": "secret123"}' # -> {"token": "abc123..."} # Create a post (logged in) curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Hello Django", "slug": "hello-django", "body": "My first post!"}' # List posts (no login needed) curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ # Publish a post (only its author can) curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/1/publish/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' # Log out curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/auth/token/revoke/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' Because pagination is switched on, the list endpoint now wraps the posts: {"count": 1, "next": null, "previous": null, "results": [...]} . You can also open http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ in the browser to use the browsable API. Log in with the link in the top-right corner (that's what api-auth/ is for). Quick recap INSTALLED_APPS lists DRF, the token app and our app; REST_FRAMEWORK sets auth, permission and pagination defaults. The project's urls.py mounts the admin, the app's API and the auth endpoints. With pagination on, list responses look like {count, next, previous, results} . Extra Practice Three small features for the finished project. Each needs only a few lines. Practice 1: Filter Posts Let clients filter the post list with ?published=true and ?author__username=alice , using the django-filter package (already in the install command). Hint: add 'django_filters' to INSTALLED_APPS , set DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS in REST_FRAMEWORK , and give PostViewSet a filterset_fields list. Show solution # add to: blogplatform/settings.py INSTALLED_APPS += [ 'django_filters' ] REST_FRAMEWORK [ 'DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS' ] = [ 'django_filters.rest_framework.DjangoFilterBackend' , ] # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) filterset_fields = [ 'published' , 'author__username' ] Practice 2: Search and Sort Add ?search=django (searches title and body) and ?ordering=title / ?ordering=-created_at to the post list, using DRF's SearchFilter and OrderingFilter . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from django_filters.rest_framework import DjangoFilterBackend from rest_framework.filters import OrderingFilter , SearchFilter # inside PostViewSet filter_backends = [ DjangoFilterBackend , SearchFilter , OrderingFilter ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' ] ordering_fields = [ 'created_at' , 'title' ] # Setting filter_backends on the view replaces the default list from settings, # which is why DjangoFilterBackend is listed again here. Practice 3: My Posts Add GET /api/posts/mine/ that returns only the logged-in user's posts, including unpublished ones. Anonymous users should get 401 . Hint: @action(detail=False, ...) makes an action on the collection, so there's no pk in the URL. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) @action ( detail = False , methods = [ 'get' ], permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ]) def mine ( self , request ): posts = self . get_queryset () . filter ( author = request . user ) page = self . paginate_queryset ( posts ) serializer = self . get_serializer ( page , many = True ) return self . get_paginated_response ( serializer . data ) Quick recap filterset_fields (django-filter) gives exact-match filters with one line. SearchFilter and OrderingFilter add ?search= and ?ordering= . @action(detail=False) adds endpoints on the collection, like /api/posts/mine/ . Summary & Cheat Sheet Topic Remember this Project vs app A project is the configuration; apps hold the code. One project, many apps. Models Classes that map to tables. Fields are columns. Migrations makemigrations writes the change, migrate applies it. Always both. ORM Lazy, chainable QuerySets. select_related / prefetch_related avoid N+1 queries. Views Functions or classes that take an HttpRequest and return an HttpResponse . DRF serializers Declare fields once; get validation and JSON in both directions. ModelViewSet One class = full CRUD. Pair it with DefaultRouter for the URLs. @action Extra endpoints on a ViewSet ( /publish/ , /unpublish/ ). Permissions IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly + a custom IsOwnerOrReadOnly protect writes. Admin Register models and customise with ModelAdmin for a free management UI. Useful Commands django-admin startproject blogplatform # new project python manage.py startapp blog # new app python manage.py makemigrations # after changing models python manage.py migrate # apply migrations python manage.py createsuperuser # admin login python manage.py shell # Python prompt with the project loaded python manage.py runserver # dev server on port 8000 Further Reading Django documentation Django REST Framework documentation QuerySet API reference drf-nested-routers : nested URLs for related resources djangorestframework-simplejwt : JWT authentication for DRF What's Next The next notebook, Deploying Applications , shows how to take a project like this one (or the FastAPI one) off your laptop and run it on a real server.

docs.text: In this notebook we build a blog platform with Django and Django REST Framework (DRF). We start with one plain JSON view and end with a token-protected REST API, nested comment URLs and a customised admin site.

docs.text: By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Create a Django project and app from scratch Define models and run database migrations Query the database with the Django ORM Write function-based and class-based views and connect them to URLs Build a REST API with DRF serializers, ViewSets and routers Protect endpoints with token authentication and permissions Manage your data with the Django admin site

docs.text: Work through it top to bottom . Each section adds to the same project, called blogplatform . The code cells are not meant to be run inside Jupyter . Create (or replace) the file and paste it in. # add to: blogplatform/settings.py means paste the cell into the existing file. # run in: python manage.py shell means type or paste it into the Django shell. Cells marked Illustration are short pieces to read, not to copy. Run terminal commands ( python manage.py ... ) from the outer blogplatform/ folder, the one that contains manage.py . Try each Exercise yourself before opening Show solution . Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read just the recaps when revising.

docs.text: A view is a Python function (or class) that receives an HttpRequest and returns an HttpResponse . JsonResponse is an HttpResponse that turns a dict into JSON for you. # file: blog/views.py (Section 1 checkpoint) from django.http import JsonResponse def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) Now connect it to a URL. The app gets its own urls.py , and the project's urls.py includes it under api/ : # file: blog/urls.py (Section 1 checkpoint; create this file) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health ), ] # file: blogplatform/urls.py (include the app URLs) from django.contrib import admin from django.urls import path , include urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), ] Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health/ and Django returns {"status": "ok", "version": "1.0.0"} . The full URL is the two pieces joined: api/ from the project's urls.py plus health/ from the app's urls.py .
docs.title: Your First View

docs.text: Add a GET /api/ping/ view that returns {"message": "pong", "timestamp": <current UTC time as a string>} . Use datetime from Python's standard library. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from datetime import datetime , timezone def ping ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "message" : "pong" , "timestamp" : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) . isoformat (), }) # add to: blog/urls.py (inside urlpatterns) # path('ping/', views.ping), Quick recap startproject makes the config package; startapp makes an app. Add the app to INSTALLED_APPS . A view takes a request and returns a response. JsonResponse(dict) returns JSON. URLs are split: the project's urls.py uses include() to hand a prefix over to the app's urls.py .

docs.text: A model is a Python class that maps to a database table. Each class attribute is a column. Django's ORM turns Python code into SQL for you. # Illustration: the smallest possible model from django.db import models class Post ( models . Model ): title = models . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) body = models . TextField () Django names the table blog_post : app name plus model name, in lowercase.
docs.title: What Is a Django Model?

docs.text: Field Python type SQL type CharField(max_length=N) str VARCHAR(N) TextField() str TEXT IntegerField() int INTEGER FloatField() float REAL BooleanField() bool BOOLEAN DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True) datetime DATETIME (set once, on create) DateTimeField(auto_now=True) datetime DATETIME (set on every save) ForeignKey(Model, on_delete=...) the related object INTEGER + foreign key constraint
