docs.title: Relationships

docs.text: Edit models.py | v python manage.py makemigrations <- writes a migration file in blog/migrations/ | v python manage.py migrate <- runs it against the database Run both commands every time you change a model. Don't edit migration files by hand unless you really know what you're doing.
docs.title: The Migration Workflow

docs.text: python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0001 # prints the SQL Django will run. Great for learning what the ORM does. Here is the full models.py for the project: # file: blog/models.py (Section 2 checkpoint) from django.db import models from django.contrib.auth.models import User class Post ( models . Model ): title = models . CharField ( max_length = 200 ) slug = models . SlugField ( unique = True ) body = models . TextField () published = models . BooleanField ( default = False ) author = models . ForeignKey ( User , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'posts' , ) created_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now_add = True ) updated_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now = True ) class Meta : ordering = [ '-created_at' ] # newest first by default def __str__ ( self ): return self . title class Comment ( models . Model ): post = models . ForeignKey ( Post , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'comments' ) author = models . ForeignKey ( User , on_delete = models . CASCADE , related_name = 'comments' ) body = models . TextField () created_at = models . DateTimeField ( auto_now_add = True ) def __str__ ( self ): return f 'Comment by { self . author } on " { self . post } "' What just happened? author links each post to Django's built-in User model, so we get user accounts and passwords for free. related_name='posts' means you can write alice.posts.all() . Likewise post.comments.all() for comments. class Meta: ordering = ['-created_at'] makes every query return the newest posts first unless you ask otherwise. __str__ controls how a post is shown in the shell and the admin site. Now create the tables: python manage.py makemigrations blog python manage.py migrate
docs.title: Inspecting the Schema

docs.text: Suppose your Post model started without slug and published . Add a slug field ( SlugField(unique=True) ) and a published boolean field (default False ), run makemigrations and migrate , and check the new columns with sqlmigrate . (The checkpoint above already includes both, so compare your answer with it.) Show solution # add to: blog/models.py (inside class Post) slug = models . SlugField ( unique = True ) published = models . BooleanField ( default = False ) # Then in the terminal: # python manage.py makemigrations blog # python manage.py migrate # python manage.py sqlmigrate blog 0002 # the number of your new migration # # If the table already has rows, makemigrations asks for a default for `slug`. # A unique field can't share one default, so the easiest fix while learning is # to delete db.sqlite3 and the files in blog/migrations/ (keep __init__.py) # and start again. Quick recap A model is a class; each field is a column. Django adds an id primary key for you. ForeignKey(..., on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='...') links tables and gives you a reverse lookup. Changed a model? makemigrations , then migrate . Every time.
docs.title: Exercise 2: Slug and Published Flag

docs.text: All the code in this section runs in the Django shell , a Python prompt with your project already loaded: python manage.py shell Start with this session. It creates the user alice and a first post, which the later examples use. Run it only once: creating alice a second time fails because usernames are unique. Since Django 5.2 the shell imports your models automatically. The import lines in the cells are still there so the code also works in older versions and in plain scripts. # run in: python manage.py shell # Only needed if you run this as a plain script instead of in the shell: # import django, os # os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE', 'blogplatform.settings') # django.setup() from django.contrib.auth.models import User from blog.models import Post , Comment # Create a user (only needed once) alice = User . objects . create_user ( username = 'alice' , password = 'secret123' ) # CREATE post = Post . objects . create ( title = 'Getting Started with Python' , slug = 'getting-started-python' , body = 'Python is a versatile language...' , author = alice , published = True , ) # READ all_posts = Post . objects . all () pub_posts = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) alice_posts = Post . objects . filter ( author__username = 'alice' ) . select_related ( 'author' ) # UPDATE post . title = 'Getting Started with Python (Revised)' post . save ()
docs.title: 3. Django ORM

docs.text: Every ORM query returns a QuerySet : a lazy, chainable list of model objects. "Lazy" means Django doesn't run any SQL until you actually need the results, for example when you loop over it, slice it or call list() on it. # run in: python manage.py shell # Nothing hits the DB yet: qs = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) # DB query fires here: for post in qs : print ( post . title )
docs.title: The QuerySet

docs.text: Here are create, read, update and delete side by side. Note the last two lines delete data; that's fine on a practice database. # run in: python manage.py shell from blog.models import Post from django.contrib.auth.models import User author = User . objects . get ( username = 'alice' ) # CREATE post = Post . objects . create ( title = 'Hello Django' , slug = 'hello-django' , body = 'My first post.' , author = author , published = True , ) # READ: all Post . objects . all () # READ: filter Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) Post . objects . filter ( author__username = 'alice' ) # <- double-underscore traverses FK # READ: single record (raises DoesNotExist if missing) post = Post . objects . get ( slug = 'hello-django' ) # UPDATE post . title = 'Hello Django (Updated)' post . save () # Bulk UPDATE (no .save() needed) Post . objects . filter ( published = False ) . update ( published = True ) # DELETE post . delete () Post . objects . filter ( published = False ) . delete ()
docs.title: CRUD Operations

docs.text: Lookup Example Meaning exact (default) filter(title='Hello') title = 'Hello' icontains filter(title__icontains='django') case-insensitive LIKE gt / gte / lt / lte filter(id__gt=5) > , >= , < , <= in filter(id__in=[1, 2, 3]) id IN (1, 2, 3) isnull filter(slug__isnull=True) IS NULL Related field filter(author__username='alice') JOIN through the foreign key
docs.title: Lookups (Filtering)

docs.text: The N+1 problem : you load N posts with one query, then touching post.author runs one more query per post . These two methods fix it: # run in: python manage.py shell # BAD (the N+1 problem): one query per post to fetch the author for post in Post . objects . all (): print ( post . author . username ) # GOOD: single JOIN query for post in Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . all (): print ( post . author . username ) # For many-to-many or reverse FK (e.g., all comments per post) posts = Post . objects . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () Rule of thumb: select_related for a foreign key you follow forwards (post -> author, one object). prefetch_related for the reverse side or many-to-many (post -> comments, many objects).
docs.title: select_related and prefetch_related

docs.text: Write one QuerySet that returns the 5 most recently created published posts whose title contains "python" (any case). Chain the methods together. Show solution # run in: python manage.py shell recent_python = ( Post . objects . filter ( published = True , title__icontains = 'python' ) . order_by ( '-created_at' )[: 5 ] ) print ( list ( recent_python )) Quick recap Model.objects gives you QuerySets: all() , filter() , exclude() , get() , order_by() . QuerySets are lazy and chainable. SQL runs only when you use the results. Double underscores do lookups ( title__icontains ) and follow relations ( author__username ). Use select_related / prefetch_related to avoid the N+1 query problem.
docs.title: Exercise 3: Recent Python Posts

docs.text: Before we bring in DRF, let's see how far plain Django gets us. This helps you appreciate what DRF does for you in the next section.
docs.title: 4. Views & URL Patterns

docs.text: A function-based view can handle several HTTP methods in one function. Check request.method to decide what to do. # Illustration (blog/views.py) from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt from django.http import JsonResponse from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods import json from .models import Post @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'POST' ]) def post_list ( request ): if request . method == 'GET' : posts = list ( Post . objects . values ( 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'published' )) return JsonResponse ( posts , safe = False ) elif request . method == 'POST' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post = Post . objects . create ( author = request . user , ** data ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id }, status = 201 ) Two things to notice: @csrf_exempt : Django protects every POST, PUT and DELETE against CSRF attacks by default. That check expects a token that only Django's own HTML forms send, so a JSON request from curl gets 403 Forbidden . We switch the check off for these demo views. DRF handles this properly for us later. author=request.user : every post needs an author. request.user is the logged-in user (or AnonymousUser if nobody is logged in, which is why the checkpoint below checks first).
docs.title: Function-Based Views (FBVs)

docs.text: # Illustration (blog/urls.py) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'posts/' , views . post_list ), # /api/posts/ path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , views . post_detail ), # /api/posts/42/ ] URL converters: Converter Matches Example <int:pk> digits /posts/42/ gives pk=42 <str:slug> anything except / /posts/hello-world/ <slug:slug> letters, digits, - , _ /posts/hello-world/ <uuid:id> a UUID /items/550e8400-.../
docs.title: URL Patterns

docs.text: # Illustration from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) # returns 404 if not found return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'body' : post . body })
docs.title: get_object_or_404

docs.text: With a class-based view, each HTTP method is its own method on the class. Django calls get() for GET requests, delete() for DELETE, and so on: # Illustration from django.views import View from django.http import HttpResponse , JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 class PostDetailView ( View ): def get ( self , request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) def delete ( self , request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) post . delete () return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) # 204 means "no content", so no body # Illustration (blog/urls.py) path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , PostDetailView . as_view ()),
docs.title: Class-Based Views (CBVs)

docs.text: Write a post_detail function-based view that handles: GET : return the post as JSON PUT : update title and body from the JSON request body DELETE : delete the post Use get_object_or_404 . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'PUT' , 'DELETE' ]) def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) if request . method == 'GET' : return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'body' : post . body }) if request . method == 'PUT' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post . title = data . get ( 'title' , post . title ) post . body = data . get ( 'body' , post . body ) post . save () return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) post . delete () # DELETE return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) Here is the full views.py and urls.py for this section. Compare how much code it takes; we'll replace all of it with a few lines of DRF in Section 6. # file: blog/views.py (Section 4 checkpoint: plain Django views) import json from django.http import HttpResponse , JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods from .models import Post def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'POST' ]) def post_list ( request ): if request . method == 'GET' : posts = list ( Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . values ( 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'author__username' , 'created_at' ) ) return JsonResponse ( posts , safe = False ) elif request . method == 'POST' : if not request . user . is_authenticated : return JsonResponse ({ 'error' : 'login required' }, status = 401 ) data = json . loads ( request . body ) post = Post . objects . create ( title = data [ 'title' ], slug = data [ 'slug' ], body = data [ 'body' ], author = request . user , ) return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }, status = 201 ) @csrf_exempt @require_http_methods ([ 'GET' , 'PUT' , 'DELETE' ]) def post_detail ( request , pk ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = pk ) if request . method == 'GET' : return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title , 'slug' : post . slug , 'body' : post . body , 'author' : post . author . username , 'published' : post . published , }) elif request . method == 'PUT' : data = json . loads ( request . body ) post . title = data . get ( 'title' , post . title ) post . body = data . get ( 'body' , post . body ) post . save () return JsonResponse ({ 'id' : post . id , 'title' : post . title }) elif request . method == 'DELETE' : post . delete () return HttpResponse ( status = 204 ) # file: blog/urls.py (Section 4 checkpoint) from django.urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health ), path ( 'posts/' , views . post_list ), # /api/posts/ path ( 'posts/<int:pk>/' , views . post_detail ), # /api/posts/42/ ] What just happened? post_list only lists published posts, and it uses .values(...) to get plain dicts that JsonResponse can serialise. A model object can't be turned into JSON directly, which is why post_detail builds its dict by hand. safe=False is needed because we return a list rather than a dict. Quick recap Function-based views branch on request.method ; class-based views have one method per HTTP verb. path('posts/<int:pk>/', view) captures part of the URL and passes it to the view. get_object_or_404 saves you the try/except for missing objects. Plain Django views mean manual JSON, manual validation and dealing with CSRF yourself. DRF fixes all three.
docs.title: Exercise 4: A Post Detail View

docs.text: Plain Django views work, but you write the JSON parsing, validation and serialisation by hand. Django REST Framework (DRF) gives you: Serializers : declare the fields once and get validation and JSON conversion Generic views / ViewSets : full CRUD in a few lines Browsable API : a clickable HTML page for every endpoint Authentication & permissions : ready-made classes you plug in
docs.title: Why DRF?

docs.text: A ModelSerializer builds its fields from a model. It plays the same role as the Pydantic ...Create / ...Response models in FastAPI, in one class: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) from rest_framework import serializers from .models import Post , Comment class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author' ] The inner Meta class connects the serializer to a model. fields lists the columns to include; read_only_fields are sent back to the client but can't be set by it.
docs.title: ModelSerializer

docs.text: Add validate_<field> methods for checks on one field, and validate for checks that involve several fields: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): title = serializers . CharField ( min_length = 5 , max_length = 200 ) class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author' ] def validate_slug ( self , value ): """Field-level validator.""" if ' ' in value : raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'Slug must not contain spaces.' ) return value def validate ( self , data ): """Object-level validator (runs after all fields pass).""" if data . get ( 'published' ) and not data . get ( 'body' ): raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'A published post must have a body.' ) return data When a check fails, DRF answers 400 Bad Request with the error message under the field name, for example {"slug": ["Slug must not contain spaces."]} .
docs.title: Validation

docs.text: A serializer can be used as a field inside another one. Here each post includes its full list of comments: # Illustration (blog/serializers.py) class CommentSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Comment fields = [ 'id' , 'body' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' ] class PostDetailSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): comments = CommentSerializer ( many = True , read_only = True ) # inline nested objects author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' , 'comments' ] source='author.username' reads a value through the relation, so the API shows "alice" instead of the author's id.
docs.title: Nested Serializers

docs.text: Add a comment_count field to PostSerializer that returns how many comments each post has. Use serializers.SerializerMethodField and write a get_comment_count method. Show solution # add to: blog/serializers.py (inside PostSerializer) comment_count = serializers . SerializerMethodField () def get_comment_count ( self , obj ): return obj . comments . count () # and add 'comment_count' to Meta.fields Here is the full serializers.py , including the exercise. PostDetailSerializer inherits from PostSerializer and just adds the comments, so the two never get out of step. # file: blog/serializers.py (Section 5 checkpoint) from rest_framework import serializers from .models import Post , Comment class CommentSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) class Meta : model = Comment fields = [ 'id' , 'body' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' ] class PostSerializer ( serializers . ModelSerializer ): author_username = serializers . CharField ( source = 'author.username' , read_only = True ) comment_count = serializers . SerializerMethodField () class Meta : model = Post fields = [ 'id' , 'title' , 'slug' , 'body' , 'published' , 'author_username' , 'created_at' , 'comment_count' , ] read_only_fields = [ 'id' , 'created_at' , 'author_username' , 'comment_count' ] def get_comment_count ( self , obj ): return obj . comments . count () def validate_slug ( self , value ): if ' ' in value : raise serializers . ValidationError ( 'Slug must not contain spaces.' ) return value class PostDetailSerializer ( PostSerializer ): """Extends PostSerializer with full comment list for detail views.""" comments = CommentSerializer ( many = True , read_only = True ) class Meta ( PostSerializer . Meta ): fields = PostSerializer . Meta . fields + [ 'comments' ] Quick recap A ModelSerializer turns model objects into JSON and validates incoming JSON. Meta.fields picks the columns; read_only_fields are output-only. validate_<field>() for one field, validate() for several. Raise serializers.ValidationError . source='author.username' and SerializerMethodField add computed fields.
docs.title: Exercise 5: Comment Count

docs.text: APIView is DRF's version of Django's View : one method per HTTP verb. On top of that, DRF parses JSON for you ( request.data ), turns Response objects into JSON, and runs authentication and permission checks. # Illustration (blog/views.py) from .models import Post from .serializers import PostSerializer from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework import status class PostListView ( APIView ): def get ( self , request ): posts = Post . objects . filter ( published = True ) serializer = PostSerializer ( posts , many = True ) return Response ( serializer . data ) def post ( self , request ): serializer = PostSerializer ( data = request . data ) if serializer . is_valid (): serializer . save ( author = request . user ) return Response ( serializer . data , status = status . HTTP_201_CREATED ) return Response ( serializer . errors , status = status . HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST )
docs.title: APIView

docs.text: A ViewSet puts all the operations for one resource in one class. A ModelViewSet gives you list , create , retrieve , update , partial_update and destroy without writing any of them: # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework import viewsets class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . all () serializer_class = PostSerializer
docs.title: ModelViewSet

docs.text: Give the ViewSet to a DefaultRouter and it creates all the URL patterns: # Illustration (blog/urls.py) from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter from . import views router = DefaultRouter () router . register ( 'posts' , views . PostViewSet , basename = 'post' ) urlpatterns = router . urls That one register call creates: URL Method Action /api/posts/ GET list /api/posts/ POST create /api/posts/{pk}/ GET retrieve /api/posts/{pk}/ PUT update /api/posts/{pk}/ PATCH partial_update /api/posts/{pk}/ DELETE destroy
docs.title: DRF Router

docs.text: For anything that isn't plain CRUD, add a method with @action . detail=True means it works on one object, so the URL includes the pk : # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework.decorators import action class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . all () serializer_class = PostSerializer @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): """POST /api/posts/{pk}/publish/ marks a post as published.""" post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' })
docs.title: Custom Actions with @action

docs.text: Add an @action called unpublish ( detail=True , methods=['post'] ) that sets post.published = False . Both /publish/ and /unpublish/ should work on the same ViewSet. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' })
docs.title: Exercise 6: Unpublish

docs.text: Replace blog/views.py and blog/urls.py with the two cells below. The comments live under each post ( /api/posts/1/comments/ ), which needs the drf-nested-routers package from the install command. Heads-up: until we add authentication in Section 7, you can read through the API but not create posts. perform_create saves self.request.user as the author, and an anonymous user can't be one, so a POST ends in a server error. That's exactly what the next section fixes. # file: blog/views.py (Section 6 checkpoint: DRF ViewSets) from django.http import JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from rest_framework import viewsets from rest_framework.decorators import action from rest_framework.response import Response from .models import Post , Comment from .serializers import PostSerializer , PostDetailSerializer , CommentSerializer def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () def get_serializer_class ( self ): # Use the detailed serializer (with comments) for single-object views if self . action == 'retrieve' : return PostDetailSerializer return PostSerializer def perform_create ( self , serializer ): # Automatically set the author to the authenticated user serializer . save ( author = self . request . user ) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' }) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' }) class CommentViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): serializer_class = CommentSerializer http_method_names = [ 'get' , 'post' , 'delete' , 'head' , 'options' ] def get_queryset ( self ): # Scope comments to the parent post return Comment . objects . filter ( post_id = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ] ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . order_by ( 'created_at' ) # oldest first def perform_create ( self , serializer ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ]) serializer . save ( author = self . request . user , post = post ) # file: blog/urls.py (Section 6 checkpoint: nested router) from django.urls import path from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter from rest_framework_nested import routers as nested_routers # pip install drf-nested-routers from . import views router = DefaultRouter () router . register ( 'posts' , views . PostViewSet , basename = 'post' ) # Nested: /api/posts/{post_pk}/comments/ posts_router = nested_routers . NestedDefaultRouter ( router , 'posts' , lookup = 'post' ) posts_router . register ( 'comments' , views . CommentViewSet , basename = 'post-comments' ) urlpatterns = [ path ( 'health/' , views . health )] + router . urls + posts_router . urls What just happened? get_serializer_class() picks the serializer per action: the detailed one (with comments) for a single post, the short one for lists. perform_create() is a hook DRF calls when saving a new object. We use it to fill in fields the client must not choose, like author . NestedDefaultRouter(router, 'posts', lookup='post') puts the comments URLs under a post, and passes the post's id to the view as self.kwargs['post_pk'] . CommentViewSet uses get_object_or_404 , so commenting on a post that doesn't exist gives 404 rather than a server error. It also sorts the comments ( order_by('created_at') ); Comment has no default ordering, and paginating an unsorted list makes DRF print a warning. Quick recap APIView : one method per verb, with request.data and Response doing the JSON work. ModelViewSet + DefaultRouter = full CRUD and all its URLs in a few lines. @action(detail=True, methods=['post']) adds extra endpoints like /publish/ . Override get_queryset , get_serializer_class and perform_create to customise a ViewSet.
docs.title: Section 6 Checkpoint

docs.text: Class How the client proves who it is SessionAuthentication Django session cookie (logging in through a browser) BasicAuthentication HTTP Basic: username and password on every request. Testing only. TokenAuthentication Authorization: Token <token> header JWTAuthentication (from djangorestframework-simplejwt ) Authorization: Bearer <jwt> header We'll use TokenAuthentication . It's like the API key from the FastAPI notebook: a random string stored in the database, one per user.
docs.title: DRF Authentication Classes

docs.text: Add this to the bottom of settings.py : # add to: blogplatform/settings.py REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication' , ], 'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly' , ], } Then run python manage.py migrate again. rest_framework.authtoken (which we added to INSTALLED_APPS in Section 1) brings its own table, authtoken_token . DRF also ships a ready-made view that swaps a username and password for a token. Add it to blogplatform/urls.py : # Illustration (blogplatform/urls.py; the final version is in Section 9) from rest_framework.authtoken import views as drf_auth_views urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), path ( 'api/auth/token/' , drf_auth_views . obtain_auth_token ), # POST {username, password} ]
docs.title: Setting Up Token Authentication

docs.text: Permission Effect AllowAny Everyone, logged in or not IsAuthenticated Must send a valid token / session IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly Anonymous users may only read (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) IsAdminUser request.user.is_staff must be True
docs.title: Built-in Permission Classes

docs.text: Only a post's author should be able to edit or delete it. Built-in classes can't know that, so we write our own: # file: blog/permissions.py from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission , SAFE_METHODS class IsOwnerOrReadOnly ( BasePermission ): """Write access only to the object's owner; read access for everyone.""" def has_object_permission ( self , request , view , obj ): if request . method in SAFE_METHODS : return True return obj . author == request . user has_object_permission runs when the view loads one specific object (retrieve, update, delete and our publish action). SAFE_METHODS is the tuple ('GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS') , the methods that don't change anything. Apply it to the ViewSet. DRF checks every class in the list, and all of them must agree: # Illustration (blog/views.py) from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly from .permissions import IsOwnerOrReadOnly class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] ...
docs.title: Custom Object-Level Permission

docs.text: DRF has no sign-up endpoint, so we write a small one. It creates the user and gives back a token straight away: # Illustration (blog/views.py; the full file is below) from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token from django.contrib.auth.models import User class RegisterView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [] # public endpoint def post ( self , request ): username = request . data . get ( 'username' ) password = request . data . get ( 'password' ) if not username or not password : return Response ({ 'error' : 'username and password required' }, status = 400 ) if User . objects . filter ( username = username ) . exists (): return Response ({ 'error' : 'username already taken' }, status = 400 ) user = User . objects . create_user ( username = username , password = password ) token = Token . objects . create ( user = user ) return Response ({ 'token' : token . key }, status = 201 ) permission_classes = [] overrides the default from settings.py , so anyone may call it. Otherwise nobody could register without already having a token.
docs.title: User Registration View

docs.text: Add a DELETE /api/auth/token/revoke/ endpoint that deletes the current user's token, so they have to log in again. It must require IsAuthenticated . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated class RevokeTokenView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ] def delete ( self , request ): request . user . auth_token . delete () return Response ( status = 204 ) # add to: blogplatform/urls.py (inside urlpatterns) # path('api/auth/token/revoke/', RevokeTokenView.as_view()), Here is the complete views.py with everything from Sections 6 and 7. Besides the new auth views, CommentViewSet now also uses IsOwnerOrReadOnly . Without it, any logged-in user could delete anyone else's comment. # file: blog/views.py (Section 7 checkpoint: full file) from django.http import JsonResponse from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404 from rest_framework import viewsets from rest_framework.decorators import action from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated , IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly from rest_framework.response import Response from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token from django.contrib.auth.models import User from .models import Post , Comment from .serializers import PostSerializer , PostDetailSerializer , CommentSerializer from .permissions import IsOwnerOrReadOnly def health ( request ): return JsonResponse ({ "status" : "ok" , "version" : "1.0.0" }) class PostViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): queryset = Post . objects . select_related ( 'author' ) . prefetch_related ( 'comments' ) . all () permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] def get_serializer_class ( self ): if self . action == 'retrieve' : return PostDetailSerializer return PostSerializer def perform_create ( self , serializer ): serializer . save ( author = self . request . user ) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'publish' ) def publish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = True post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'published' }) @action ( detail = True , methods = [ 'post' ], url_path = 'unpublish' ) def unpublish ( self , request , pk = None ): post = self . get_object () post . published = False post . save () return Response ({ 'status' : 'unpublished' }) class CommentViewSet ( viewsets . ModelViewSet ): serializer_class = CommentSerializer permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly , IsOwnerOrReadOnly ] http_method_names = [ 'get' , 'post' , 'delete' , 'head' , 'options' ] def get_queryset ( self ): return Comment . objects . filter ( post_id = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ] ) . select_related ( 'author' ) . order_by ( 'created_at' ) # oldest first def perform_create ( self , serializer ): post = get_object_or_404 ( Post , pk = self . kwargs [ 'post_pk' ]) serializer . save ( author = self . request . user , post = post ) class RegisterView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [] # public: anyone can register def post ( self , request ): username = request . data . get ( 'username' ) password = request . data . get ( 'password' ) if not username or not password : return Response ({ 'error' : 'username and password required' }, status = 400 ) if User . objects . filter ( username = username ) . exists (): return Response ({ 'error' : 'username already taken' }, status = 400 ) user = User . objects . create_user ( username = username , password = password ) token = Token . objects . create ( user = user ) return Response ({ 'token' : token . key }, status = 201 ) class RevokeTokenView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ] def delete ( self , request ): request . user . auth_token . delete () return Response ( status = 204 ) Quick recap Authentication answers "who are you?"; permissions answer "are you allowed?". Set defaults in REST_FRAMEWORK in settings.py ; override per view with permission_classes . Clients send Authorization: Token <key> . Get the key from /api/auth/token/ or /api/auth/register/ . Object-level rules ("only the author") go in has_object_permission .

docs.text: Django comes with a complete web admin site at /admin/ . You don't write any frontend code; you just register your models. python manage.py createsuperuser # creates an admin user python manage.py runserver # open http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/
docs.title: What Is the Admin?

docs.text: # Illustration (blog/admin.py, simplest version) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment admin . site . register ( Post ) admin . site . register ( Comment ) That's enough to get list, add, edit and delete pages for both models.
docs.title: Basic Registration

docs.text: A ModelAdmin class controls the columns, filters, search box and more. An inline shows related objects (here, a post's comments) on the same page: # Illustration (blog/admin.py) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment class CommentInline ( admin . TabularInline ): model = Comment extra = 0 # don't show blank rows by default readonly_fields = [ 'author' , 'created_at' ] @admin . register ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'title' , 'author' , 'published' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'published' , 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' , 'author__username' ] prepopulated_fields = { 'slug' : ( 'title' ,)} # auto-fills slug from title inlines = [ CommentInline ] actions = [ 'make_published' ] @admin . action ( description = 'Mark selected posts as published' ) def make_published ( self , request , queryset ): queryset . update ( published = True ) @admin.action(description=...) is the current way to name a bulk action. Older code sets make_published.short_description = ... after the function, which still works.
docs.title: Customising the Admin

docs.text: Option Effect list_display Columns shown in the list of objects list_filter Filter panel in the sidebar search_fields Adds a search box (uses LIKE queries) ordering Default sort order prepopulated_fields Fills one field from another as you type inlines Shows related objects on the same page actions Bulk actions in the list view readonly_fields Fields shown but not editable
docs.title: Common ModelAdmin Options

docs.text: Register Comment with a CommentAdmin that shows post , author and created_at as columns, can be filtered by created_at , and can be searched by body and author__username . (Remove the plain admin.site.register(Comment) line, since a model can only be registered once.) Show solution # add to: blog/admin.py @admin . register ( Comment ) class CommentAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'post' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'body' , 'author__username' ] # file: blog/admin.py (Section 8 checkpoint) from django.contrib import admin from .models import Post , Comment class CommentInline ( admin . TabularInline ): model = Comment extra = 0 readonly_fields = [ 'author' , 'created_at' ] @admin . register ( Post ) class PostAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'title' , 'author' , 'published' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'published' , 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' , 'author__username' ] prepopulated_fields = { 'slug' : ( 'title' ,)} inlines = [ CommentInline ] actions = [ 'make_published' ] @admin . action ( description = 'Mark selected posts as published' ) def make_published ( self , request , queryset ): queryset . update ( published = True ) @admin . register ( Comment ) class CommentAdmin ( admin . ModelAdmin ): list_display = [ 'post' , 'author' , 'created_at' ] list_filter = [ 'created_at' ] search_fields = [ 'body' , 'author__username' ] Quick recap python manage.py createsuperuser , then log in at /admin/ . @admin.register(Model) + a ModelAdmin class to customise the pages. list_display , list_filter , search_fields and inlines cover most needs.

Compared with Section 7 we've added SessionAuthentication (so you can log in to the browsable API) and pagination. # add to: blogplatform/settings.py (final version of the parts we changed) INSTALLED_APPS = [ 'django.contrib.admin' , 'django.contrib.auth' , 'django.contrib.contenttypes' , 'django.contrib.sessions' , 'django.contrib.messages' , 'django.contrib.staticfiles' , # third-party 'rest_framework' , 'rest_framework.authtoken' , # local 'blog' , ] REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.TokenAuthentication' , 'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication' , ], 'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly' , ], 'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS' : 'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination' , 'PAGE_SIZE' : 10 , }

docs.text: # file: blogplatform/urls.py (final) from django.contrib import admin from django.urls import path , include from rest_framework.authtoken import views as drf_auth_views from blog.views import RegisterView , RevokeTokenView urlpatterns = [ path ( 'admin/' , admin . site . urls ), path ( 'api/' , include ( 'blog.urls' )), path ( 'api/auth/register/' , RegisterView . as_view ()), path ( 'api/auth/token/' , drf_auth_views . obtain_auth_token ), path ( 'api/auth/token/revoke/' , RevokeTokenView . as_view ()), path ( 'api-auth/' , include ( 'rest_framework.urls' )), ]
docs.title: blogplatform/urls.py

docs.text: # Register curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/auth/register/ \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username": "alice", "password": "secret123"}' # -> {"token": "abc123..."} # Create a post (logged in) curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Hello Django", "slug": "hello-django", "body": "My first post!"}' # List posts (no login needed) curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ # Publish a post (only its author can) curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/1/publish/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' # Log out curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/auth/token/revoke/ \ -H 'Authorization: Token abc123...' Because pagination is switched on, the list endpoint now wraps the posts: {"count": 1, "next": null, "previous": null, "results": [...]} . You can also open http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/posts/ in the browser to use the browsable API. Log in with the link in the top-right corner (that's what api-auth/ is for). Quick recap INSTALLED_APPS lists DRF, the token app and our app; REST_FRAMEWORK sets auth, permission and pagination defaults. The project's urls.py mounts the admin, the app's API and the auth endpoints. With pagination on, list responses look like {count, next, previous, results} .

docs.text: Let clients filter the post list with ?published=true and ?author__username=alice , using the django-filter package (already in the install command). Hint: add 'django_filters' to INSTALLED_APPS , set DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS in REST_FRAMEWORK , and give PostViewSet a filterset_fields list. Show solution # add to: blogplatform/settings.py INSTALLED_APPS += [ 'django_filters' ] REST_FRAMEWORK [ 'DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS' ] = [ 'django_filters.rest_framework.DjangoFilterBackend' , ] # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) filterset_fields = [ 'published' , 'author__username' ]
docs.title: Practice 1: Filter Posts

docs.text: Add ?search=django (searches title and body) and ?ordering=title / ?ordering=-created_at to the post list, using DRF's SearchFilter and OrderingFilter . Show solution # add to: blog/views.py from django_filters.rest_framework import DjangoFilterBackend from rest_framework.filters import OrderingFilter , SearchFilter # inside PostViewSet filter_backends = [ DjangoFilterBackend , SearchFilter , OrderingFilter ] search_fields = [ 'title' , 'body' ] ordering_fields = [ 'created_at' , 'title' ] # Setting filter_backends on the view replaces the default list from settings, # which is why DjangoFilterBackend is listed again here.
docs.title: Practice 2: Search and Sort

docs.text: Add GET /api/posts/mine/ that returns only the logged-in user's posts, including unpublished ones. Anonymous users should get 401 . Hint: @action(detail=False, ...) makes an action on the collection, so there's no pk in the URL. Show solution # add to: blog/views.py (inside PostViewSet) @action ( detail = False , methods = [ 'get' ], permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated ]) def mine ( self , request ): posts = self . get_queryset () . filter ( author = request . user ) page = self . paginate_queryset ( posts ) serializer = self . get_serializer ( page , many = True ) return self . get_paginated_response ( serializer . data ) Quick recap filterset_fields (django-filter) gives exact-match filters with one line. SearchFilter and OrderingFilter add ?search= and ?ordering= . @action(detail=False) adds endpoints on the collection, like /api/posts/mine/ .
docs.title: Practice 3: My Posts

docs.text: Topic Remember this Project vs app A project is the configuration; apps hold the code. One project, many apps. Models Classes that map to tables. Fields are columns. Migrations makemigrations writes the change, migrate applies it. Always both. ORM Lazy, chainable QuerySets. select_related / prefetch_related avoid N+1 queries. Views Functions or classes that take an HttpRequest and return an HttpResponse . DRF serializers Declare fields once; get validation and JSON in both directions. ModelViewSet One class = full CRUD. Pair it with DefaultRouter for the URLs. @action Extra endpoints on a ViewSet ( /publish/ , /unpublish/ ). Permissions IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly + a custom IsOwnerOrReadOnly protect writes. Admin Register models and customise with ModelAdmin for a free management UI.

docs.text:
Event-Driven Programming in Python "Don't call us, we'll call you." (the Hollywood Principle, also known as Inversion of Control) In most programs you've written so far, you decide the order things happen. In an event-driven program, events decide: a button click, a message arriving, a timer going off. This notebook builds the idea up one step at a time, from plain callbacks to an event emitter, a home-made event loop, and finally Python's own asyncio . You already live in an event-driven world: You don't keep checking whether someone texted you. Your phone notifies you. A waiter doesn't ask "ready to order?" every second. You signal them. A fire alarm doesn't walk from room to room. The smoke triggers it. The idea is the same every time: react when something happens instead of constantly checking. Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Pass functions around as callbacks, including separate success and error callbacks Explain why deeply nested callbacks ("callback hell") are hard to work with Build an event emitter (the Observer pattern) and register listeners with a decorator Describe what an event loop does by building a small one yourself Write coroutines with async def / await and run them concurrently with asyncio.gather and asyncio.create_task Handle errors and timeouts in async code Use three common async patterns: an async event emitter, producer/consumer queues, and retry with backoff Prerequisites Python 3.10 or newer Functions, including *args , **kwargs and lambda Classes and OOP basics (see the OOP notebook) Decorators help, but aren't required How to Use This Notebook Run the cells from top to bottom . Later cells reuse things defined earlier, such as EventEmitter . The asyncio cells use await directly at the top level of a cell. That works in Jupyter. In a normal .py script you'd put the code in an async def main() and call asyncio.run(main()) . Some examples use random numbers or timings, so your output can differ a little from the saved output. That's expected. Try It cells are for you. Write your answer first, then open Show solution to compare. Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read only the recaps when revising before an exam. What We'll Cover Section Topic Main idea 1 Callbacks Functions that respond to events 2 Building an Event System The Observer pattern in action 3 The Event Loop The engine behind event-driven code 4 asyncio and async / await Python's built-in async framework 5 Real-World Patterns Putting it all together Warm-Up: Synchronous vs Event-Driven Thinking Two quick questions before any code. Think about your answer, then open it. Question 1: What's wrong with this restaurant? Synchronous Restaurant: 1. Waiter takes Order A 2. Waiter walks to kitchen, WAITS until food is cooked 3. Waiter delivers Order A 4. Waiter takes Order B 5. Waiter walks to kitchen, WAITS until food is cooked 6. Waiter delivers Order B Show answer The waiter is blocked . While waiting for one order, they can't serve anyone else. A real restaurant is event-driven: Waiter takes Order A, sends it to the kitchen Waiter takes Order B, sends it to the kitchen Waiter takes Order C, sends it to the kitchen Kitchen signals "Order A ready!", waiter delivers it Kitchen signals "Order C ready!", waiter delivers it Kitchen signals "Order B ready!", waiter delivers it The waiter reacts to events (food being ready) instead of standing still until each order is done. Question 2: Which of these are event-driven? A) A for loop that processes every item in a list B) A button click handler on a web page C) Reading a file line by line D) A chat app that shows messages when they arrive E) A security camera that records when motion is detected Show answer B, D and E are event-driven. B : the code waits for a click, then reacts. D : messages arrive as events, and the UI reacts by showing them. E : motion triggers an event, and recording is the reaction. A and C are sequential : they process things in a fixed order that the program decides. Quick recap Synchronous code does one thing at a time and waits (blocks) until each step is finished. Event-driven code reacts when something happens instead of waiting or constantly checking. 1. Callback Functions: The Building Block A callback is a function you hand to another function, so that it can be called back later, when something happens. You: "When the food is ready, call me back." Kitchen: "Sure. I'll call your function when it's done." This works because in Python functions are first-class objects : you can store them in variables and pass them around like any other value. # Functions are objects! You can assign them to variables, pass them around... def greet ( name ): return f "Hello, { name } !" # Assign a function to a variable (NO parentheses = the function itself) say_hello = greet print ( say_hello ( "Alice" )) # "Hello, Alice!" # Functions have attributes just like any object print ( f "Function name: { greet . __name__ } " ) print ( f "Type: { type ( greet ) } " ) print ( f "Same object? { say_hello is greet } " ) Hello, Alice! Function name: greet Type: <class 'function'> Same object? True Notice that say_hello = greet has no parentheses . We're not calling greet , we're giving the same function a second name. The () is what actually runs a function. 1.1 Your First Callback # A simple callback example: a function that "calls back" when it's done def download_file ( url , on_complete ): """Simulates downloading a file, then calls the callback.""" print ( f "Downloading from { url } ..." ) # Simulate the download result data = f "<contents of { url } >" # Call the callback with the result! on_complete ( data ) # Define what should happen when the download finishes def handle_download ( data ): print ( f "Download complete! Got: { data } " ) def save_to_disk ( data ): print ( f "Saving to disk: { data } " ) # Pass DIFFERENT callbacks to get DIFFERENT behaviors! download_file ( "https://example.com/file.txt" , handle_download ) print () download_file ( "https://example.com/file.txt" , save_to_disk ) Downloading from https://example.com/file.txt... Download complete! Got: <contents of https://example.com/file.txt> Downloading from https://example.com/file.txt... Saving to disk: <contents of https://example.com/file.txt> download_file doesn't know or care what on_complete does. It does its job and then calls whatever function it was given. Pass a different function and you get different behaviour, without changing download_file at all. That's separation of concerns : the downloader handles downloading, and the callback decides what to do with the result. 1.2 Callbacks with Lambda Functions For short, one-line callbacks you can use a lambda (a small function without a name) instead of a full def : def process_numbers ( numbers , transform ): """Apply a transformation callback to each number.""" return [ transform ( n ) for n in numbers ] nums = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] # Lambda callbacks for different transformations doubled = process_numbers ( nums , lambda x : x * 2 ) squared = process_numbers ( nums , lambda x : x ** 2 ) as_text = process_numbers ( nums , lambda x : f "# { x } " ) print ( f "Doubled: { doubled } " ) print ( f "Squared: { squared } " ) print ( f "As text: { as_text } " ) Doubled: [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] Squared: [1, 4, 9, 16, 25] As text: ['#1', '#2', '#3', '#4', '#5'] 1.3 Callbacks for Success and Failure Real operations can succeed or fail . A common pattern is to pass two callbacks: one for each outcome. import random def fetch_user ( user_id , on_success , on_error ): """Simulates fetching a user from a database.""" print ( f "Fetching user { user_id } ..." ) # Simulate random success/failure if random . random () > 0.3 : # 70% chance of success user = { "id" : user_id , "name" : "Alice" , "role" : "admin" } on_success ( user ) else : on_error ( f "User { user_id } not found in database" ) # Define our callbacks def handle_user ( user ): print ( f "Got user: { user [ 'name' ] } (role: { user [ 'role' ] } )" ) def handle_error ( error ): print ( f "ERROR: { error } " ) # Run it a few times to see both outcomes! for i in range ( 5 ): fetch_user ( 42 , handle_user , handle_error ) print () Fetching user 42... Got user: Alice (role: admin) Fetching user 42... Got user: Alice (role: admin) Fetching user 42... ERROR: User 42 not found in database Fetching user 42... Got user: Alice (role: admin) Fetching user 42... Got user: Alice (role: admin) Your output will differ each time you run this, because of random . The point is the split of jobs: fetch_user decides which callback to call, and the caller decides what each callback does. Try It: Callback Calculator Complete the calculate function below. It should: Run operation(a, b) Pass the answer to on_result Pass the error to on_error if something goes wrong (for example, dividing by zero) def calculate ( a , b , operation , on_result , on_error ): """Perform a calculation and call the appropriate callback.""" try : # YOUR CODE HERE: call the operation and pass result to on_result pass except Exception as e : # YOUR CODE HERE: pass the error to on_error pass # Test it! calculate ( 10 , 3 , lambda a , b : a + b , on_result = lambda r : print ( f "Result: { r } " ), on_error = lambda e : print ( f "Error: { e } " )) calculate ( 10 , 0 , lambda a , b : a / b , on_result = lambda r : print ( f "Result: { r } " ), on_error = lambda e : print ( f "Error: { e } " )) # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # got = [] # calculate(6, 7, lambda a, b: a * b, on_result=got.append, on_error=got.append) # assert got == [42] # calculate(1, 0, lambda a, b: a / b, on_result=got.append, on_error=got.append) # assert isinstance(got[-1], ZeroDivisionError) # print("✓ Callback calculator works!") Show solution def calculate ( a , b , operation , on_result , on_error ): try : result = operation ( a , b ) on_result ( result ) except Exception as e : on_error ( e ) 1.4 Callback Hell (The Problem) Callbacks are fine for one step. They get ugly when each step needs the result of the previous one, because every step has to be nested inside the one before: # Callback Hell: nested callbacks become hard to read and maintain def step1 ( callback ): print ( "Step 1: Authenticating..." ) callback ( "auth_token_123" ) def step2 ( token , callback ): print ( f "Step 2: Fetching data with { token } ..." ) callback ({ "users" : [ "Alice" , "Bob" ]}) def step3 ( data , callback ): print ( f "Step 3: Processing { len ( data [ 'users' ]) } users..." ) callback ( "done" ) # The "pyramid of doom" - each step nests inside the previous one step1 ( lambda token : step2 ( token , lambda data : step3 ( data , lambda result : print ( f "Final result: { result } " ) ) ) ) # Imagine 10 steps deep... This is called "Callback Hell" # async/await (Section 4) fixes this: the same steps read top to bottom. Step 1: Authenticating... Step 2: Fetching data with auth_token_123... Step 3: Processing 2 users... Final result: done Only three steps, and it's already hard to see what runs when. Each step lives inside the previous step's lambda, so the code drifts to the right like a pyramid. Add error handling at every level and it gets much worse. Keep this picture in mind: in Section 4 we'll write the same flow with async / await . Quick recap A callback is a function passed to another function, to be called later. Functions are objects: greet is the function itself, greet() calls it. Success/error callback pairs let the caller decide how to handle each outcome. Nesting many callbacks inside each other leads to "callback hell". 2. Building an Event System (Observer Pattern) One callback is useful, but real applications have many events , and each event can have many listeners . Let's build an event emitter : an object that lets you register callbacks for named events ( on ), and emits an event, calling every callback registered for it ( emit ). This is the Observer pattern . The emitter doesn't know who's listening; it just tells everyone who signed up. class EventEmitter : """A simple event system: register callbacks and emit events.""" def __init__ ( self ): self . _listeners = {} # {event_name: [list of callbacks]} def on ( self , event , callback ): """Register a callback for an event.""" if event not in self . _listeners : self . _listeners [ event ] = [] self . _listeners [ event ] . append ( callback ) return self # allows chaining: emitter.on('a', f).on('b', g) def emit ( self , event , * args , ** kwargs ): """Trigger an event, calling all registered callbacks.""" if event in self . _listeners : for callback in self . _listeners [ event ]: callback ( * args , ** kwargs ) def off ( self , event , callback ): """Remove a specific callback from an event.""" if event in self . _listeners : self . _listeners [ event ] . remove ( callback ) # Let's use it! emitter = EventEmitter () # Register multiple listeners for the same event emitter . on ( "user_login" , lambda user : print ( f "Welcome back, { user } !" )) emitter . on ( "user_login" , lambda user : print ( f "[LOG] { user } logged in" )) emitter . on ( "user_login" , lambda user : print ( f "[ANALYTICS] Login event for { user } " )) # One event triggers ALL registered callbacks! print ( "--- User logs in ---" ) emitter . emit ( "user_login" , "Alice" ) --- User logs in --- Welcome back, Alice! [LOG] Alice logged in [ANALYTICS] Login event for Alice Three listeners, one emit , three reactions. The code that emits "user_login" doesn't need to know anything about logging or analytics. Those parts of the program simply subscribe. 2.1 Real-World Example: Online Store Events class OnlineStore : """An online store powered by events.""" def __init__ ( self ): self . events = EventEmitter () self . inventory = { "laptop" : 5 , "phone" : 10 , "tablet" : 3 } self . revenue = 0 def purchase ( self , item , price ): if item not in self . inventory or self . inventory [ item ] <= 0 : self . events . emit ( "purchase_failed" , item , "Out of stock" ) return self . inventory [ item ] -= 1 self . revenue += price self . events . emit ( "purchase_complete" , item , price ) # Emit low stock warning if needed if self . inventory [ item ] <= 2 : self . events . emit ( "low_stock" , item , self . inventory [ item ]) # Create store and wire up event handlers store = OnlineStore () # Different parts of the system listen to different events store . events . on ( "purchase_complete" , lambda item , price : print ( f " Receipt: { item } purchased for $ { price } " )) store . events . on ( "purchase_complete" , lambda item , price : print ( f " [ANALYTICS] Sale: { item } @ $ { price } " )) store . events . on ( "purchase_failed" , lambda item , reason : print ( f " FAILED: { item } - { reason } " )) store . events . on ( "low_stock" , lambda item , qty : print ( f " WARNING: { item } is low! Only { qty } left!" )) # Simulate purchases print ( "Customer 1 buys a tablet:" ) store . purchase ( "tablet" , 499 ) print ( "

Only 2 left! Customer 2 buys a tablet: Receipt: tablet purchased for $499 [ANALYTICS] Sale: tablet @ $499 WARNING: tablet is low! Only 1 left! Receipts, analytics and warnings are wired up outside the class. To add, say, an email when stock runs low, you'd add one more store.events.on(...) line and leave OnlineStore untouched. Show solution class ChatRoom : def __init__ ( self , name ): self . name = name self . events = EventEmitter () self . users = [] def join ( self , username ): self . users . append ( username ) self . events . emit ( "user_joined" , username ) def send_message ( self , username , text ): self . events . emit ( "message" , username , text ) def leave ( self , username ): self . users . remove ( username ) self . events . emit ( "user_left" , username ) 2.2 Decorator Syntax for Event Registration Writing emitter.on("event", func) after every function gets repetitive. A decorator lets you register a function right where you define it: class DecoratorEventEmitter ( EventEmitter ): """EventEmitter with decorator support.""" def listener ( self , event ): """Decorator to register a function as an event listener.""" def decorator ( func ): self . on ( event , func ) return func return decorator # Now we can use @ syntax! server = DecoratorEventEmitter () @server . listener ( "request" ) def log_request ( method , path ): print ( f "[LOG] { method } { path } " ) @server . listener ( "request" ) def check_auth ( method , path ): if path . startswith ( "/admin" ): print ( f "[AUTH] Checking credentials for { path } " ) @server . listener ( "error" ) def handle_server_error ( code , message ): print ( f "[ERROR { code } ] { message } " ) # Simulate server events print ( "--- Normal request ---" ) server . emit ( "request" , "GET" , "/home" ) print ( " 
 --- Admin request ---" ) server . emit ( "request" , "POST" , "/admin/users" ) print ( " 
 --- Error ---" ) server . emit ( "error" , 404 , "Page not found" ) --- Normal request --- [LOG] GET /home --- Admin request --- [LOG] POST /admin/users [AUTH] Checking credentials for /admin/users --- Error --- [ERROR 404] Page not found @server.listener("request") calls server.on("request", log_request) for you and then returns the function unchanged, so log_request is still a normal function you can call yourself. Web frameworks such as Flask and FastAPI use exactly this trick to register routes ( @app.get("/") ). Quick recap An event emitter keeps a dictionary of event name -> list of callbacks . on() subscribes a callback, emit() calls every subscriber, off() unsubscribes. The code that emits an event doesn't need to know who is listening (loose coupling). A decorator can register a listener at the point where the function is defined. 3. The Event Loop: The Engine Behind It All An event loop is a loop that: waits for events to occur, sends each event to the right handler, and goes back to waiting. while running: event = wait_for_next_event() handler = find_handler(event) handler(event) Every GUI app, web server and game engine has one. Let's build a simple one. import time from collections import deque class SimpleEventLoop : """A minimal event loop to understand the concept.""" def __init__ ( self ): self . _queue = deque () # Events waiting to be processed self . _handlers = {} # {event_type: handler_function} self . _running = False self . _timers = [] # Scheduled events def register ( self , event_type , handler ): """Register a handler for an event type.""" self . _handlers [ event_type ] = handler def post ( self , event_type , data = None ): """Add an event to the queue.""" self . _queue . append (( event_type , data )) def schedule ( self , delay , event_type , data = None ): """Schedule an event for the future.""" fire_at = time . time () + delay self . _timers . append (( fire_at , event_type , data )) self . _timers . sort ( key = lambda t : t [ 0 ]) # Keep sorted by time def run ( self ): """Run the event loop until no events remain.""" self . _running = True print ( "Event loop started!" ) while self . _running : # Check if any timers have fired now = time . time () while self . _timers and self . _timers [ 0 ][ 0 ] <= now : _ , event_type , data = self . _timers . pop ( 0 ) self . _queue . append (( event_type , data )) # Process one event from the queue if self . _queue : event_type , data = self . _queue . popleft () if event_type == "__STOP__" : self . _running = False print ( "Event loop stopped!" ) break handler = self . _handlers . get ( event_type ) if handler : handler ( data ) else : print ( f "No handler for event: { event_type } " ) # If nothing to do right now but timers pending, wait a bit elif self . _timers : time . sleep ( 0.01 ) else : # No events, no timers: we're done break print ( "Event loop finished." ) # Create and configure our event loop loop = SimpleEventLoop () loop . register ( "greet" , lambda data : print ( f " Hello, { data } !" )) loop . register ( "alarm" , lambda data : print ( f " ALARM: { data } " )) loop . register ( "tick" , lambda data : print ( f " Tick # { data } " )) # Queue up some events loop . post ( "greet" , "Alice" ) loop . post ( "greet" , "Bob" ) loop . post ( "tick" , 1 ) # Schedule a delayed event (0.5 seconds from now) loop . schedule ( 0.5 , "alarm" , "Wake up!" ) loop . schedule ( 0.3 , "tick" , 2 ) # Run it! loop . run () Event loop started! Hello, Alice! Hello, Bob! Tick #1 Tick #2 ALARM: Wake up! Event loop finished. Look at the order. The three posted events run first, in the order they were queued. The scheduled events wait until their time comes, so Tick #2 (0.3 s) fires before the alarm (0.5 s), even though the alarm was scheduled first. When the queue is empty and no timers are left, the loop ends. (You could also stop it early by posting a "__STOP__" event.) How This Connects to asyncio Our SimpleEventLoop is a toy version of what Python's asyncio does for real: Our SimpleEventLoop asyncio loop.post(event) puts work in the queue asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules a coroutine Handlers run when their event comes up Coroutines resume when what they're waiting for is ready loop.schedule(delay, ...) asyncio.sleep(delay) and other timers loop.run() asyncio.run(main()) The event queue The loop's internal queue of ready work One big difference: our handlers always run from start to finish. An asyncio coroutine can pause in the middle at an await and let other code run. That's what we'll look at next. Quick recap An event loop repeatedly takes the next event and runs its handler. Events can be queued straight away or scheduled for later with a timer. asyncio is a production-quality event loop; coroutines are what it runs. 4. asyncio : Python's Async Framework asyncio is Python's built-in library for writing concurrent code with the async / await syntax. "Concurrent" here means many tasks make progress during the same period of time, by taking turns while the others are waiting. Key Vocabulary Term What it means Analogy Coroutine A function that can pause and resume A bookmark in a book async def Defines a coroutine function "This function can pause" await Pause here until the result is ready "I'll wait here, others can go ahead" Event loop Schedules and runs coroutines The restaurant manager Task A coroutine scheduled to run concurrently An order ticket 4.1 Your First Coroutine import asyncio # A coroutine is defined with 'async def' async def say_hello ( name , delay ): print ( f "Hello, { name } ! (waiting { delay } s...)" ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) # Non-blocking pause! print ( f "Goodbye, { name } ! (after { delay } s)" ) return f " { name } done" # In Jupyter, we can use 'await' directly at the top level result = await say_hello ( "Alice" , 1 ) print ( f "Result: { result } " ) Hello, Alice! (waiting 1s...) Goodbye, Alice! (after 1s) Result: Alice done 4.2 await vs No await The most common beginner mistake: forgetting await . What happens then? async def greet (): return "Hello!" # WITHOUT await: you get a coroutine OBJECT, not the result! result_wrong = greet () print ( f "Without await: { result_wrong } " ) print ( f "Type: { type ( result_wrong ) } " ) # WITH await: you get the actual return value result_right = await greet () print ( f " 
 With await: { result_right } " ) print ( f "Type: { type ( result_right ) } " ) # Clean up the unawaited coroutine result_wrong . close () Without await: <coroutine object greet at 0x10bd8ac80> Type: <class 'coroutine'> With await: Hello! Type: <class 'str'> Calling an async def function does not run it. It only builds a coroutine object, like a recipe that hasn't been cooked yet. await is what actually runs it and hands you the return value. The .close() at the end tidies up the coroutine we never ran, so Python doesn't warn about it. Now remember the pyramid from Section 1.4? Here are the same three steps written with async / await : # The callback-hell example from Section 1.4, rewritten with async/await async def authenticate (): print ( "Step 1: Authenticating..." ) return "auth_token_123" async def fetch_data ( token ): print ( f "Step 2: Fetching data with { token } ..." ) return { "users" : [ "Alice" , "Bob" ]} async def process ( data ): print ( f "Step 3: Processing { len ( data [ 'users' ]) } users..." ) return "done" token = await authenticate () data = await fetch_data ( token ) result = await process ( data ) print ( f "Final result: { result } " ) Step 1: Authenticating... Step 2: Fetching data with auth_token_123... Step 3: Processing 2 users... Final result: done Same steps, same output, but each step is one line and the code reads top to bottom. You could also wrap all three lines in a single try/except to handle errors, which is very awkward with nested callbacks. 4.3 Running Tasks Concurrently with asyncio.gather Here's where async really pays off: doing several things during the same wait. import asyncio import time async def make_coffee ( order ): print ( f " Starting coffee: { order } " ) await asyncio . sleep ( 2 ) # Takes 2 seconds print ( f " Coffee ready: { order } " ) return f " { order } (hot)" # SEQUENTIAL: One at a time (slow!) print ( "=== Sequential (one at a time) ===" ) start = time . time () coffee1 = await make_coffee ( "Espresso" ) coffee2 = await make_coffee ( "Latte" ) coffee3 = await make_coffee ( "Cappuccino" ) print ( f "Total time: { time . time () - start : .1f } s" ) print ( f "Orders: { [ coffee1 , coffee2 , coffee3 ] } " ) print ( " 
 === Concurrent (all at once!) ===" ) start = time . time () # asyncio.gather runs all coroutines concurrently! results = await asyncio . gather ( make_coffee ( "Espresso" ), make_coffee ( "Latte" ), make_coffee ( "Cappuccino" ), ) print ( f "Total time: { time . time () - start : .1f } s" ) print ( f "Orders: { results } " ) === Sequential (one at a time) === Starting coffee: Espresso Coffee ready: Espresso Starting coffee: Latte Coffee ready: Latte Starting coffee: Cappuccino Coffee ready: Cappuccino Total time: 6.0s Orders: ['Espresso (hot)', 'Latte (hot)', 'Cappuccino (hot)'] === Concurrent (all at once!) === Starting coffee: Espresso Starting coffee: Latte Starting coffee: Cappuccino Coffee ready: Espresso Coffee ready: Latte Coffee ready: Cappuccino Total time: 2.0s Orders: ['Espresso (hot)', 'Latte (hot)', 'Cappuccino (hot)'] Sequential : about 6 seconds (2 + 2 + 2) Concurrent : about 2 seconds, because all three coffees wait at the same time While one coroutine is sleeping (in real code: waiting for the network or the disk), the event loop runs the others. gather returns the results in the same order you passed the coroutines in. 4.4 asyncio.create_task : Start Now, Collect Later gather starts coroutines and waits for them in one go. create_task splits that into two steps: it schedules a coroutine to start as soon as the event loop gets a chance , and gives you back a Task object you can await later. async def background_job ( name , duration ): print ( f " [ { name } ] Started" ) await asyncio . sleep ( duration ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Finished after { duration } s" ) return name async def main (): print ( "Creating tasks..." ) # create_task schedules the coroutine to run WITHOUT waiting task1 = asyncio . create_task ( background_job ( "Backup" , 2 )) task2 = asyncio . create_task ( background_job ( "Email" , 1 )) task3 = asyncio . create_task ( background_job ( "Report" , 3 )) print ( "Tasks created! Doing other work..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( "Still working..." ) # Now wait for all tasks to finish results = await asyncio . gather ( task1 , task2 , task3 ) print ( f " 
 All done! Completed: { results } " ) await main () Creating tasks... Tasks created! Doing other work... [Backup] Started [Email] Started [Report] Started Still working... [Email] Finished after 1s [Backup] Finished after 2s [Report] Finished after 3s All done! Completed: ['Backup', 'Email', 'Report'] Look at the output order. "Tasks created! Doing other work..." is printed before any task starts. Creating a task only schedules it; the tasks actually start at the next await ( asyncio.sleep(0.5) ), when main hands control back to the event loop. Always keep a reference to the tasks you create (here task1 , task2 , task3 ) and await them at some point. The event loop only keeps a weak reference to a task, so a task nobody refers to can disappear before it finishes. 4.5 Error Handling in Async Code async def risky_operation ( name , should_fail = False ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) if should_fail : raise ConnectionError ( f " { name } : Connection refused!" ) return f " { name } : Success!" # Method 1: try/except (just like sync code!) print ( "=== try/except ===" ) try : result = await risky_operation ( "API Call" , should_fail = True ) except ConnectionError as e : print ( f "Caught error: { e } " ) # Method 2: gather with return_exceptions=True print ( " 
 === gather with return_exceptions ===" ) results = await asyncio . gather ( risky_operation ( "Task A" , should_fail = False ), risky_operation ( "Task B" , should_fail = True ), risky_operation ( "Task C" , should_fail = False ), return_exceptions = True # Don't let one failure crash everything ) for r in results : if isinstance ( r , Exception ): print ( f " FAILED: { r } " ) else : print ( f " OK: { r } " ) === try/except === Caught error: API Call: Connection refused! === gather with return_exceptions === OK: Task A: Success! FAILED: Task B: Connection refused! OK: Task C: Success! Without return_exceptions=True , the first exception would be raised straight out of gather and you wouldn't get the other results back. With it, each exception is returned in the results list in its normal position, so you can check every result one by one. 4.6 Timeouts: Don't Wait Forever async def slow_api_call (): """Simulates a very slow API.""" print ( "Calling slow API..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 10 ) # This takes 10 seconds! return "data" # Use asyncio.wait_for to set a timeout try : result = await asyncio . wait_for ( slow_api_call (), timeout = 2.0 ) print ( f "Got: { result } " ) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( "Timed out after 2 seconds! The API was too slow." ) Calling slow API... Timed out after 2 seconds! The API was too slow. wait_for cancels slow_api_call when the 2 seconds are up, so this cell takes about 2 seconds, not 10. (Since Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is just another name for the built-in TimeoutError .)
