docs.title: Quick Mental Exercise

docs.text: Whenever you design a program with classes, ask these four questions: What things exist? Those become classes. What does each thing know? Those become attributes. What can each thing do? Those become methods. How are the things connected? That tells you whether to use composition or inheritance. Keep these questions in mind; we'll answer them again in the mini-project at the end.
docs.title: From the Real World to Code

docs.text: Everything in Python is an object: numbers, strings, lists, functions, even classes. Before writing our own classes, we need to be clear about how Python stores objects and what a variable really is. A variable is a name that points to an object . Two names can point to the same object. # Object Identity: Every object has a unique ID a = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] b = a # b references the SAME object as a c = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] # c is a NEW object with same content print ( f "a = { a } " ) print ( f "b = { b } " ) print ( f "c = { c } " ) print () print ( f "id(a) = { id ( a ) } " ) print ( f "id(b) = { id ( b ) } " ) print ( f "id(c) = { id ( c ) } " ) print () print ( f "a is b: { a is b } " ) # True - same object print ( f "a is c: { a is c } " ) # False - different objects print ( f "a == c: { a == c } " ) # True - equal values a = [1, 2, 3] b = [1, 2, 3] c = [1, 2, 3] id(a) = 4459232064 id(b) = 4459232064 id(c) = 4459126144 a is b: True a is c: False a == c: True a and b are two names for one list, so they have the same id . c looks the same but is a separate list. That's the difference between is (same object?) and == (same value?). # Mutability: Lists are mutable, strings/tuples are not my_list = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] original_id = id ( my_list ) my_list . append ( 4 ) # Modifies in place print ( f "After append: { my_list } " ) print ( f "Same object? { id ( my_list ) == original_id } " ) # True! # Contrast with strings (immutable) my_string = "hello" string_id = id ( my_string ) my_string = my_string + " world" # Creates NEW object print ( f " \n After concatenation: { my_string } " ) print ( f "Same object? { id ( my_string ) == string_id } " ) # False! After append: [1, 2, 3, 4] Same object? True After concatenation: hello world Same object? False A list can be changed in place , so it keeps its identity. A string can't be changed, so + builds a brand-new string and the name now points to that. This matters for functions too. Default argument values are created once , when the function is defined, so a mutable default gets shared between calls: # Reference traps: Mutable default arguments def add_item_bad ( item , items = []): """BAD: Default list is shared across calls!""" items . append ( item ) return items def add_item_good ( item , items = None ): """GOOD: Create new list if not provided.""" if items is None : items = [] items . append ( item ) return items # Watch the difference print ( "Bad function:" ) print ( add_item_bad ( "a" )) # ['a'] print ( add_item_bad ( "b" )) # ['a', 'b'] - Oops! print ( " \n Good function:" ) print ( add_item_good ( "a" )) # ['a'] print ( add_item_good ( "b" )) # ['b'] - Correct! Bad function: ['a'] ['a', 'b'] Good function: ['a'] ['b']
docs.title: 1. Quick Warm-Up: Object Identity, Mutability & References

docs.text: Write down what you think will be printed, then run the cell to check. # Try to predict before running! x = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] y = x x . append ( 4 ) y = y + [ 5 ] print ( f "x = { x } " ) print ( f "y = { y } " ) print ( f "x is y: { x is y } " ) # Why are they different? # Hint: x.append() modifies in place, y + [5] creates a new list x = [1, 2, 3, 4] y = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] x is y: False Quick recap A variable is a name pointing to an object. is checks for the same object; == checks for equal values. Lists, dicts and sets are mutable (change in place). Strings, numbers and tuples are immutable . Never use [] or {} as a default argument. Use None and create the object inside the function.

docs.text: A class is a blueprint. An object (also called an instance ) is one thing built from that blueprint. One Student class, many student objects.
docs.title: 2. Classes & Objects

docs.text: When you write Student("Alice", ...) , Python creates an empty object and immediately calls __init__ on it. self is that new object, so self.name = name stores the name on that particular student . class Student : """Represents a student enrolled in a course.""" def __init__ ( self , name : str , student_id : str , gpa : float = 0.0 ): """ Initialize a new Student instance. Args: name: Student's full name student_id: Unique identifier gpa: Grade point average (default 0.0) """ self . name = name # Instance attribute self . student_id = student_id # Instance attribute self . gpa = gpa # Instance attribute with default def is_honor_roll ( self ) -> bool : """Check if student qualifies for honor roll.""" return self . gpa >= 3.5 # Creating instances alice = Student ( "Alice Johnson" , "STU001" , 3.8 ) bob = Student ( "Bob Smith" , "STU002" , 2.9 ) print ( f " { alice . name } (GPA: { alice . gpa } )" ) print ( f "Honor roll? { alice . is_honor_roll () } " ) print () print ( f " { bob . name } (GPA: { bob . gpa } )" ) print ( f "Honor roll? { bob . is_honor_roll () } " ) Alice Johnson (GPA: 3.8) Honor roll? True Bob Smith (GPA: 2.9) Honor roll? False
docs.title: 2.1 The __init__ Method and Instance Attributes

docs.text: Instance attributes (set on self ) belong to one object. Alice's balance is not Bob's balance. Class attributes (written directly in the class body) are shared by every object of that class. class BankAccount : """A simple bank account with class-level tracking.""" # Class attributes: shared by ALL instances bank_name = "Python National Bank" total_accounts = 0 def __init__ ( self , owner : str , balance : float = 0.0 ): # Instance attributes: unique to each instance self . owner = owner self . balance = balance self . account_number = BankAccount . total_accounts + 1 # Increment class attribute BankAccount . total_accounts += 1 def deposit ( self , amount : float ) -> None : """Add money to the account.""" if amount > 0 : self . balance += amount # Create accounts acc1 = BankAccount ( "Alice" , 1000 ) acc2 = BankAccount ( "Bob" , 500 ) print ( f "Bank: { BankAccount . bank_name } " ) # Access via class print ( f "Total accounts: { BankAccount . total_accounts } " ) print () print ( f "Account { acc1 . account_number } : { acc1 . owner } - $ { acc1 . balance } " ) print ( f "Account { acc2 . account_number } : { acc2 . owner } - $ { acc2 . balance } " ) # Both instances share the same class attribute assert acc1 . bank_name == acc2 . bank_name == BankAccount . bank_name print ( " \n ✓ Class attribute shared correctly" ) Bank: Python National Bank Total accounts: 2 Account 1: Alice - $1000 Account 2: Bob - $500 ✓ Class attribute shared correctly
docs.title: 2.2 Class Attributes vs Instance Attributes

docs.text: Python classes can have three kinds of methods: Kind First parameter Use it when... Instance method self the method needs this object's data (most methods) Class method ( @classmethod ) cls the method works with the class itself, e.g. an alternative way to create objects Static method ( @staticmethod ) none it's a helper that belongs with the class but needs no object or class data import datetime class Employee : """Demonstrates different method types.""" company = "Tech Corp" employee_count = 0 def __init__ ( self , name : str , hire_year : int ): self . name = name self . hire_year = hire_year Employee . employee_count += 1 # Instance method: operates on self def years_employed ( self ) -> int : """Calculate years with company.""" return datetime . date . today () . year - self . hire_year # Class method: operates on class, not instance @classmethod def get_company_info ( cls ) -> str : """Return company information.""" return f " { cls . company } - { cls . employee_count } employees" # Alternative constructor using classmethod @classmethod def from_string ( cls , data : str ) -> "Employee" : """Create employee from 'name,year' string.""" name , year = data . split ( "," ) return cls ( name . strip (), int ( year . strip ())) # Static method: utility function, no self or cls @staticmethod def is_valid_year ( year : int ) -> bool : """Check if hire year is reasonable.""" current_year = datetime . date . today () . year return 1990 <= year <= current_year # Using instance method emp1 = Employee ( "Alice" , 2020 ) print ( f " { emp1 . name } - { emp1 . years_employed () } years employed" ) # Using class method print ( Employee . get_company_info ()) # Using classmethod as alternative constructor emp2 = Employee . from_string ( "Bob, 2022" ) print ( f "Created from string: { emp2 . name } ( { emp2 . hire_year } )" ) # Using static method print ( f "Is 2020 valid? { Employee . is_valid_year ( 2020 ) } " ) print ( f "Is 1800 valid? { Employee . is_valid_year ( 1800 ) } " ) Alice - 6 years employed Tech Corp - 1 employees Created from string: Bob (2022) Is 2020 valid? True Is 1800 valid? False
docs.title: 2.3 Methods: Instance, Class, and Static

docs.text: __repr__ : Unambiguous representation for developers (debugging) __str__ : Readable representation for users (display) print() and f-strings use __str__ . The interactive shell, the debugger and lists use __repr__ . Rule of thumb: __repr__ should look like the code that would recreate the object. class Point : """A 2D point with proper string representations.""" def __init__ ( self , x : float , y : float ): self . x = x self . y = y def __repr__ ( self ) -> str : """Developer representation - can recreate object.""" return f "Point( { self . x } , { self . y } )" def __str__ ( self ) -> str : """User-friendly representation.""" return f "( { self . x } , { self . y } )" p = Point ( 3.5 , 4.2 ) print ( f "repr: { repr ( p ) } " ) # Point(3.5, 4.2) print ( f "str: { str ( p ) } " ) # (3.5, 4.2) print ( f "print: { p } " ) # Uses __str__ # In a list, __repr__ is used points = [ Point ( 1 , 2 ), Point ( 3 , 4 )] print ( f "List: { points } " ) repr: Point(3.5, 4.2) str: (3.5, 4.2) print: (3.5, 4.2) List: [Point(1, 2), Point(3, 4)]
docs.title: 2.4 __repr__ vs __str__

docs.text: Create a Book class with: title , author and pages as instance attributes total_books as a class attribute that counts how many books have been created a __repr__ that returns Book('Title', 'Author', pages) an is_long() method that returns True if the book has more than 300 pages # Your code here: class Book : total_books = 0 def __init__ ( self , title : str , author : str , pages : int ): # TODO: Initialize attributes pass def __repr__ ( self ) -> str : # TODO: Return representation pass def is_long ( self ) -> bool : # TODO: Check if pages > 300 pass # Test your implementation: # book1 = Book("Python Crash Course", "Eric Matthes", 544) # book2 = Book("Clean Code", "Robert Martin", 464) # print(book1) # print(f"Is long? {book1.is_long()}") # print(f"Total books: {Book.total_books}") Show solution class Book : total_books = 0 def __init__ ( self , title : str , author : str , pages : int ): self . title = title self . author = author self . pages = pages Book . total_books += 1 def __repr__ ( self ) -> str : return f "Book( { self . title !r} , { self . author !r} , { self . pages } )" def is_long ( self ) -> bool : return self . pages > 300 Quick recap A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it. __init__ runs when an object is created and stores its data on self . Instance attributes belong to one object; class attributes are shared by all objects. Instance methods get self , class methods get cls , static methods get neither. __str__ is for users, __repr__ is for developers.
docs.title: Try It: Create a Book Class

docs.text: Encapsulation means keeping an object's data and the code that works on it together, and controlling how that data can be changed from outside. Python doesn't have true private like Java. It relies on naming conventions instead: Name Meaning balance Public. Anyone can read and change it. _balance Internal. "Please don't touch this from outside." Python won't stop you; it's a convention. __balance Name-mangled to _ClassName__balance to avoid clashes in subclasses. Rarely needed.
docs.title: 3. Encapsulation & Properties

docs.text: A property looks like a normal attribute to whoever uses the class, but behind the scenes it runs a method. That lets you add validation or calculations without changing how the attribute is used. class Temperature : """Temperature with validation using properties.""" def __init__ ( self , celsius : float = 0.0 ): self . _celsius = celsius # Protected attribute @property def celsius ( self ) -> float : """Get temperature in Celsius.""" return self . _celsius @celsius . setter def celsius ( self , value : float ) -> None : """Set temperature with validation.""" if value < - 273.15 : raise ValueError ( "Temperature below absolute zero is not possible" ) self . _celsius = value @property def fahrenheit ( self ) -> float : """Get temperature in Fahrenheit (computed property).""" return self . _celsius * 9 / 5 + 32 @fahrenheit . setter def fahrenheit ( self , value : float ) -> None : """Set temperature via Fahrenheit.""" self . celsius = ( value - 32 ) * 5 / 9 # Uses celsius setter validation # Usage looks like simple attributes temp = Temperature ( 25 ) print ( f "Celsius: { temp . celsius } °C" ) print ( f "Fahrenheit: { temp . fahrenheit } °F" ) temp . fahrenheit = 98.6 print ( f " \n After setting to 98.6°F:" ) print ( f "Celsius: { temp . celsius : .1f } °C" ) # Validation works try : temp . celsius = - 300 except ValueError as e : print ( f " \n ✓ Validation error: { e } " ) Celsius: 25°C Fahrenheit: 77.0°F After setting to 98.6°F: Celsius: 37.0°C ✓ Validation error: Temperature below absolute zero is not possible temp.fahrenheit is never stored anywhere. It's calculated from _celsius every time you read it. And because the Fahrenheit setter goes through the Celsius setter, the absolute-zero check protects both.
docs.title: 3.1 The @property Decorator

docs.text: Properties are a good place to enforce rules about your data. If every change goes through a setter, invalid data can never get into the object, not even through __init__ . class User : """User with validated email and age.""" def __init__ ( self , username : str , email : str , age : int ): self . username = username self . email = email # Uses setter self . age = age # Uses setter @property def email ( self ) -> str : return self . _email @email . setter def email ( self , value : str ) -> None : if "@" not in value or "." not in value . split ( "@" )[ - 1 ]: raise ValueError ( f "Invalid email format: { value } " ) self . _email = value . lower () . strip () @property def age ( self ) -> int : return self . _age @age . setter def age ( self , value : int ) -> None : if not isinstance ( value , int ): raise TypeError ( "Age must be an integer" ) if not 0 <= value <= 150 : raise ValueError ( "Age must be between 0 and 150" ) self . _age = value @property def is_adult ( self ) -> bool : """Read-only computed property.""" return self . _age >= 18 # Valid user user = User ( "alice" , "Alice@Example.COM" , 25 ) print ( f "Username: { user . username } " ) print ( f "Email: { user . email } " ) # Normalized to lowercase print ( f "Age: { user . age } " ) print ( f "Is adult: { user . is_adult } " ) # Test validations test_cases = [ ( "invalid_email" , "bademail" , 20 ), ( "invalid_age_type" , "valid@email.com" , "twenty" ), ( "invalid_age_range" , "valid@email.com" , - 5 ), ] print ( " \n Validation tests:" ) for name , email , age in test_cases : try : User ( name , email , age ) except ( ValueError , TypeError ) as e : print ( f " ✓ { name } : { e } " ) Username: alice Email: alice@example.com Age: 25 Is adult: True Validation tests: ✓ invalid_email: Invalid email format: bademail ✓ invalid_age_type: Age must be an integer ✓ invalid_age_range: Age must be between 0 and 150 Quick recap A leading underscore ( _name ) means "internal". It's a convention, not a lock. @property runs code when an attribute is read; @x.setter runs code when it's assigned. Put validation in setters, and assign through them in __init__ , so bad data never gets in.
docs.title: 3.2 Validation Rules with Properties

docs.text: Inheritance lets a new class (the child ) reuse everything from an existing class (the parent ) and add or change only what's different. Polymorphism means you can call the same method on different kinds of objects and each one does the right thing for itself. In the loop below, describe() doesn't care whether it's dealing with a rectangle or a circle. Shape is an abstract base class ( ABC ): you can't create a plain Shape , and every child must implement the methods marked @abstractmethod .
docs.title: 4. Inheritance & Polymorphism

docs.text: import math from abc import ABC , abstractmethod class Shape ( ABC ): """Abstract base class for shapes.""" def __init__ ( self , name : str ): self . name = name @abstractmethod def area ( self ) -> float : """Calculate and return the area.""" pass @abstractmethod def perimeter ( self ) -> float : """Calculate and return the perimeter.""" pass def describe ( self ) -> str : """Common method for all shapes.""" return f " { self . name } : area= { self . area () : .2f } , perimeter= { self . perimeter () : .2f } " class Rectangle ( Shape ): """Rectangle implementation.""" def __init__ ( self , width : float , height : float ): super () . __init__ ( "Rectangle" ) # Call parent __init__ self . width = width self . height = height def area ( self ) -> float : return self . width * self . height def perimeter ( self ) -> float : return 2 * ( self . width + self . height ) class Circle ( Shape ): """Circle implementation.""" def __init__ ( self , radius : float ): super () . __init__ ( "Circle" ) self . radius = radius def area ( self ) -> float : return math . pi * self . radius ** 2 def perimeter ( self ) -> float : return 2 * math . pi * self . radius # Polymorphism in action: same interface, different implementations shapes = [ Rectangle ( 5 , 3 ), Circle ( 4 ), Rectangle ( 2 , 2 )] for shape in shapes : print ( shape . describe ()) # Verify inheritance rect = Rectangle ( 10 , 5 ) print ( f " \n Is Rectangle a Shape? { isinstance ( rect , Shape ) } " ) print ( f "Is Rectangle a Rectangle? { isinstance ( rect , Rectangle ) } " ) Rectangle: area=15.00, perimeter=16.00 Circle: area=50.27, perimeter=25.13 Rectangle: area=4.00, perimeter=8.00 Is Rectangle a Shape? True Is Rectangle a Rectangle? True
docs.title: 4.1 Base Class and Child Class

docs.text: A child class can override a parent method (replace it completely) or extend it (call the parent's version with super() and add to it). class Vehicle : """Base class for vehicles.""" def __init__ ( self , brand : str , model : str , year : int ): self . brand = brand self . model = model self . year = year def start ( self ) -> str : return f "Starting { self . brand } { self . model } " def info ( self ) -> str : return f " { self . year } { self . brand } { self . model } " class ElectricCar ( Vehicle ): """Electric car with battery.""" def __init__ ( self , brand : str , model : str , year : int , battery_kwh : float ): super () . __init__ ( brand , model , year ) # Call parent __init__ self . battery_kwh = battery_kwh def start ( self ) -> str : # Override parent method return f "🔋 Silently starting { self . brand } { self . model } " def info ( self ) -> str : # Extend parent method base_info = super () . info () # Get parent's info return f " { base_info } (Electric, { self . battery_kwh } kWh)" def charge ( self , kwh : float ) -> str : """New method specific to ElectricCar.""" return f "Charging { kwh } kWh" # Regular vehicle car = Vehicle ( "Honda" , "Civic" , 2022 ) print ( car . start ()) print ( car . info ()) print () # Electric car tesla = ElectricCar ( "Tesla" , "Model 3" , 2023 , 75 ) print ( tesla . start ()) # Overridden print ( tesla . info ()) # Extended with super() print ( tesla . charge ( 50 )) # New method Starting Honda Civic 2022 Honda Civic 🔋 Silently starting Tesla Model 3 2023 Tesla Model 3 (Electric, 75 kWh) Charging 50 kWh
docs.title: 4.2 Method Overriding and super()

docs.text: "Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking the program." In plain words: if your code works with a parent class, it must keep working when you hand it a child class. The classic counter-example: in maths a square is a rectangle, so it's tempting to write class Square(Rectangle) . But code using a rectangle expects that changing the width leaves the height alone. A square can't keep that promise. # BAD: Violates LSP class RectangleBad : def __init__ ( self , width : float , height : float ): self . _width = width self . _height = height @property def width ( self ) -> float : return self . _width @width . setter def width ( self , value : float ) -> None : self . _width = value @property def height ( self ) -> float : return self . _height @height . setter def height ( self , value : float ) -> None : self . _height = value def area ( self ) -> float : return self . _width * self . _height class SquareBad ( RectangleBad ): """Violates LSP: changing width also changes height.""" def __init__ ( self , side : float ): super () . __init__ ( side , side ) @RectangleBad . width . setter def width ( self , value : float ) -> None : self . _width = value self . _height = value # Forces square constraint @RectangleBad . height . setter def height ( self , value : float ) -> None : self . _height = value self . _width = value # Forces square constraint def calculate_expected_area ( shape : RectangleBad ) -> float : """Function that expects normal Rectangle behavior.""" shape . width = 5 shape . height = 4 # Expect area to be 5 * 4 = 20 return shape . area () rect = RectangleBad ( 3 , 3 ) square = SquareBad ( 3 ) print ( f "Rectangle area: { calculate_expected_area ( rect ) } " ) # 20 ✓ print ( f "Square area: { calculate_expected_area ( square ) } " ) # 16 ✗ (LSP violated!) print ( " \n ⚠️ Square violates LSP: behavior changed unexpectedly" ) Rectangle area: 20 Square area: 16 ⚠️ Square violates LSP: behavior changed unexpectedly The function was written for rectangles and got a wrong answer from a "rectangle". The fix is to stop pretending a square is a rectangle and give both a common parent instead: # GOOD: LSP-compliant design using shared base from abc import ABC , abstractmethod class ShapeLSP ( ABC ): """Abstract base for shapes - LSP compliant.""" @abstractmethod def area ( self ) -> float : pass class RectangleGood ( ShapeLSP ): """Rectangle that doesn't promise width/height independence.""" def __init__ ( self , width : float , height : float ): self . width = width self . height = height def area ( self ) -> float : return self . width * self . height class SquareGood ( ShapeLSP ): """Square as its own type, not a Rectangle subclass.""" def __init__ ( self , side : float ): self . side = side def area ( self ) -> float : return self . side ** 2 # Both work correctly with the interface shapes_lsp = [ RectangleGood ( 5 , 4 ), SquareGood ( 4 )] for s in shapes_lsp : print ( f " { s . __class__ . __name__ } : area = { s . area () } " ) print ( " \n ✓ LSP compliant: each shape behaves consistently" ) RectangleGood: area = 20 SquareGood: area = 16 ✓ LSP compliant: each shape behaves consistently Quick recap A child class inherits everything from its parent and can override or extend it. super() calls the parent's version of a method. An abstract base class defines methods every child must implement. Polymorphism: the same method call does different things depending on the object's class. Liskov Substitution Principle: a child must work anywhere its parent is expected. If it can't, don't inherit.
docs.title: 4.3 Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

docs.text: Relationship Example Inheritance "is-a" A Dog is an Animal Composition "has-a" A Car has an Engine With composition, a class holds other objects as attributes and asks them to do the work. You can swap one part (say, a bigger SSD) without touching the rest. Prefer composition over inheritance. It's more flexible and keeps classes loosely connected. Use inheritance only when the "is-a" relationship is genuinely true.
docs.title: 5. Composition vs Inheritance

docs.text: class CPU : """Central Processing Unit component.""" def __init__ ( self , brand : str , cores : int , speed_ghz : float ): self . brand = brand self . cores = cores self . speed_ghz = speed_ghz def process ( self , task : str ) -> str : return f "CPU processing ' { task } ' on { self . cores } cores at { self . speed_ghz } GHz" class RAM : """Memory component.""" def __init__ ( self , size_gb : int , type_ : str = "DDR4" ): self . size_gb = size_gb self . type_ = type_ def load ( self , data : str ) -> str : return f "Loading ' { data } ' into { self . size_gb } GB { self . type_ } RAM" class Storage : """Storage component.""" def __init__ ( self , size_gb : int , type_ : str = "SSD" ): self . size_gb = size_gb self . type_ = type_ def save ( self , file : str ) -> str : return f "Saving ' { file } ' to { self . size_gb } GB { self . type_ } " class Computer : """Computer composed of components (has-a relationship).""" def __init__ ( self , name : str , cpu : CPU , ram : RAM , storage : Storage ): self . name = name self . cpu = cpu # Has-a CPU self . ram = ram # Has-a RAM self . storage = storage # Has-a Storage def run_program ( self , program : str ) -> None : """Run a program using all components.""" print ( f "--- { self . name } running ' { program } ' ---" ) print ( self . storage . save ( program )) print ( self . ram . load ( program )) print ( self . cpu . process ( program )) def specs ( self ) -> str : """Return computer specifications.""" return ( f " { self . name } : { self . cpu . brand } { self . cpu . cores } -core, " f " { self . ram . size_gb } GB RAM, { self . storage . size_gb } GB { self . storage . type_ } " ) # Build a computer using composition gaming_pc = Computer ( name = "Gaming Rig" , cpu = CPU ( "AMD Ryzen 9" , 12 , 4.8 ), ram = RAM ( 32 , "DDR5" ), storage = Storage ( 2000 , "NVMe SSD" ) ) print ( gaming_pc . specs ()) print () gaming_pc . run_program ( "Cyberpunk 2077" ) Gaming Rig: AMD Ryzen 9 12-core, 32GB RAM, 2000GB NVMe SSD --- Gaming Rig running 'Cyberpunk 2077' --- Saving 'Cyberpunk 2077' to 2000GB NVMe SSD Loading 'Cyberpunk 2077' into 32GB DDR5 RAM CPU processing 'Cyberpunk 2077' on 12 cores at 4.8GHz Computer doesn't know how to process, load or save anything. It hands each job to the part that does. Want a faster machine? Pass in a different CPU object; the Computer class doesn't change. Quick recap Inheritance models "is-a"; composition models "has-a". Composition lets you swap parts without changing the class that uses them, so reach for it first.
docs.title: 5.1 Composition Example: Computer System

docs.text: Many classes exist mainly to hold data. Writing __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ for each of them gets repetitive. The @dataclass decorator writes those for you from the type-annotated fields.
docs.title: 6. Dataclasses

docs.text: from dataclasses import dataclass , field from typing import List # Regular class (lots of boilerplate) class ProductOld : def __init__ ( self , name : str , price : float , quantity : int = 0 ): self . name = name self . price = price self . quantity = quantity def __repr__ ( self ): return f "ProductOld(name= { self . name !r} , price= { self . price } , quantity= { self . quantity } )" def __eq__ ( self , other ): if not isinstance ( other , ProductOld ): return NotImplemented return ( self . name , self . price , self . quantity ) == ( other . name , other . price , other . quantity ) # Dataclass (same functionality, less code!) @dataclass class Product : """Product with auto-generated __init__, __repr__, __eq__.""" name : str price : float quantity : int = 0 # Default value def total_value ( self ) -> float : """You can still add custom methods.""" return self . price * self . quantity # Usage laptop = Product ( "MacBook Pro" , 2499.99 , 5 ) mouse = Product ( "Magic Mouse" , 99.99 ) print ( laptop ) # Auto __repr__ print ( f "Total value: $ { laptop . total_value () : .2f } " ) # Auto __eq__ mouse2 = Product ( "Magic Mouse" , 99.99 ) print ( f " \n mouse == mouse2: { mouse == mouse2 } " ) # True Product(name='MacBook Pro', price=2499.99, quantity=5) Total value: $12499.95 mouse == mouse2: True
docs.title: 6.1 Basic Dataclass

docs.text: With frozen=True the fields can't be changed after the object is created, just like a tuple. Frozen objects are also hashable, so they can be used as dictionary keys or put in sets. @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class Coordinate : """Immutable coordinate - cannot be modified after creation.""" latitude : float longitude : float def distance_to ( self , other : "Coordinate" ) -> float : """Simplified distance calculation (not real geo distance).""" import math return math . sqrt ( ( self . latitude - other . latitude ) ** 2 + ( self . longitude - other . longitude ) ** 2 ) # Create immutable coordinates home = Coordinate ( 27.7172 , 85.3240 ) # Kathmandu office = Coordinate ( 27.6915 , 85.3420 ) print ( f "Home: { home } " ) print ( f "Distance: { home . distance_to ( office ) : .4f } " ) # Cannot modify frozen dataclass try : home . latitude = 28.0 # Will raise FrozenInstanceError except Exception as e : print ( f " \n ✓ Cannot modify frozen: { type ( e ) . __name__ } " ) # Frozen dataclasses can be used as dict keys or set elements locations = { home : "Home" , office : "Office" } print ( f " \n Locations dict: { locations } " ) Home: Coordinate(latitude=27.7172, longitude=85.324) Distance: 0.0314 ✓ Cannot modify frozen: FrozenInstanceError Locations dict: {Coordinate(latitude=27.7172, longitude=85.324): 'Home', Coordinate(latitude=27.6915, longitude=85.342): 'Office'}
docs.title: 6.2 Frozen Dataclass (Immutable)

docs.text: Remember the mutable-default trap from Section 1? Dataclasses protect you from it: items: list = [] is an error. Use field(default_factory=list) so each object gets its own new list. from dataclasses import dataclass , field from typing import List , Dict @dataclass class ShoppingCart : """Shopping cart with mutable defaults done right.""" customer_name : str # WRONG: items: List[str] = [] # Would share list across instances! # RIGHT: Use field with default_factory items : List [ str ] = field ( default_factory = list ) prices : Dict [ str , float ] = field ( default_factory = dict ) def add_item ( self , item : str , price : float ) -> None : self . items . append ( item ) self . prices [ item ] = price def total ( self ) -> float : return sum ( self . prices . values ()) # Each instance gets its own list/dict cart1 = ShoppingCart ( "Alice" ) cart1 . add_item ( "Laptop" , 999.99 ) cart1 . add_item ( "Mouse" , 49.99 ) cart2 = ShoppingCart ( "Bob" ) cart2 . add_item ( "Keyboard" , 129.99 ) print ( f "Cart 1 ( { cart1 . customer_name } ): { cart1 . items } = $ { cart1 . total () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Cart 2 ( { cart2 . customer_name } ): { cart2 . items } = $ { cart2 . total () : .2f } " ) # Verify they're independent assert cart1 . items is not cart2 . items print ( " \n ✓ Each cart has independent items list" ) Cart 1 (Alice): ['Laptop', 'Mouse'] = $1049.98 Cart 2 (Bob): ['Keyboard'] = $129.99 ✓ Each cart has independent items list Quick recap @dataclass generates __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ from the fields. frozen=True makes objects read-only and hashable. Use field(default_factory=list) (or dict ) for mutable defaults. Use __post_init__ if you need to validate fields after creation.

docs.text: "Dunder" is short for d ouble under score, as in __len__ . You almost never call them directly. Python calls them for you: len(x) calls x.__len__() , for item in x calls x.__iter__() , and so on. Implement them, and your objects work with Python's built-in syntax.
docs.title: 7. Dunder Methods You Actually Use

docs.text: class Playlist : """A playlist that behaves like a container.""" def __init__ ( self , name : str ): self . name = name self . _songs : List [ str ] = [] def add ( self , song : str ) -> None : self . _songs . append ( song ) def __len__ ( self ) -> int : """Enable len(playlist).""" return len ( self . _songs ) def __iter__ ( self ): """Enable for song in playlist.""" return iter ( self . _songs ) def __contains__ ( self , song : str ) -> bool : """Enable 'song in playlist'.""" return song in self . _songs def __getitem__ ( self , index : int ) -> str : """Enable playlist[0].""" return self . _songs [ index ] def __repr__ ( self ) -> str : return f "Playlist(' { self . name } ', { len ( self ) } songs)" # Create and populate playlist playlist = Playlist ( "Road Trip Mix" ) playlist . add ( "Hotel California" ) playlist . add ( "Bohemian Rhapsody" ) playlist . add ( "Stairway to Heaven" ) # Now use Python's built-in operations print ( f "Playlist: { playlist } " ) print ( f "Length: { len ( playlist ) } " ) # __len__ print ( f "First song: { playlist [ 0 ] } " ) # __getitem__ print ( f "Contains 'Yesterday': { 'Yesterday' in playlist } " ) # __contains__ print ( f "Contains 'Hotel California': { 'Hotel California' in playlist } " ) print ( " \n All songs:" ) for song in playlist : # __iter__ print ( f " ♪ { song } " ) Playlist: Playlist('Road Trip Mix', 3 songs) Length: 3 First song: Hotel California Contains 'Yesterday': False Contains 'Hotel California': True All songs: ♪ Hotel California ♪ Bohemian Rhapsody ♪ Stairway to Heaven
docs.title: 7.1 Container Methods: __len__, __iter__, __contains__

docs.text: from functools import total_ordering @total_ordering # Generates other comparisons from __eq__ and __lt__ class Version : """Software version with comparison support.""" def __init__ ( self , major : int , minor : int , patch : int ): self . major = major self . minor = minor self . patch = patch def __repr__ ( self ) -> str : return f "Version( { self . major } , { self . minor } , { self . patch } )" def __str__ ( self ) -> str : return f " { self . major } . { self . minor } . { self . patch } " def __eq__ ( self , other : object ) -> bool : """Enable == comparison.""" if not isinstance ( other , Version ): return NotImplemented return ( self . major , self . minor , self . patch ) == ( other . major , other . minor , other . patch ) def __lt__ ( self , other : "Version" ) -> bool : """Enable < comparison. @total_ordering provides <=, >, >=.""" if not isinstance ( other , Version ): return NotImplemented return ( self . major , self . minor , self . patch ) < ( other . major , other . minor , other . patch ) def __hash__ ( self ) -> int : """Make hashable for use in sets/dicts.""" return hash (( self . major , self . minor , self . patch )) # Create versions v1 = Version ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) v2 = Version ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) v3 = Version ( 2 , 0 , 0 ) v4 = Version ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) print ( f "v1 = { v1 } , v2 = { v2 } , v3 = { v3 } " ) print ( f "v2 == v4: { v2 == v4 } " ) print ( f "v1 < v2: { v1 < v2 } " ) print ( f "v3 > v2: { v3 > v2 } " ) # Sorting works automatically versions = [ v3 , v1 , v2 ] print ( f " \n Sorted: { sorted ( versions ) } " ) v1 = 1.0.0, v2 = 1.2.3, v3 = 2.0.0 v2 == v4: True v1 < v2: True v3 > v2: True Sorted: [Version(1, 0, 0), Version(1, 2, 3), Version(2, 0, 0)] With @total_ordering we only wrote __eq__ and __lt__ ; Python filled in <= , > and >= . Because < works, sorted() works too. Watch out: if you define __eq__ , Python removes the default __hash__ . Define __hash__ as well if the objects need to go in a set or be used as dict keys. Quick recap Dunder methods let your objects work with len() , for , in , [] , == , < and sorted() . With @total_ordering you only need __eq__ and __lt__ . If you define __eq__ , also define __hash__ when objects must be hashable.

docs.text: Time to put everything together. We'll build the core of a food-delivery app like Foodmandu. Going back to our four design questions: Question Answer What things exist? Customer , MenuItem , Order , discount rules What does each thing know? prices, categories, customer details, items in an order What can each thing do? add items, calculate totals, apply discounts, complete an order How are they connected? an Order has a customer and menu items (composition); each discount rule is a DiscountStrategy (inheritance)
docs.title: 8. Real-Life Mini-Project: Food Delivery Order System

docs.text: from dataclasses import dataclass , field from typing import List , Optional from abc import ABC , abstractmethod from datetime import datetime from enum import Enum class Category ( Enum ): """Menu item categories.""" APPETIZER = "appetizer" MAIN = "main" DESSERT = "dessert" BEVERAGE = "beverage" @dataclass class MenuItem : """A single menu item with pricing.""" name : str price : float category : Category is_vegetarian : bool = False def __post_init__ ( self ): if self . price < 0 : raise ValueError ( "Price cannot be negative" ) def __str__ ( self ) -> str : veg = " (V)" if self . is_vegetarian else "" return f " { self . name }{ veg } - $ { self . price : .2f } " @dataclass class Customer : """A customer with loyalty status.""" name : str email : str phone : str is_premium : bool = False orders_count : int = 0 def __str__ ( self ) -> str : status = "Premium" if self . is_premium else "Regular" return f " { self . name } ( { status } - { self . orders_count } orders)" # Abstract base for discount strategies (Strategy Pattern preview) class DiscountStrategy ( ABC ): """Abstract discount strategy.""" @abstractmethod def calculate_discount ( self , subtotal : float , customer : Customer ) -> float : """Return discount amount.""" pass @property @abstractmethod def name ( self ) -> str : pass class NoDiscount ( DiscountStrategy ): """No discount applied.""" def calculate_discount ( self , subtotal : float , customer : Customer ) -> float : return 0.0 @property def name ( self ) -> str : return "No discount" class PremiumDiscount ( DiscountStrategy ): """10% off for premium customers.""" def calculate_discount ( self , subtotal : float , customer : Customer ) -> float : if customer . is_premium : return subtotal * 0.10 return 0.0 @property def name ( self ) -> str : return "Premium 10 % o ff" class BulkDiscount ( DiscountStrategy ): """15% off for orders over $50.""" def calculate_discount ( self , subtotal : float , customer : Customer ) -> float : if subtotal >= 50 : return subtotal * 0.15 return 0.0 @property def name ( self ) -> str : return "Bulk 15 % o ff (orders $50+)" print ( "✓ Core classes defined" ) ✓ Core classes defined
docs.title: 8.1 Core Classes

docs.text: class Order : """ An order that HAS-A customer and HAS MenuItems (composition). Demonstrates encapsulation and composition. """ _order_counter = 0 # Class attribute for order numbering TAX_RATE = 0.13 # 13% tax def __init__ ( self , customer : Customer , discount_strategy : DiscountStrategy = None ): Order . _order_counter += 1 self . _order_id = Order . _order_counter self . _customer = customer # Composition: Order HAS-A Customer self . _items : List [ tuple [ MenuItem , int ]] = [] # (item, quantity) self . _discount_strategy = discount_strategy or NoDiscount () self . _created_at = datetime . now () self . _is_completed = False @property def order_id ( self ) -> int : return self . _order_id @property def customer ( self ) -> Customer : return self . _customer @property def is_completed ( self ) -> bool : return self . _is_completed def add_item ( self , item : MenuItem , quantity : int = 1 ) -> None : """Add item to order.""" if self . _is_completed : raise ValueError ( "Cannot modify completed order" ) if quantity < 1 : raise ValueError ( "Quantity must be at least 1" ) self . _items . append (( item , quantity )) @property def subtotal ( self ) -> float : """Calculate subtotal before tax and discount.""" return sum ( item . price * qty for item , qty in self . _items ) @property def discount_amount ( self ) -> float : """Calculate discount based on strategy.""" return self . _discount_strategy . calculate_discount ( self . subtotal , self . _customer ) @property def tax_amount ( self ) -> float : """Calculate tax on discounted amount.""" return ( self . subtotal - self . discount_amount ) * self . TAX_RATE @property def total ( self ) -> float : """Calculate final total.""" return self . subtotal - self . discount_amount + self . tax_amount def complete ( self ) -> None : """Mark order as completed.""" self . _is_completed = True self . _customer . orders_count += 1 # Container methods def __len__ ( self ) -> int : """Return number of line items.""" return len ( self . _items ) def __iter__ ( self ): """Iterate over items.""" return iter ( self . _items ) def __str__ ( self ) -> str : lines = [ f "═══ Order # { self . _order_id } ═══" , f "Customer: { self . _customer . name } " , f "Date: { self . _created_at . strftime ( '%Y-%m- %d %H:%M' ) } " , "─" * 30 , ] for item , qty in self . _items : lines . append ( f " { qty } x { item . name : <20 } $ { item . price * qty : .2f } " ) lines . extend ([ "─" * 30 , f " { 'Subtotal:' : <22 } $ { self . subtotal : .2f } " , f " { self . _discount_strategy . name : <22 } -$ { self . discount_amount : .2f } " , f " { 'Tax (13%):' : <22 } $ { self . tax_amount : .2f } " , "═" * 30 , f " { 'TOTAL:' : <22 } $ { self . total : .2f } " , ]) return " \n " . join ( lines ) print ( "✓ Order class defined" ) ✓ Order class defined
docs.title: 8.2 The Order Class (Composition)

docs.text: Create a Counter class that: starts at 0, or at a value you pass in has increment() , decrement() and reset() methods has a read-only value property Hint : Store the count in self._value and expose it with @property (no setter). Expected : after two increment() calls, c.value is 2 . # Exercise 1: Your code here class Counter : pass # Test (uncomment when ready): # c = Counter() # c.increment() # c.increment() # assert c.value == 2 # c.decrement() # assert c.value == 1 # c.reset() # assert c.value == 0 # print("✓ Exercise 1 passed!") Show solution class Counter : def __init__ ( self , start : int = 0 ): self . _start = start self . _value = start @property def value ( self ) -> int : return self . _value def increment ( self ) -> None : self . _value += 1 def decrement ( self ) -> None : self . _value -= 1 def reset ( self ) -> None : self . _value = self . _start

docs.text: Add a from_fahrenheit(cls, f) classmethod to convert from Fahrenheit. Hint : Formula is (f - 32) * 5/9 Expected : Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212).celsius → 100.0 # Exercise 2: Your code here class TemperatureEx2 : def __init__ ( self , celsius : float ): self . celsius = celsius # TODO: Add from_fahrenheit classmethod # Test: # t = TemperatureEx2.from_fahrenheit(212) # assert t.celsius == 100.0 # print("✓ Exercise 2 passed!") Show solution class TemperatureEx2 : def __init__ ( self , celsius : float ): self . celsius = celsius @classmethod def from_fahrenheit ( cls , f : float ) -> "TemperatureEx2" : return cls (( f - 32 ) * 5 / 9 )

Expected : Setting password to "abc" should raise ValueError. # Exercise 3: Your code here class UserAccount : pass # Test: # user = UserAccount("alice", "secure123") # Should work # try: # user.password = "short" # Should raise ValueError # print("✗ Should have raised ValueError") # except ValueError: # print("✓ Exercise 3 passed!") Show solution class UserAccount : def __init__ ( self , username : str , password : str ): self . username = username self . password = password # goes through the setter @property def password ( self ) -> str : return self . _password @password . setter def password ( self , value : str ) -> None : if len ( value ) < 8 : raise ValueError ( "Password must be at least 8 characters" ) self . _password = value

docs.text: Topic Remember this Objects & references Variables are names pointing to objects. is = same object, == = same value. Classes class Name: + __init__(self, ...) . self is the object being created or used. Attributes Instance attributes on self ; class attributes in the class body, shared by all. Methods instance ( self ), @classmethod ( cls ), @staticmethod (neither). Encapsulation _name for internal data, @property + setter for validation. Inheritance class Child(Parent): , super().method() to reuse the parent's version. Polymorphism Same method name, different behaviour per class. LSP A child must work anywhere the parent works. Composition "has-a". Prefer it over inheritance. Dataclasses @dataclass , frozen=True , field(default_factory=list) , __post_init__ . Dunder methods __repr__ , __str__ , __len__ , __iter__ , __contains__ , __getitem__ , __eq__ , __lt__ , __hash__ .

docs.text: PRG 400: Advanced Python – Course Project Welcome to the PRG 400 course project. Over the next few weeks you'll build a production-grade web application the way professional teams do: a clean architecture, sensible design patterns, tests, containers and a real deployment. The point isn't just to get something working. You'll apply SOLID principles , the 12-Factor App methodology and modular design so that your app is maintainable and deployable by someone who has never met you. At a Glance What A layered Python web API (routes → services → repositories) backed by a database Framework FastAPI (recommended), Flask or Django (see Core Requirements below) Runs in Docker + Docker Compose (app + PostgreSQL) Timeline Weeks 2–8, with a deliverable every week Tests pytest , at least 60% overall coverage Ends with A live public URL, a 7–10 minute presentation and a 4–6 page final report Biggest marks SOLID principles in code (20%), repository & service layer (15%), testing (15%) Objectives By the end of this project you will be able to: Architect a clean, modular Python web application that follows the SOLID principles Apply 12-Factor App practices for configuration, logging and environments Build a RESTful API backend with FastAPI or Flask Containerise your application with Docker and Docker Compose Write unit and integration tests with meaningful coverage Deploy your application to a cloud platform Document your architecture decisions and reflect on the engineering trade-offs Core Requirements Every project must include: Requirement Details Web framework FastAPI (recommended) or Django or Flask Database PostgreSQL or SQLite (via SQLAlchemy ORM) Containerisation Dockerfile + docker-compose.yml Configuration Environment variables via .env (never hardcoded) Testing Unit tests with pytest (minimum 60% coverage) Logging Structured logging (no bare print() statements in production code) Code quality ruff or flake8 linting, black formatting Documentation README.md with setup, architecture and API docs SOLID Principles in Your Project Your project must visibly apply all five SOLID principles. You'll be marked on how deliberately and correctly you use each one, not on whether the words appear in your code. S: Single Responsibility Principle A class or module should have only one reason to change. Each module should own one concern . A route handler shouldn't also format data, validate input and write to the database. Split those jobs across layers: app/ ├── api/routes/ # HTTP layer only: receives requests, returns responses ├── services/ # Business logic only: applies the domain rules ├── repositories/ # Data access only: talks to the database ├── models/ # Domain entities: data shapes and validation └── core/ # App-wide concerns: config, logging, exceptions O: Open/Closed Principle Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. Design your core logic so you can add features without editing existing code . Abstract base classes, dependency injection and the strategy pattern all help here. Example: a NotificationService that works with any NotificationChannel (email, SMS, webhook). Adding a new channel means writing a new class; the service itself never changes. from abc import ABC , abstractmethod class NotificationChannel ( ABC ): @abstractmethod def send ( self , recipient : str , message : str ) -> None : ... class EmailChannel ( NotificationChannel ): def send ( self , recipient : str , message : str ) -> None : print ( f "[email] to { recipient } : { message } " ) # real code would send an email class SMSChannel ( NotificationChannel ): def send ( self , recipient : str , message : str ) -> None : print ( f "[sms] to { recipient } : { message } " ) # real code would send an SMS class NotificationService : def __init__ ( self , channel : NotificationChannel ): self . _channel = channel def notify ( self , recipient : str , message : str ) -> None : self . _channel . send ( recipient , message ) NotificationService ( EmailChannel ()) . notify ( "asha@example.com" , "Your order has shipped" ) NotificationService ( SMSChannel ()) . notify ( "+977-9800000000" , "Your order has shipped" ) [email] to asha@example.com: Your order has shipped [sms] to +977-9800000000: Your order has shipped L: Liskov Substitution Principle Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness. If you use inheritance or abstract classes, every subclass must honour the full contract of its parent. A subclass should never demand more from its callers (stricter preconditions), promise less (weaker postconditions), or raise exceptions the parent wouldn't. What to watch for: if you find yourself writing if isinstance(obj, SubclassX) inside shared logic, you're probably breaking LSP. I: Interface Segregation Principle Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large "god" interface. If a class only needs to read from a repository, it should depend on something like Readable , not on a full CRUD repository. from typing import Protocol class Readable ( Protocol ): def get ( self , id : int ): ... class Writable ( Protocol ): def save ( self , entity ): ... def delete ( self , id : int ): ... class ReadWriteRepository ( Readable , Writable , Protocol ): ... D: Dependency Inversion Principle High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. Your service layer should never import a concrete database class directly. Pass dependencies in through the constructor or FastAPI's Depends() system. from typing import Protocol class UserRepository ( Protocol ): # the abstraction def get ( self , user_id : int ) -> dict : ... class PostgresUserRepository : # a concrete, low-level detail def get ( self , user_id : int ) -> dict : return { "id" : user_id , "source" : "postgres" } # Bad: the high-level service creates its own low-level dependency class UserServiceBad : def __init__ ( self ): self . repo = PostgresUserRepository () # tightly coupled # Good: the service depends on the abstraction, injected from outside class UserService : def __init__ ( self , repo : UserRepository ): self . repo = repo service = UserService ( PostgresUserRepository ()) # or a fake repo in your tests print ( service . repo . get ( 1 )) {'id': 1, 'source': 'postgres'} 12-Factor App Methodology Your application must follow the 12-Factor App principles. Here's what each factor means for your project. Factor What you must do I. Codebase One Git repo, one app. No sharing code between apps by copy-paste. II. Dependencies Declare every dependency in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml . Assume nothing is pre-installed. III. Config Load all config (DB URLs, secrets, ports) from environment variables. Use python-dotenv locally. Never commit .env . IV. Backing Services Treat your database, cache or email provider as attached resources, swappable through config rather than code changes. V. Build, Release, Run The Dockerfile separates build from run. docker compose manages the release and run stages. VI. Processes Your app must be stateless. No in-memory session state; keep state in the database or cache. VII. Port Binding Your app exposes itself on a port (e.g. 8000 ) set by an environment variable, not hardcoded. VIII. Concurrency Design so that several workers can run in parallel. Avoid global mutable state. IX. Disposability The app starts fast and shuts down gracefully. Handle SIGTERM for a clean shutdown. X. Dev/Prod Parity Docker Compose keeps local development close to production. No "works on my machine". XI. Logs Log to stdout / stderr as structured events (JSON preferred). Don't write log files yourself. XII. Admin Processes Run DB migrations as one-off tasks (e.g. alembic upgrade head ), not as part of app startup. Required Project Structure Your repository must follow this structure. You may add to it, but don't remove any of the required parts. your-project/ │ ├── app/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── main.py # App entry point, FastAPI/Flask app factory │ │ │ ├── api/ │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── routes/ # Route handlers (one file per resource) │ │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ │ └── items.py │ │ └── dependencies.py # FastAPI Depends() injections │ │ │ ├── core/ │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── config.py # Pydantic BaseSettings — loads from env │ │ ├── logging.py # Structured logger setup │ │ └── exceptions.py # Custom exception classes │ │ │ ├── models/ │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── domain.py # Pure domain entities (Pydantic / dataclasses) │ │ └── orm.py # SQLAlchemy ORM models │ │ │ ├── repositories/ │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── base.py # Abstract base repository (interface) │ │ └── item_repository.py # Concrete implementation │ │ │ └── services/ │ ├── __init__.py │ └── item_service.py # Business logic, depends on repository interface │ ├── tests/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── conftest.py # Pytest fixtures, test DB setup │ ├── unit/ │ │ └── test_item_service.py │ └── integration/ │ └── test_item_routes.py │ ├── migrations/ # Alembic migration scripts │ ├── env.py │ └── versions/ │ ├── .env.example # Template for env vars — committed to repo ├── .env # Actual secrets — NEVER committed (in .gitignore) ├── .gitignore ├── Dockerfile ├── docker-compose.yml ├── docker-compose.test.yml # Separate compose for running tests ├── requirements.txt ├── pyproject.toml # Linting, formatting, test config ├── alembic.ini └── README.md # Your project's own README Dockerfile Requirements Your Dockerfile must use a multi-stage build , like this one: # Stage 1: Builder — install dependencies FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder WORKDIR /app # Install dependencies into a virtual environment RUN python -m venv /opt/venv ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # Stage 2: Runtime — lean final image FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime WORKDIR /app # Copy only the venv and app code — no build tools in production image COPY --from = builder /opt/venv /opt/venv COPY ./app ./app ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED = 1 ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE = 1 # Run as non-root user (security best practice) RUN adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 CMD [ "uvicorn" , "app.main:app" , "--host" , "0.0.0.0" , "--port" , "8000" ] Your docker-compose.yml must define at least: an app service (your web application) a db service (PostgreSQL) proper use of environment , depends_on , volumes and healthcheck Configuration: The Right Way Use Pydantic BaseSettings (from the pydantic-settings package) to load all configuration from environment variables: # app/core/config.py from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings , SettingsConfigDict class Settings ( BaseSettings ): model_config = SettingsConfigDict ( env_file = ".env" ) app_name : str = "My App" database_url : str secret_key : str debug : bool = False port : int = 8000 settings = Settings () Your .env.example (committed) should list every variable with a placeholder value: DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb SECRET_KEY=changeme DEBUG=false PORT=8000 Your .env (never committed) holds the real values for local development. Week 2: Architecture Design & Proposal Choose your project domain (see Sample Project Ideas below) Define your data models, API endpoints and service boundaries Sketch your layered architecture (routes → services → repositories) Identify which SOLID principles apply where Deliverables: 1–2 page Architecture Proposal Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD) Endpoint design table (method, path, description, auth required) Week 3: Literature & Technical Review Review 2–3 open-source Python web applications on GitHub Evaluate their architecture: Do they follow SRP? Are the services testable? Is config handled properly? Identify what you'll do differently or improve on Deliverables: Technical Review Report (2–3 pages) Annotated links to the reviewed repositories, with critique notes Week 4: Project Scaffold & Core Models Initialise your repository with the required folder structure Set up Dockerfile , docker-compose.yml and .env.example Implement the domain models and ORM models Configure Alembic and create your first migration Deliverables: Running Docker Compose stack (app + db) At least one Alembic migration applied GET /health endpoint returning {"status": "ok"} Week 5: Repository & Service Layer Implement an abstract base repository and at least one concrete repository Implement the service layer with dependency injection Write unit tests for the service layer using mock repositories Demonstrate the Dependency Inversion and Open/Closed principles in code Deliverables: Working service + repository layer with tests Test coverage report showing ≥ 50% coverage on the service layer Week 6: API Layer & Integration Implement all API routes using FastAPI/Flask Connect routes → services → repositories through dependency injection Add request validation (Pydantic schemas) Add structured logging to all service operations Deliverables: All planned endpoints implemented and testable by hand in Swagger UI or Postman Integration tests for at least 3 endpoints Week 7: Hardening, Testing & Documentation Reach ≥ 60% overall test coverage Add error handling (custom exceptions, correct HTTP status codes) Write your project's own README.md : setup guide, environment variables, how to run tests, API reference Run the linter ( ruff / flake8 ) and formatter ( black ) with zero errors Deliverables: Test coverage report (HTML output from pytest --cov ) Clean linting output Complete project README.md Week 8: Deployment, Demo & Submission Deploy using one of: Railway , Render , Fly.io or a VPS with Docker The live application must be reachable at a public URL Present your application (7–10 minutes): demo, architecture walkthrough and reflection Submit the final report Deliverables: Live deployment URL Final Project Report (4–6 pages), see the structure below Presentation slides Final GitHub repository (clean commit history, no secrets committed) Final Project Report Structure Your report must cover: Project Overview : What does your app do? Who is it for? Architecture Diagram : A layered diagram showing routes, services, repositories and the DB SOLID Principles Applied : One section per principle: where it appears, why you used it, what problem it solves 12-Factor Compliance : Which factors you implemented and how Testing Strategy : What you tested, how, and your coverage results Deployment : The platform you chose, the deployment steps, any challenges Reflection : What you'd do differently, and what you learned Sample Project Ideas Pick a domain that interests you. The technical requirements are the same whichever you choose. Domain Project Idea Healthcare Patient appointment scheduling API Finance Personal budget tracker with category analysis Education Course enrollment and grade management system E-Commerce Product catalog and order management API Productivity Task manager with priority queues and deadlines IoT / Monitoring Sensor data ingestion and threshold alerting API HR Employee leave request and approval workflow Library Book lending and reservation management system Recommended Tools & Libraries Purpose Recommended Web framework FastAPI (preferred), Flask ORM SQLAlchemy 2.x Migrations Alembic Validation Pydantic v2 Testing pytest, pytest-cov, httpx (for FastAPI) Mocking pytest-mock, unittest.mock Config pydantic-settings, python-dotenv Logging Python logging module with a JSON formatter ( python-json-logger ) Linting ruff Formatting black Containerisation Docker, Docker Compose API docs Swagger UI (built into FastAPI), Postman Deployment Railway, Render, Fly.io Diagramming draw.io, Lucidchart, Mermaid (in Markdown) Evaluation Criteria Component Weight Key Rubric Points Architecture Proposal & ERD 10% Clarity of design, layer separation, endpoint planning Technical Review Report 5% Depth of analysis, actionable takeaways SOLID Principles (in code) 20% Correct and intentional application of all 5 principles 12-Factor Compliance 10% Config from env, stateless design, Docker parity, structured logs Repository & Service Layer 15% Abstraction quality, dependency injection, testability API Layer & Functionality 10% Correctness, validation, error handling, HTTP semantics Testing & Coverage 15% Coverage ≥ 60%, meaningful tests (not just happy path) Deployment & Presentation 10% Live app, clear demo, architecture explanation Final Report 5% Completeness, reflection quality, accuracy Total 100% Academic Integrity All code must be your own work. You may use libraries, documentation and AI tools as references, but you must be able to explain every line of your code. Copying code from other students or repositories without attribution is a violation of academic policy. If you use an AI coding assistant, say so in your report and describe how you used it. Frequently Asked Questions Can I use AI tools like Copilot or ChatGPT? Yes, as references. You must be able to explain every line, and you must mention the AI use in your report (see Academic Integrity above). Which database should I use? PostgreSQL or SQLite, through the SQLAlchemy ORM. Your docker-compose.yml must include a PostgreSQL db service. Do I commit my .env file? No. Commit .env.example with placeholder values; keep .env out of Git via .gitignore . What coverage do I need? At least 50% on the service layer by Week 5, and at least 60% overall by Week 7. Where can I deploy? Railway, Render, Fly.io or a VPS running Docker. The app must be reachable at a public URL. How long is the presentation? 7–10 minutes: a demo, an architecture walkthrough and your reflection. Getting Started Once you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, clone your repository and get the stack running: # Clone your repo git clone https://github.com/your-org/your-repo.git cd your-repo # Copy the example env file, then edit .env with your local values cp .env.example .env # Build and start the stack docker compose up --build # In a separate terminal: run migrations docker compose exec app alembic upgrade head # Run tests docker compose -f docker-compose.test.yml run --rm test Your app will be at http://localhost:8000 , and the API docs at http://localhost:8000/docs . Submission Checklist Tick these off before your final submission in Week 8. Code & repository [ ] Repository follows the required project structure [ ] All five SOLID principles applied deliberately (and explained in the report) [ ] Config loaded from environment variables; .env.example committed, .env not committed [ ] Structured logging, no bare print() in production code [ ] ruff / flake8 and black run with zero errors [ ] Clean commit history with no secrets committed Containers & deployment [ ] Multi-stage Dockerfile [ ] docker-compose.yml with app and db services, using environment , depends_on , volumes and healthcheck [ ] Alembic migrations run as a one-off task [ ] App deployed and reachable at a public URL Testing [ ] Unit tests for the service layer using mock repositories [ ] Integration tests for at least 3 endpoints [ ] At least 60% overall coverage, with the HTML coverage report Documents [ ] Project README.md : setup, environment variables, how to run tests, API reference [ ] Final report (4–6 pages) covering all seven sections [ ] Presentation slides for a 7–10 minute demo Good engineers don't just write code that works. They write code that is readable, testable, maintainable and deployable by someone who has never met them.
docs.title: Project Description (PRG400)

docs.text: Welcome to the PRG 400 course project. Over the next few weeks you'll build a production-grade web application the way professional teams do: a clean architecture, sensible design patterns, tests, containers and a real deployment. The point isn't just to get something working. You'll apply SOLID principles , the 12-Factor App methodology and modular design so that your app is maintainable and deployable by someone who has never met you.
docs.title: PRG 400: Advanced Python – Course Project

docs.text: What A layered Python web API (routes → services → repositories) backed by a database Framework FastAPI (recommended), Flask or Django (see Core Requirements below) Runs in Docker + Docker Compose (app + PostgreSQL) Timeline Weeks 2–8, with a deliverable every week Tests pytest , at least 60% overall coverage Ends with A live public URL, a 7–10 minute presentation and a 4–6 page final report Biggest marks SOLID principles in code (20%), repository & service layer (15%), testing (15%)
docs.title: At a Glance

docs.text: By the end of this project you will be able to: Architect a clean, modular Python web application that follows the SOLID principles Apply 12-Factor App practices for configuration, logging and environments Build a RESTful API backend with FastAPI or Flask Containerise your application with Docker and Docker Compose Write unit and integration tests with meaningful coverage Deploy your application to a cloud platform Document your architecture decisions and reflect on the engineering trade-offs

docs.text: Every project must include: Requirement Details Web framework FastAPI (recommended) or Django or Flask Database PostgreSQL or SQLite (via SQLAlchemy ORM) Containerisation Dockerfile + docker-compose.yml Configuration Environment variables via .env (never hardcoded) Testing Unit tests with pytest (minimum 60% coverage) Logging Structured logging (no bare print() statements in production code) Code quality ruff or flake8 linting, black formatting Documentation README.md with setup, architecture and API docs
