docs.text: Risk What happens 1. Hallucinations The AI invents functions, parameters or libraries that don't exist. It sounds confident. It's wrong. 2. Outdated code Training has a cutoff. You may get Pydantic v1 code when you use v2, or old Django patterns. 3. Security holes SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, missing permission checks. 4. Skill atrophy If you accept code you don't understand, you stop learning and come to depend on the tool. 5. Licensing / IP The AI may reproduce copyrighted code from its training data. Know your organisation's AI policy.
docs.title: The Five Biggest Risks of Vibe Coding

docs.text: Each snippet below contains a mistake an AI really does make. Try to spot it before reading the comment. # Spot the hallucinations: each snippet contains a typical AI mistake. print ( "=" * 60 ) print ( "HALLUCINATION EXAMPLES: spot the bug" ) print ( "=" * 60 ) # Example 1: non-existent FastAPI parameter example_1 = ''' # AI generated this. What's wrong? from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get("/items") async def get_items(limit: int = Query(default=10, max_value=100)): ... # Bug: FastAPI's Query uses `le=` not `max_value=` # Correct: Query(default=10, le=100) # (Query is also never imported.) ''' # Example 2: invented Django ORM method example_2 = ''' # AI generated this. What's wrong? # "Use the .recent() manager method to get the latest 5 posts." posts = Post.objects.recent(5) # Bug: .recent() does not exist! # Correct: Post.objects.order_by('-created_at')[:5] ''' # Example 3: outdated Pydantic API example_3 = ''' # AI generated this Pydantic v2 code. What's wrong? from pydantic import BaseModel class User(BaseModel): name: str age: int @validator("age") # Bug: @validator is the Pydantic v1 API def age_must_be_positive(cls, v): ... # (deprecated in v2, and not imported here) # Correct v2: @field_validator("age") + @classmethod ''' # Example 4: insecure advice example_4 = ''' # AI said: "Here's how to hash a password securely" import hashlib def hash_password(password: str) -> str: return hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() # WRONG! # MD5 is cryptographically broken. # Never use MD5 or SHA1 for passwords. # Correct: use bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt. ''' examples = [ ( "FastAPI - wrong Query parameter name" , "max_value= doesn't exist -> use le=" ), ( "Django ORM - invented method" , ".recent() doesn't exist -> use .order_by()" ), ( "Pydantic v2 - outdated decorator" , "@validator is the v1 API -> use @field_validator" ), ( "Security - broken hash function" , "MD5 is broken for passwords -> use bcrypt or argon2" ), ] print ( " \n Hallucination Summary:" ) print ( "-" * 60 ) for i , ( category , fix ) in enumerate ( examples , 1 ): print ( f " { i } . { category } " ) print ( f " Fix: { fix } " ) print () ============================================================ HALLUCINATION EXAMPLES: spot the bug ============================================================ Hallucination Summary: ------------------------------------------------------------ 1. FastAPI - wrong Query parameter name Fix: max_value= doesn't exist -> use le= 2. Django ORM - invented method Fix: .recent() doesn't exist -> use .order_by() 3. Pydantic v2 - outdated decorator Fix: @validator is the v1 API -> use @field_validator 4. Security - broken hash function Fix: MD5 is broken for passwords -> use bcrypt or argon2

These map to categories from the OWASP Top 10 (2021 numbering). # OWASP Top 10 issues that show up in AI-generated code. print ( "Common OWASP Issues in AI-Generated Python Code" ) print ( "=" * 60 ) security_issues = [ { "owasp" : "A01 - Broken Access Control" , "ai_code" : "@app.delete('/users/ {user_id} ') 
 def delete_user(user_id: int, db=Depends(get_db)): 
 # No check if current user == user_id or is admin!" , "fix" : "Always verify current_user.id == user_id or current_user.is_admin" , }, { "owasp" : "A02 - Cryptographic Failures" , "ai_code" : "token = base64.b64encode(str(user.id).encode()).decode() # NOT a token!" , "fix" : "Use a signed JWT (e.g. PyJWT) or secrets.token_urlsafe() for random tokens" , }, { "owasp" : "A03 - Injection" , "ai_code" : "cursor.execute(f " SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ' {name} ' " )" , "fix" : "Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('...WHERE name = %s ', (name,))" , }, { "owasp" : "A05 - Security Misconfiguration" , "ai_code" : "SECRET_KEY = 'dev-secret-key-12345' # Hardcoded in settings.py" , "fix" : "SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY'] # From env vars" , }, { "owasp" : "A09 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures" , "ai_code" : "print(f'Login attempt: {username} / {password} ')" , "fix" : "Never log passwords. Log: 'Login attempt for user {username} '" , }, ] for issue in security_issues : print ( f " 
 { issue [ 'owasp' ] } " ) print ( f " AI Generated: { issue [ 'ai_code' ] . splitlines ()[ 0 ] } " ) print ( f " Fix: { issue [ 'fix' ] } " ) Common OWASP Issues in AI-Generated Python Code ============================================================ A01 - Broken Access Control AI Generated: @app.delete('/users/{user_id}') Fix: Always verify current_user.id == user_id or current_user.is_admin A02 - Cryptographic Failures AI Generated: token = base64.b64encode(str(user.id).encode()).decode() # NOT a token! Fix: Use a signed JWT (e.g. PyJWT) or secrets.token_urlsafe() for random tokens A03 - Injection AI Generated: cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'") Fix: Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('...WHERE name = %s', (name,)) A05 - Security Misconfiguration AI Generated: SECRET_KEY = 'dev-secret-key-12345' # Hardcoded in settings.py Fix: SECRET_KEY = os.environ['DJANGO_SECRET_KEY'] # From env vars A09 - Security Logging and Monitoring Failures AI Generated: print(f'Login attempt: {username} / {password}') Fix: Never log passwords. Log: 'Login attempt for user {username}'

docs.text: The function below is the A03 example in runnable form, using an in-memory SQLite database. Pass it the name x' OR '1'='1 and it returns every user. Rewrite it with a parameterised query so that input returns nothing. import sqlite3 conn = sqlite3 . connect ( ":memory:" ) conn . execute ( "CREATE TABLE users (name TEXT, email TEXT)" ) conn . executemany ( "INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)" , [( "alice" , "alice@example.com" ), ( "bob" , "bob@example.com" )]) def find_user_unsafe ( name : str ): return conn . execute ( f "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ' { name } '" ) . fetchall () print ( find_user_unsafe ( "alice" )) print ( find_user_unsafe ( "x' OR '1'='1" )) # leaks every row # Exercise 7: your code here def find_user_safe ( name : str ): ... # Tests (uncomment when ready): # assert find_user_safe("alice") == [("alice", "alice@example.com")] # assert find_user_safe("x' OR '1'='1") == [] # print("Exercise 7 passed") [('alice', 'alice@example.com')] [('alice', 'alice@example.com'), ('bob', 'bob@example.com')] Show solution def find_user_safe ( name : str ): # The ? placeholder sends name as data, never as part of the SQL text. return conn . execute ( "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?" , ( name ,)) . fetchall () assert find_user_safe ( "alice" ) == [( "alice" , "alice@example.com" )] assert find_user_safe ( "x' OR '1'='1" ) == [] print ( "Exercise 7 passed" ) Quick recap The big five risks: hallucinations, outdated code, security holes, skill atrophy, licensing. Hallucinations look plausible: max_value= , .recent() , @validator in v2. Check AI code against the OWASP list: access control, crypto, injection, config, logging. Parameterised queries, hashed passwords (bcrypt/argon2) and secrets from env vars are non-negotiable.

docs.text: AI assistants keep getting better, but they still struggle with these: Area Why it still needs you Problem understanding The AI doesn't know what your users or business actually need. It optimises for the prompt, not the real problem. System architecture Monolith or microservices? Event-driven or request-response? These need domain knowledge and long-term thinking. Debugging complex systems Race conditions, memory leaks and intermittent failures in distributed systems need careful investigation and intuition. Communication & requirements Turning fuzzy stakeholder wishes into a precise spec is a human conversation. Ethical & product judgement "Should we build this?" "Is this use of data appropriate?" The AI can't answer these responsibly. Security review Threat modelling, penetration testing and understanding business risk need real expertise.
docs.title: The Human Edge

docs.text: Programmer How much AI helps Risk Strong fundamentals A lot: it speeds up what they already know how to do Low: they spot mistakes Intermediate Quite a lot: it fills knowledge gaps quickly Medium: may miss subtle issues Beginner (weak fundamentals) Less than you'd think: they can't tell if it's right High: blind trust in wrong code The paradox of vibe coding: AI is most valuable to those who need it least, and most dangerous to those who need it most.
docs.title: Fundamentals Make AI More Useful

docs.text: Think of a project you've worked on. Which parts would AI have helped with most? Which parts would have been dangerous to hand over? If AI can write code, what should computer science education focus on? How do you check that AI-generated code is correct? Quick recap AI can't understand your users, choose your architecture, or make ethical calls for you. Hard debugging and security review still need human expertise. Strong fundamentals are what make AI useful; without them, AI is a risk.

docs.text: Never accept code you don't understand. If you can't explain a function line by line, keep asking the AI to explain it until you can. Always run the code. AI code can look right and still be wrong. Test it with real inputs. Security-review everything , especially authentication, database queries, input validation and secret handling. Pin your library versions. The AI may be writing for a different version than the one you have installed. Iterate with feedback. Paste the actual error message back to the AI. The best follow-up prompts include it. Use AI for what it's good at: boilerplate, documentation, tests and refactoring. Keep system design for yourself. Keep building your fundamentals. The more you know, the better you'll be at working with AI.

 Step 1: Observe unexpected behaviour" ) result = calculate_discount_buggy ( 100 , 20 ) # Expecting $80, passing 20% print ( f " Price: $100, Discount: 20%" ) print ( f " Expected: $80.00" ) print ( f " Got: $ { result : .2f } <- wrong: 20 was treated as 2000%" ) # Step 3: Good prompt to AI (include context + error) prompt_to_ai = ''' My Python function returns wrong results. Here's the code: def calculate_discount(price: float, discount_pct: float) -> float: return price - (price * discount_pct) When I call calculate_discount(100, 20), I expect $80.00 (20 % o ff). But I get -1900.0. What's wrong and how do I fix it? ''' print ( " 
 Step 2: Craft a precise prompt to AI" ) print ( "-" * 40 ) print ( "Good prompt includes:" ) print ( " - the actual code" ) print ( " - the inputs used" ) print ( " - the expected output" ) print ( " - the actual output received" ) # Step 4: AI explains and provides fix print ( " 
 Step 3: AI Response (simulated)" ) print ( "-" * 40 ) print ( "The bug: discount_pct should be divided by 100 if passed as" ) print ( "a percentage (0-100) rather than a fraction (0.0-1.0)." ) # Step 5: Apply and verify the fix def calculate_discount_fixed ( price : float , discount_pct : float ) -> float : """Calculate price after discount. discount_pct is 0-100 (e.g., 20 = 20%).""" if not ( 0 <= discount_pct <= 100 ): raise ValueError ( f "discount_pct must be between 0 and 100, got { discount_pct } " ) return price * ( 1 - discount_pct / 100 ) print ( " 
 Step 4: Apply and verify the fix" ) print ( "-" * 40 ) test_cases = [ ( 100.0 , 20 , 80.0 ), ( 200.0 , 50 , 100.0 ), ( 99.99 , 10 , 89.991 ), ( 0.0 , 100 , 0.0 ), ] all_pass = True for price , pct , expected in test_cases : result = calculate_discount_fixed ( price , pct ) passed = abs ( result - expected ) < 0.001 status = "PASS" if passed else "FAIL" print ( f " { status } discount( { price } , { pct } %) = $ { result : .3f } (expected $ { expected : .3f } )" ) if not passed : all_pass = False print ( f " 
 All tests passed: { all_pass } " ) Debugging Workflow with AI Assistance ============================================================ Step 1: Observe unexpected behaviour Price: $100, Discount: 20% Expected: $80.00 Got: $-1900.00 <- wrong: 20 was treated as 2000% Step 2: Craft a precise prompt to AI ---------------------------------------- Good prompt includes: - the actual code - the inputs used - the expected output - the actual output received Step 3: AI Response (simulated) ---------------------------------------- The bug: discount_pct should be divided by 100 if passed as a percentage (0-100) rather than a fraction (0.0-1.0). docs.text:
Deep Dive: asyncio in Python "Concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once. Parallelism is about doing lots of things at once." (Rob Pike) The Event-Driven Programming notebook gave you a first look at async and await . This notebook goes deeper into Python's asyncio library: running tasks together, timeouts and cancellation, sharing resources safely, mixing blocking code with async code, and finally a small web crawler that uses all of it. Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook you will be able to: Explain why async code helps with I/O-bound work (and why it doesn't speed up CPU-bound work) Write coroutines and explain what can be await ed Run work concurrently with gather , create_task , TaskGroup and as_completed Control running tasks with timeouts, cancellation, shield and wait Coordinate coroutines with queues, locks, semaphores and events Use async generators, async comprehensions and async context managers Call blocking code from async code with asyncio.to_thread and executors Combine all of this in a rate-limited async web crawler Prerequisites Python 3.11 or newer recommended ( TaskGroup needs 3.11; the notebook falls back to gather on 3.10) Functions, classes and exception handling Generators ( yield ) help, but aren't required The Event-Driven Programming notebook (callbacks, event loops, first steps with async / await ) How to Use This Notebook Run the cells from top to bottom . Later cells reuse imports ( asyncio , random , time ) and helpers from earlier cells. The cells use await directly at the top level. That works in Jupyter. In a normal .py script you'd put the code in async def main() and call asyncio.run(main()) (see Section 2.4). Many examples use random delays, so the order of lines and the timings in your output will differ a little from the saved output. That's expected. Try It cells are for you. Write your answer first, then open Show solution to compare. Each section ends with a Quick recap . Read only the recaps when revising before an exam. What We'll Cover Section Topic 1 Why Async? The I/O Problem 2 Coroutines and await : The Basics 3 Running Concurrently: gather , create_task , TaskGroup 4 Controlling Execution: Timeouts, Cancellation, Shielding 5 Coordination: Queues, Locks, Semaphores, Events 6 Async Iteration: async for , async with 7 Bridging Sync and Async: Threads and Processes 8 Real-World Project: Async Web Crawler Warm-Up Quiz: Concurrency Intuition Think about each question before opening the answer. Q1: You need to download 100 images from the internet. What's the bottleneck? A) Your CPU can't process the pixels fast enough B) Your program is waiting for each download to finish before starting the next C) Python is too slow Show answer B. During a download the CPU is mostly idle; it's just waiting for data to arrive over the network. That's called an I/O-bound problem, and it's exactly what asyncio is designed for. Q2: What's the difference between concurrency and parallelism? Show answer Concurrency : one cook switching between several dishes (tasks take turns). Parallelism : several cooks, each working on their own dish at the same moment. asyncio gives you concurrency on a single thread. For true parallelism you need several processes ( multiprocessing ). Concurrency Parallelism Threads 1 (in asyncio) Multiple (or multiple processes) Best for I/O-bound work (network, disk) CPU-bound work (maths, image processing) Python tool asyncio multiprocessing Q3: How long does this cell take to run? Write down your guess before you run it. The last line prints the actual time. import time start = time . time () time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second print ( f "Took { time . time () - start : .1f } s" ) Took 3.0s Show answer About 3 seconds. time.sleep is blocking : the whole program stops at each call, so the three waits add up. With asyncio , the same three waits can overlap and take about 1 second : await asyncio . gather ( asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), ) Quick recap I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting; that waiting is what async code overlaps. Concurrency = taking turns on one thread. Parallelism = running at the same moment on several cores. time.sleep blocks everything; await asyncio.sleep lets other tasks run meanwhile. 1. Why Async? The I/O Problem Let's see the problem with synchronous I/O for ourselves. First, three "network calls" made the normal way: import time def fetch_data_sync ( source , delay ): """Simulates a synchronous network call.""" print ( f " [ { source } ] Requesting..." ) time . sleep ( delay ) # BLOCKS the entire program! print ( f " [ { source } ] Done ( { delay } s)" ) return f " { source } _data" print ( "=== Synchronous (blocking) ===" ) start = time . time () r1 = fetch_data_sync ( "Database" , 1.0 ) r2 = fetch_data_sync ( "API" , 1.5 ) r3 = fetch_data_sync ( "Cache" , 0.5 ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " 
 Results: { [ r1 , r2 , r3 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { elapsed : .1f } s (1.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 3.0s expected)" ) === Synchronous (blocking) === [Database] Requesting... [Database] Done (1.0s) [API] Requesting... [API] Done (1.5s) [Cache] Requesting... [Cache] Done (0.5s) Results: ['Database_data', 'API_data', 'Cache_data'] Total time: 3.0s (1.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 3.0s expected) Each call has to finish before the next one starts, so the waits add up. Now the same three calls written with asyncio : import asyncio async def fetch_data_async ( source , delay ): """Simulates an async network call.""" print ( f " [ { source } ] Requesting..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) # Non-blocking! Other tasks can run. print ( f " [ { source } ] Done ( { delay } s)" ) return f " { source } _data" print ( "=== Asynchronous (non-blocking) ===" ) start = time . time () r1 , r2 , r3 = await asyncio . gather ( fetch_data_async ( "Database" , 1.0 ), fetch_data_async ( "API" , 1.5 ), fetch_data_async ( "Cache" , 0.5 ), ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " 
 Results: { [ r1 , r2 , r3 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { elapsed : .1f } s (max of 1.0, 1.5, 0.5 = 1.5s expected)" ) === Asynchronous (non-blocking) === [Database] Requesting... [API] Requesting... [Cache] Requesting... [Cache] Done (0.5s) [Database] Done (1.0s) [API] Done (1.5s) Results: ['Database_data', 'API_data', 'Cache_data'] Total time: 1.5s (max of 1.0, 1.5, 0.5 = 1.5s expected) 3.0 s vs 1.5 s. The async version takes only as long as the slowest call, because all three waits happen at the same time. How It Works Under the Hood Synchronous: Asynchronous: t=0 [DB starts] t=0 [DB starts] [API starts] [Cache starts] t=1 [DB done] t=0.5 [Cache done] [API starts] t=1 [DB done] t=2.5 [API done] t=1.5 [API done] [Cache starts] t=3 [Cache done] Total: 1.5s Total: 3.0s The event loop interleaves the waiting: while one coroutine is waiting for I/O, the others get to run. Quick recap Blocking calls run one after another, so total time = sum of all waits. With asyncio.gather , waits overlap, so total time = the longest single wait. 2. Coroutines and await : The Basics 2.1 Anatomy of a Coroutine # A coroutine function is defined with 'async def' async def my_coroutine (): print ( "Coroutine started" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) # Yield control to the event loop print ( "Coroutine resumed" ) return 42 # Calling it returns a coroutine OBJECT: it does NOT execute yet! coro = my_coroutine () print ( f "Type: { type ( coro ) } " ) print ( f "It hasn't printed anything yet!" ) # 'await' actually executes it result = await coro print ( f "Result: { result } " ) Type: <class 'coroutine'> It hasn't printed anything yet! Coroutine started Coroutine resumed Result: 42 Calling my_coroutine() only creates a coroutine object; none of the code inside runs yet. That's why "Coroutine started" appears after our two print lines. The code runs when we await it. 2.2 What Can You await ? You can only await awaitable objects. There are three kinds: # 1. Coroutines (from 'async def') async def get_value (): return "from coroutine" result1 = await get_value () print ( f "1. Coroutine: { result1 } " ) # 2. Tasks (scheduled coroutines) async def delayed_value (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) return "from task" task = asyncio . create_task ( delayed_value ()) result2 = await task print ( f "2. Task: { result2 } " ) # 3. Futures (low-level, rarely used directly) loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () future = loop . create_future () future . set_result ( "from future" ) result3 = await future print ( f "3. Future: { result3 } " ) # NOT awaitable (this would raise TypeError): # await 42 # await "hello" # await [1, 2, 3] 1. Coroutine: from coroutine 2. Task: from task 3. Future: from future In everyday code you'll await coroutines and tasks. Futures are the low-level building block that tasks are built on; libraries use them, but application code rarely creates one directly. Inside async code, get the current loop with asyncio.get_running_loop() . The older asyncio.get_event_loop() is deprecated in many situations. 2.3 The Golden Rule of await Every await is a checkpoint where the event loop may switch to another task. No await means no switching, which means no concurrency. async def cooperative (): """Good: yields control regularly.""" for i in range ( 3 ): print ( f " Cooperative: step { i } " ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) # Yield control, even with 0 delay! async def greedy (): """Bad: hogs the event loop with CPU-bound work.""" total = 0 for i in range ( 3 ): print ( f " Greedy: step { i } " ) # No await here! Other tasks are BLOCKED until this finishes. for _ in range ( 1_000_000 ): # CPU-bound work total += 1 return total async def other_task (): print ( " Other: I want to run!" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) print ( " Other: I finally ran!" ) # With the cooperative coroutine, other_task gets interleaved print ( "=== Cooperative ===" ) await asyncio . gather ( cooperative (), other_task ()) print ( " 
 === Greedy ===" ) results = await asyncio . gather ( greedy (), other_task ()) # Notice: other_task only runs AFTER greedy finishes! === Cooperative === Cooperative: step 0 Other: I want to run! Cooperative: step 1 Other: I finally ran! Cooperative: step 2 === Greedy === Greedy: step 0 Greedy: step 1 Greedy: step 2 Other: I want to run! Other: I finally ran! In the cooperative run, other_task gets a turn between the steps. In the greedy run, greedy never reaches an await , so other_task has to wait until it's completely finished. asyncio uses cooperative multitasking : a task only gives up control when it reaches an await . One long block of synchronous code freezes everything else. For heavy blocking work inside async code, use asyncio.to_thread() (Section 7). 2.4 asyncio.run() : The Entry Point In Jupyter we can await at the top level. Done! If you call asyncio.run() inside Jupyter you get RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop . All results lost! === return_exceptions=True (resilient) === OK: A ok FAILED: B failed! OK: C ok Be careful with the default behaviour. Controlling Execution: Timeouts, Cancellation, Shielding 4.1 Timeouts with asyncio.wait_for async def slow_query (): print ( " Query started..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 5 ) # Takes 5 seconds return "query result" # Set a 2-second timeout print ( "=== wait_for timeout ===" ) try : result = await asyncio . wait_for ( slow_query (), timeout = 2.0 ) print ( f " Result: { result } " ) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( " Timed out! Query took too long." ) print ( " The coroutine was automatically CANCELLED." ) === wait_for timeout === Query started... Timed out! Query took too long. The coroutine was automatically CANCELLED. When the timeout runs out, wait_for cancels slow_query and raises a timeout error, so the cell takes about 2 seconds instead of 5. (Since Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is just another name for the built-in TimeoutError .) 4.2 Task Cancellation async def long_running_job (): try : print ( " Job: Starting..." ) for i in range ( 10 ): print ( f " Job: Step { i + 1 } /10" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( " Job: Completed!" ) # This won't print except asyncio . CancelledError : # This is where you do cleanup! print ( " Job: CANCELLED! Cleaning up resources..." ) raise # Re-raise to properly cancel async def supervisor (): task = asyncio . create_task ( long_running_job ()) # Let it run for 1.5 seconds, then cancel await asyncio . sleep ( 1.5 ) print ( " Supervisor: Cancelling the job!" ) task . cancel () try : await task except asyncio . CancelledError : print ( " Supervisor: Job was successfully cancelled." ) await supervisor () Job: Starting... Job: Step 1/10 Job: Step 2/10 Job: Step 3/10 Supervisor: Cancelling the job! Job: CANCELLED! Cleaning up resources... Supervisor: Job was successfully cancelled. task.cancel() doesn't stop the task instantly. It raises CancelledError inside the task at its next await . The task can catch it to clean up (close files, release connections), but it should then re-raise it so the cancellation actually completes. 4.3 Shielding Tasks from Cancellation Sometimes a piece of work must not be cancelled , for example saving data to a database: async def critical_save ( data ): """This MUST complete even if the parent is cancelled.""" print ( f " Saving ' { data } ' to database..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) print ( f " Save complete!" ) return True async def process_with_save (): print ( " Processing..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) # Shield protects the inner coroutine from cancellation try : result = await asyncio . shield ( critical_save ( "important_data" )) print ( f " Save result: { result } " ) except asyncio . CancelledError : print ( " Process was cancelled, but save continues in background!" ) raise task = asyncio . create_task ( process_with_save ()) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.8 ) # Let it start the save task . cancel () try : await task except asyncio . CancelledError : pass # Give the shielded save time to complete await asyncio . sleep ( 1.5 ) print ( " All done." ) Processing... Saving 'important_data' to database... Process was cancelled, but save continues in background! Save complete! All done. Cancelling task cancels process_with_save , which was waiting on the shield. The inner critical_save is protected, so it keeps running in the background and "Save complete!" still appears. The final asyncio.sleep(1.5) is only there to give it time to finish before the cell ends. 4.4 asyncio.wait : Fine-Grained Control wait gives you more control than gather : you can wait for the first task to complete, the first one to raise an exception, or all of them. async def racer ( name , speed ): await asyncio . sleep ( speed ) return f " { name } finished in { speed } s!" tasks = [ asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Alice" , 2.0 )), asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Bob" , 1.0 )), asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Charlie" , 1.5 )), ] # FIRST_COMPLETED: returns as soon as ONE task finishes done , pending = await asyncio . wait ( tasks , return_when = asyncio . FIRST_COMPLETED ) print ( "First to finish:" ) for task in done : print ( f " { task . result () } " ) print ( f " 
 Still running: { len ( pending ) } tasks" ) # Clean up: wait for the rest remaining_done , _ = await asyncio . wait ( pending ) print ( " 
 Remaining results:" ) for task in remaining_done : print ( f " { task . result () } " ) First to finish: Bob finished in 1.0s! Still running: 2 tasks Remaining results: Alice finished in 2.0s! Charlie finished in 1.5s! wait returns two sets of tasks, done and pending , rather than results; call .result() on each finished task. Sets have no order, so the remaining results may print in either order. Quick recap asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout) cancels the coroutine if it takes too long. task.cancel() raises CancelledError inside the task; clean up, then re-raise. asyncio.shield() protects inner work from being cancelled along with its caller. asyncio.wait() returns (done, pending) sets and can stop at the first finished task. 5. Coordination: Queues, Locks, Semaphores, Events When coroutines share data or resources, they need ways to coordinate. asyncio provides the same tools you'd find in threading, in async form. 5.1 asyncio.Queue : Producer/Consumer async def producer ( queue , n_items ): for i in range ( n_items ): item = f "item- { i } " await asyncio . sleep ( random . uniform ( 0.1 , 0.5 )) await queue . put ( item ) print ( f " [Producer] Put: { item } (queue size: { queue . qsize () } )" ) async def consumer ( queue , name ): while True : item = await queue . get () # Blocks until an item is available if item is None : # Poison pill = stop signal print ( f " [ { name } ] Received stop signal. Shutting down." ) break # Process the item process_time = random . uniform ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Processing: { item } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( process_time ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Done: { item } ( { process_time : .1f } s)" ) queue . task_done () # Bounded queue: maxsize prevents producer from getting too far ahead queue = asyncio .  All work complete!" ) [Producer] Put: item-0 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-0... [Producer] Put: item-1 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Processing: item-1... [Worker-A] Done: item-0 (0.5s) [Producer] Put: item-2 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-2... [Producer] Put: item-3 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Done: item-1 (0.8s) [Worker-B] Processing: item-3... [Worker-A] Done: item-2 (0.6s) [Producer] Put: item-4 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-4... [Producer] Put: item-5 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Done: item-3 (0.8s) [Worker-B] Processing: item-5... [Worker-A] Done: item-4 (0.5s) [Worker-B] Done: item-5 (0.4s) [Worker-A] Received stop signal. Shutting down. [Worker-B] Received stop signal. Shutting down. All work complete! maxsize=3 means put waits when the queue is full, so a fast producer can't run far ahead of the consumers. queue.join() waits until every item has been marked done with task_done() . Only then do we send one None (the stop signal, or poison pill ) per worker. 5.2 asyncio.Lock : Mutual Exclusion # Shared counter WITHOUT a lock: race condition! counter_no_lock = 0 async def increment_unsafe ( n ): global counter_no_lock for _ in range ( n ): temp = counter_no_lock await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) # Context switch point! counter_no_lock = temp + 1 counter_no_lock = 0 await asyncio . gather ( increment_unsafe ( 100 ), increment_unsafe ( 100 ), ) print ( f "Without lock: counter = { counter_no_lock } (expected 200)" ) # Shared counter WITH a lock: safe! counter_with_lock = 0 lock = asyncio . Lock () async def increment_safe ( n ): global counter_with_lock for _ in range ( n ): async with lock : # Only one coroutine can enter at a time temp = counter_with_lock await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) counter_with_lock = temp + 1 counter_with_lock = 0 await asyncio . gather ( increment_safe ( 100 ), increment_safe ( 100 ), ) print ( f "With lock: counter = { counter_with_lock } (expected 200)" ) Without lock: counter = 100 (expected 200) With lock: counter = 200 (expected 200) Without the lock, both coroutines read the same value, pause at await asyncio.sleep(0) , and then both write temp + 1 , so half of the increments are lost. Inside async with lock , only one coroutine at a time can run the read-pause-write steps. So yes, single-threaded async code can still have race conditions, but only at await points. 5.3 asyncio.Semaphore : Rate Limiting A semaphore limits how many coroutines can use a resource at the same time. Async Iteration: async for and async with 6.1 Async Generators async def event_stream ( source , count = 5 ): """Simulates a stream of events arriving over time.""" for i in range ( count ): await asyncio . sleep ( random . uniform ( 0.2 , 0.8 )) event = { "source" : source , "id" : i , "value" : random . randint ( 1 , 100 ), } yield event # 'yield' in an 'async def' = async generator # Consume with 'async for' print ( "Receiving events:" ) async for event in event_stream ( "sensor-1" , count = 5 ): print ( f " Event # { event [ 'id' ] } : value= { event [ 'value' ] } " ) Receiving events: Event #0: value=85 Event #1: value=40 Event #2: value=56 Event #3: value=52 Event #4: value=15 An async def that contains yield is an async generator . async for awaits each item, so while the loop waits for the next event, other tasks can run. 6.2 Async Comprehensions async def get_price ( item ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) prices = { "apple" : 1.50 , "banana" : 0.75 , "cherry" : 3.00 , "date" : 5.50 } return prices . get ( item , 0 ) # Async list comprehension (awaits inside the comprehension!) items = [ "apple" , "banana" , "cherry" , "date" ] prices = [ await get_price ( item ) for item in items ] print ( f "Prices: { dict ( zip ( items , prices )) } " ) # Async generator comprehension with 'async for' async def number_stream ( n ): for i in range ( n ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.05 ) yield i # Filter even numbers from the async stream evens = [ x async for x in number_stream ( 10 ) if x % 2 == 0 ] print ( f "Even numbers: { evens } " ) Prices: {'apple': 1.5, 'banana': 0.75, 'cherry': 3.0, 'date': 5.5} Even numbers: [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] Careful: [await get_price(item) for item in items] awaits the calls one after another , so it's sequential (4 × 0.1 s). To fetch all the prices at the same time, you'd write await asyncio.gather(*(get_price(item) for item in items)) . 6.3 Async Context Managers ( async with ) Use async with when setting up or tearing down a resource involves async operations. from contextlib import asynccontextmanager # Method 1: Class-based (implement __aenter__ and __aexit__) class AsyncTimer : """Times an async block.""" def __init__ ( self , label ): self . label = label async def __aenter__ ( self ): self . start = time . time () print ( f " [ { self . label } ] Timer started" ) return self async def __aexit__ ( self , exc_type , exc_val , exc_tb ): elapsed = time . time () - self . start print ( f " [ { self . label } ] Timer stopped: { elapsed : .2f } s" ) async with AsyncTimer ( "fetch" ) as timer : await asyncio . sleep ( 0.7 ) print ( " Doing work..." ) # Method 2: Decorator-based (simpler for most cases) @asynccontextmanager async def managed_connection ( db_name ): print ( f " Connecting to { db_name } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.3 ) conn = { "db" : db_name , "status" : "connected" } try : yield conn # Hand the connection to the caller finally : print ( f " Disconnecting from { db_name } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) print ( f " Disconnected." ) print () async with managed_connection ( "mydb" ) as conn : print ( f " Using connection: { conn } " ) [fetch] Timer started Doing work... [fetch] Timer stopped: 0.70s Connecting to mydb... Using connection: {'db': 'mydb', 'status': 'connected'} Disconnecting from mydb... Disconnected. Two ways to write the same idea: Class-based : write __aenter__ (setup) and __aexit__ (teardown). @asynccontextmanager : write one async generator. The code before yield is the setup, the code after it is the teardown. Putting the teardown in finally makes sure it runs even if the block raises an error. Quick recap An async def with yield is an async generator; consume it with async for . await inside a list comprehension runs the calls sequentially; use gather to run them concurrently. Async context managers handle async setup/teardown; @asynccontextmanager is the short way to write one. 7. Bridging Sync and Async: Threads and Processes Sometimes you need to call blocking code from async code (for example a library that has no async version), or start async code from normal synchronous code. 7.1 asyncio.to_thread : Run Blocking Code Without Freezing the Loop import hashlib def cpu_heavy_work ( data ): """Simulates CPU-bound work (blocking!).""" result = data for _ in range ( 100_000 ): result = hashlib . sha256 ( result . encode ()) . hexdigest () return result [: 16 ] def blocking_io (): """Simulates blocking I/O (like a non-async database driver).""" time . sleep ( 1 ) return "data from blocking call" # BAD: calling blocking functions directly freezes the event loop # GOOD: run them in a thread with to_thread() print ( "Running blocking + async work concurrently:" ) start = time . time () results = await asyncio . gather ( asyncio . to_thread ( cpu_heavy_work , "hello" ), # Runs in a thread asyncio . to_thread ( blocking_io ), # Runs in a thread asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), # Runs in the event loop ) print ( f " 
 Hash result: { results [ 0 ] } " ) print ( f "IO result: { results [ 1 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { time . time () - start : .1f } s (all ran concurrently!)" ) Running blocking + async work concurrently: Hash result: 3b2d9ab4b38fe0bc IO result: data from blocking call Total time: 1.0s (all ran concurrently!) The event loop stays free while the two threads work, so the sleep, the blocking I/O and the hashing all overlap. One caveat: because of Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), only one thread runs Python code at a time. Moving cpu_heavy_work to a thread stops it from freezing the loop, but it does not make CPU-heavy Python code faster. For real CPU speed-ups you need separate processes. 7.2 loop.run_in_executor : Thread Pools and Process Pools run_in_executor lets you choose the pool the work runs in. Here's a thread pool: from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor def compute ( n ): """A CPU-bound function.""" return sum ( i * i for i in range ( n )) # Using a custom thread pool loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () with ThreadPoolExecutor ( max_workers = 4 ) as pool : results = await asyncio . gather ( loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 1_000_000 ), loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 2_000_000 ), loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 3_000_000 ), ) for i , r in enumerate ( results ): print ( f " Result { i } : { r : , } " ) Result 0: 333,332,833,333,500,000 Result 1: 2,666,664,666,667,000,000 Result 2: 8,999,995,500,000,500,000 We print the results with {r:,} . Formatting with {r:,.0f} would first turn these big integers into floats and print slightly wrong digits at the end. For CPU-bound work, swap in a ProcessPoolExecutor so each job runs in its own process, on its own core. Process pools need the worker function to be importable by the child processes, so they don't work reliably with functions defined in a notebook. Use them from a .py script like this: # cpu_jobs.py import asyncio from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def compute ( n ): return sum ( i * i for i in range ( n )) async def main (): loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () with ProcessPoolExecutor () as pool : results = await asyncio . gather ( * ( loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , n ) for n in ( 1_000_000 , 2_000_000 , 3_000_000 )) ) print ( results ) if __name__ == "__main__" : asyncio . run ( main ()) When to Use What Situation Solution Blocking I/O (file reads, a non-async database driver) asyncio.to_thread() or a ThreadPoolExecutor CPU-bound computation ProcessPoolExecutor or multiprocessing Async-native I/O ( aiohttp , asyncpg ) Just await it directly Calling async code from sync code asyncio.run() Quick recap Never call blocking functions directly in async code; they freeze the event loop. asyncio.to_thread(func, *args) runs a blocking function in a thread and lets you await the result. Threads keep the loop responsive but don't speed up CPU-bound Python code (GIL). Use processes for that. loop.run_in_executor(pool, func, *args) lets you pick a thread pool or a process pool. 8. Real-World Project: Async Web Crawler Let's put everything together. We'll build a simulated web crawler that: starts from a list of seed URLs, fetches pages concurrently, with a semaphore limiting how many fetches run at once, reads the links on each page, uses a queue to keep track of the pages still to visit (the crawl frontier ), stops following links beyond a maximum depth, and stops after a maximum number of pages, retries a failed fetch a couple of times before giving up on that page. Instead of a real network we use FAKE_WEB , a dictionary of pages and their links, so the crawler runs anywhere. import asyncio import random import time # Simulated web: maps each URL to the links on that page FAKE_WEB = { "/" : [ "/about" , "/products" , "/blog" ], "/about" : [ "/about/team" , "/about/history" , "/" ], "/products" : [ "/products/1" , "/products/2" , "/products/3" ], "/blog" : [ "/blog/post-1" , "/blog/post-2" , "/" ], "/about/team" : [ "/about" ], "/about/history" : [ "/about" , "/" ], "/products/1" : [ "/products" , "/" ], "/products/2" : [ "/products" , "/products/1" ], "/products/3" : [ "/products" ], "/blog/post-1" : [ "/blog" , "/blog/post-2" ], "/blog/post-2" : [ "/blog" , "/" ], } async def fetch_page ( url , semaphore ): """Simulate fetching a web page.""" async with semaphore : delay = random . uniform ( 0.1 , 0.5 ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) if random . random () < 0.1 : # 10% chance of failure raise ConnectionError ( f "Failed to fetch { url } " ) links = FAKE_WEB . get ( url , []) size = random . randint ( 500 , 5000 ) return { "url" : url , "links" : links , "size" : size , "latency" : round ( delay , 3 )} async def fetch_with_retry ( url , semaphore , worker_id , attempts = 3 ): """Try a fetch up to `attempts` times before giving up.""" for attempt in range ( 1 , attempts + 1 ): try : return await fetch_page ( url , semaphore ) except ConnectionError as e : print ( f " [W { worker_id } ] ERROR (attempt { attempt } / { attempts } ): { e } " ) return None # every attempt failed async def crawl ( seeds , max_pages = 15 , max_depth = 2 , max_concurrent = 3 ): """Crawl starting from the seed URLs.""" visited = set () results = [] queue = asyncio . Queue () # holds (url, depth) pairs semaphore = asyncio . Semaphore ( max_concurrent ) for url in seeds : queue . put_nowait (( url , 0 )) async def worker ( worker_id ): while True : url , depth = await queue . get () try : if url in visited or len ( visited ) >= max_pages : continue # skip it (the finally block still runs) visited . add ( url ) page = await fetch_with_retry ( url , semaphore , worker_id ) if page is None : continue results . append ( page ) print ( f " [W { worker_id } ] Crawled { url } (depth { depth } , " f " { page [ 'size' ] } B, { page [ 'latency' ] } s, { len ( page [ 'links' ]) } links)" ) # Queue the links we found, unless we're already at max depth if depth < max_depth : for link in page [ "links" ]: if link not in visited : queue . put_nowait (( link , depth + 1 )) finally : queue . task_done () # mark this queue item as handled workers = [ asyncio . create_task ( worker ( i )) for i in range ( max_concurrent )] # join() returns once every queued URL has been handled # (including all the links discovered along the way) await queue . join () # The workers are now idle, waiting on an empty queue, so stop them for w in workers : w . cancel () await asyncio . gather ( * workers , return_exceptions = True ) return results # Run the crawler! print ( "Starting web crawler... 
 " ) start = time . time () pages = await crawl ([ "/" ], max_pages = 11 , max_depth = 2 , max_concurrent = 3 ) elapsed = time . time () - start total_bytes = sum ( p [ "size" ] for p in pages ) avg_latency = sum ( p [ "latency" ] for p in pages ) / len ( pages ) if pages else 0 print ( f " 
 { '=' * 50 } " ) print ( "CRAWL REPORT" ) print ( f " { '=' * 50 } " ) print ( f " Pages crawled: { len ( pages ) } " ) print ( f " Total data: { total_bytes : , } bytes" ) print ( f " Avg latency: { avg_latency : .3f } s" ) print ( f " Wall clock time: { elapsed : .1f } s" ) print ( f " Sequential est: ~ { sum ( p [ 'latency' ] for p in pages ) : .1f } s" ) Starting web crawler... [W0] Crawled / (depth 0, 1638B, 0.357s, 3 links) [W0] Crawled /about (depth 1, 1862B, 0.209s, 3 links) [W2] Crawled /blog (depth 1, 1888B, 0.346s, 3 links) [W1] ERROR (attempt 1/3): Failed to fetch /products [W2] Crawled /about/history (depth 2, 1348B, 0.145s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /about/team (depth 2, 3923B, 0.474s, 1 links) [W1] Crawled /products (depth 1, 4847B, 0.278s, 3 links) [W2] Crawled /blog/post-1 (depth 2, 800B, 0.255s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /blog/post-2 (depth 2, 3632B, 0.199s, 2 links) [W2] ERROR (attempt 1/3): Failed to fetch /products/2 [W1] Crawled /products/1 (depth 2, 4731B, 0.487s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /products/3 (depth 2, 4505B, 0.355s, 1 links) [W2] Crawled /products/2 (depth 2, 4574B, 0.227s, 2 links) ================================================== CRAWL REPORT ================================================== Pages crawled: 11 Total data: 33,748 bytes Avg latency: 0.303s Wall clock time: 1.8s Sequential est: ~3.3s How the pieces fit together: The queue holds (url, depth) pairs waiting to be crawled. Three workers take URLs off it. The visited set makes sure no page is crawled twice, even though many pages link back to / . Every queue.get() is matched by a queue.task_done() in a finally block, even when a URL is skipped. That's what lets await queue.join() know when all the work, including newly discovered links, is finished. Once the queue is drained, the workers are just waiting forever on queue.get() , so we cancel them. The semaphore caps how many fetches run at once. Here it matches the number of workers; in a bigger crawler you might have many workers sharing a smaller limit. Your report will differ between runs because of the random delays and failures. Try changing max_depth to 1 and see which pages drop out. Quick recap A queue plus a fixed number of worker tasks is the standard shape for an async crawler or job runner. Pair every queue.get() with queue.task_done() (in finally ) so queue.join() knows when the work is done. Cancel idle workers after join() , then gather them so their cancellation is cleaned up. Final Challenge: Async Job Scheduler Build an async job scheduler that: accepts jobs with priorities (higher priority runs first), limits concurrency with a semaphore, supports a timeout per job, collects results and errors separately, and prints some statistics at the end. Store each success as {"name": ..., "result": ...} in self.results and each failure as {"name": ..., "error": ...} in self.errors , using the string "timeout" as the error for jobs that time out. import asyncio import random import time class AsyncJobScheduler : def __init__ ( self , max_concurrent = 3 , default_timeout = 5.0 ): self . max_concurrent = max_concurrent self . default_timeout = default_timeout self . jobs = [] # List of (priority, name, coro_func, timeout) self . results = [] self . errors = [] def add_job ( self , name , coro_func , priority = 0 , timeout = None ): """Add a job. Higher priority = runs first.""" # YOUR CODE HERE pass async def run_all ( self ): """Run all jobs respecting priority, concurrency, and timeouts.""" # YOUR CODE HERE: # 1. Sort jobs by priority (highest first) # 2. Create a semaphore # 3. For each job, create a task that: # a. Acquires the semaphore # b. Runs the coroutine with wait_for (timeout) # c. Stores result or error # 4. Gather all tasks # 5. Return (results, errors) pass # --- Test jobs --- async def fast_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.3 ) return "fast result" async def slow_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 3 ) return "slow result" async def flaky_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) if random . random () < 0.5 : raise RuntimeError ( "Random failure!" ) return "flaky result" # --- Build and run --- scheduler = AsyncJobScheduler ( max_concurrent = 2 , default_timeout = 2.0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-1" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-2" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Slow-1" , slow_job , priority = 0 ) # Will timeout! scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-1" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) # Highest priority scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-2" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-3" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # results, errors = await scheduler.run_all() # assert len(results) + len(errors) == 6 # assert {"name": "Slow-1", "error": "timeout"} in errors # assert [name for _, name, _, _ in scheduler.jobs][:2] == ["Flaky-1", "Flaky-2"] # highest priority first # print(f"✓ Successes: {len(results)}, Failures: {len(errors)}") Show solution class AsyncJobScheduler : def __init__ ( self , max_concurrent = 3 , default_timeout = 5.0 ): self . max_concurrent = max_concurrent self . default_timeout = default_timeout self . jobs = [] self . results = [] self . errors = [] def add_job ( self , name , coro_func , priority = 0 , timeout = None ): timeout = timeout or self . default_timeout self . jobs . append (( priority , name , coro_func , timeout )) async def _run_job ( self , name , coro_func , timeout , semaphore ): async with semaphore : try : print ( f " [ { name } ] Starting..." ) result = await asyncio . wait_for ( coro_func (), timeout = timeout ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Success: { result } " ) self . results . append ({ "name" : name , "result" : result }) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( f " [ { name } ] TIMEOUT after { timeout } s" ) self . errors . append ({ "name" : name , "error" : "timeout" }) except Exception as e : print ( f " [ { name } ] FAILED: { e } " ) self . errors . append ({ "name" : name , "error" : str ( e )}) async def run_all ( self ): self . results . clear () self . errors . clear () # Sort by priority (highest first) self . jobs . sort ( key = lambda j : j [ 0 ], reverse = True ) sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( self . max_concurrent ) tasks = [ self . _run_job ( name , coro_func , timeout , sem ) for _ , name , coro_func , timeout in self . jobs ] start = time . time () await asyncio . gather ( * tasks ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " 
 { '=' * 40 } " ) print ( f "JOB REPORT ( { elapsed : .1f } s total)" ) print ( f " { '=' * 40 } " ) print ( f " Successes: { len ( self . results ) } " ) print ( f " Failures: { len ( self . errors ) } " ) for e in self . errors : print ( f " - { e [ 'name' ] } : { e [ 'error' ] } " ) return self . results , self . errors scheduler = AsyncJobScheduler ( max_concurrent = 2 , default_timeout = 2.0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-1" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-2" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Slow-1" , slow_job , priority = 0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-1" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-2" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-3" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) results , errors = await scheduler . run_all () Quick recap Sorting the jobs before creating the tasks, plus a semaphore, makes higher-priority jobs start first. wait_for gives every job its own timeout; try/except around it keeps one bad job from stopping the rest. Quiz: Test Your Knowledge For each question, predict the answer first , then run the cell (where there is one) and open the answer. Q1: What's the output order? async def f ( label , delay ): print ( f "start { label } " ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) print ( f "end { label } " ) results = await asyncio . gather ( f ( "X" , 1 ), f ( "Y" , 0.5 ), f ( "Z" , 0.1 )) start X start Y start Z end Z end Y end X Show answer start X start Y start Z end Z (0.1s) end Y (0.5s) end X (1.0s) All three start immediately, because gather runs them concurrently. They finish in order of their sleep time. Q2: Will this code finish? To be safe, the cell stops waiting after 2 seconds, so a hang can't freeze your notebook. lock = asyncio . Lock () async def task_a (): async with lock : await task_b () async def task_b (): async with lock : print ( "done" ) try : await asyncio . wait_for ( task_a (), timeout = 2 ) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( "Still waiting after 2 seconds..." ) Still waiting after 2 seconds... Show answer No, it deadlocks. task_a holds the lock and then calls task_b , which tries to take the same lock. asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant (the task that holds it can't take it a second time), so task_b waits forever. Without the wait_for timeout, the cell would never finish. Fix: restructure the code so the lock isn't held while calling task_b , or avoid taking the same lock twice. Q3: What's wrong with this code? Assume fetch(url) is a coroutine that takes about 1 second. async def fetch_all ( urls ): results = [] for url in urls : result = await fetch ( url ) results . append ( result ) return results Show answer It's sequential. The for loop awaits each fetch() one at a time, so 10 URLs take about 10 seconds. To fetch them concurrently: async def fetch_all ( urls ): return await asyncio . gather ( * [ fetch ( url ) for url in urls ]) This is the most common asyncio performance mistake. Q4: When should you use asyncio.to_thread() ? Show answer When you need to call a blocking function from async code without freezing the event loop. Common cases: Database drivers that aren't async ( sqlite3 , psycopg2 ) File I/O ( open , read , write ) Third-party libraries that don't support async CPU-heavy work, to keep the loop responsive (it won't run faster, because of the GIL) def read_file ( path ): with open ( path ) as f : return f . read () # Instead of: data = read_file ( "big_file.csv" ) # blocks the event loop # Do: data = await asyncio . to_thread ( read_file , "big_file.csv" ) # runs in a thread Quick recap Coroutines in gather start together and finish in order of how long they wait. asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: taking it twice in the same task deadlocks. Awaiting inside a for loop is sequential; use gather to overlap the waits. asyncio.to_thread is for blocking calls you can't make async. Summary & Cheat Sheet Core Patterns import asyncio # Define a coroutine async def work (): await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) return "done" # Run from a .py script (not inside Jupyter) asyncio . run ( work ()) # Run concurrently results = await asyncio . gather ( a (), b (), c ()) # Start in the background, await later (keep the reference!) task = asyncio . create_task ( work ()) result = await task # Structured concurrency (3.11+) async with asyncio . TaskGroup () as tg : t1 = tg . create_task ( a ()) t2 = tg . create_task ( b ()) # Process results as they complete for coro in asyncio . as_completed ([ a (), b (), c ()]): result = await coro Control Flow # Timeout await asyncio . wait_for ( slow (), timeout = 5.0 ) # Cancellation task . cancel () # Shield from cancellation await asyncio . shield ( critical_operation ()) # Wait for the first one (or all) done , pending = await asyncio . wait ( tasks , return_when = asyncio . FIRST_COMPLETED ) Coordination # Queue (producer/consumer) queue = asyncio . Queue ( maxsize = 10 ) await queue . put ( item ) item = await queue . get () queue . task_done () # Lock (one at a time): create it ONCE and share it lock = asyncio . Lock () async with lock : ... # critical section # Semaphore (at most 5 at a time): create it ONCE and share it sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( 5 ) async with sem : ... # rate-limited work # Event (signalling) event = asyncio . Event () await event . wait () # block until set event . set () # release all waiters Bridging Sync and Async # Blocking function -> awaitable result = await asyncio . to_thread ( blocking_func , arg1 , arg2 ) # Async code -> from a sync script's entry point asyncio . run ( main ()) Common Mistakes Mistake Fix Forgetting await Always await coroutine calls await inside a loop, one call at a time Use gather() instead Calling time.sleep() Use await asyncio.sleep() Blocking I/O in async code Use asyncio.to_thread() Creating a new Lock / Semaphore on every use Create it once and share it Not handling CancelledError Catch it to clean up, then re-raise Further Reading Official asyncio docs Real Python: Async IO in Python Python Concurrency with asyncio (book) Popular async libraries: aiohttp (HTTP), asyncpg (PostgreSQL), aiofiles (file I/O), aiocache (caching) What's Next This notebook and the Event-Driven Programming notebook together take you from callbacks all the way to production-style async patterns. You'll use these ideas again in the FastAPI notebook, where endpoints can be async def functions running on exactly this kind of event loop.

Parallelism : several cooks, each working on their own dish at the same moment. asyncio gives you concurrency on a single thread. For true parallelism you need several processes ( multiprocessing ). The last line prints the actual time. import time start = time . time () time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second time . sleep ( 1 ) # wait 1 second print ( f "Took { time . time () - start : .1f } s" ) Took 3.0s Show answer About 3 seconds. time.sleep is blocking : the whole program stops at each call, so the three waits add up. With asyncio , the same three waits can overlap and take about 1 second : await asyncio . gather ( asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), ) Quick recap I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting; that waiting is what async code overlaps. Concurrency = taking turns on one thread. Parallelism = running at the same moment on several cores. time.sleep blocks everything; await asyncio.sleep lets other tasks run meanwhile.

docs.text: Let's see the problem with synchronous I/O for ourselves. First, three "network calls" made the normal way: import time def fetch_data_sync ( source , delay ): """Simulates a synchronous network call.""" print ( f " [ { source } ] Requesting..." ) time . sleep ( delay ) # BLOCKS the entire program! print ( f " [ { source } ] Done ( { delay } s)" ) return f " { source } _data" print ( "=== Synchronous (blocking) ===" ) start = time . time () r1 = fetch_data_sync ( "Database" , 1.0 ) r2 = fetch_data_sync ( "API" , 1.5 ) r3 = fetch_data_sync ( "Cache" , 0.5 ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " \n Results: { [ r1 , r2 , r3 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { elapsed : .1f } s (1.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 3.0s expected)" ) === Synchronous (blocking) === [Database] Requesting... [Database] Done (1.0s) [API] Requesting... [API] Done (1.5s) [Cache] Requesting... [Cache] Done (0.5s) Results: ['Database_data', 'API_data', 'Cache_data'] Total time: 3.0s (1.0 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 3.0s expected) Each call has to finish before the next one starts, so the waits add up. Now the same three calls written with asyncio : import asyncio async def fetch_data_async ( source , delay ): """Simulates an async network call.""" print ( f " [ { source } ] Requesting..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) # Non-blocking! Other tasks can run. print ( f " [ { source } ] Done ( { delay } s)" ) return f " { source } _data" print ( "=== Asynchronous (non-blocking) ===" ) start = time . time () r1 , r2 , r3 = await asyncio . gather ( fetch_data_async ( "Database" , 1.0 ), fetch_data_async ( "API" , 1.5 ), fetch_data_async ( "Cache" , 0.5 ), ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " \n Results: { [ r1 , r2 , r3 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { elapsed : .1f } s (max of 1.0, 1.5, 0.5 = 1.5s expected)" ) === Asynchronous (non-blocking) === [Database] Requesting... [API] Requesting... [Cache] Requesting... [Cache] Done (0.5s) [Database] Done (1.0s) [API] Done (1.5s) Results: ['Database_data', 'API_data', 'Cache_data'] Total time: 1.5s (max of 1.0, 1.5, 0.5 = 1.5s expected) 3.0 s vs 1.5 s. The async version takes only as long as the slowest call, because all three waits happen at the same time.
