docs.text: Synchronous: Asynchronous: t=0 [DB starts] t=0 [DB starts] [API starts] [Cache starts] t=1 [DB done] t=0.5 [Cache done] [API starts] t=1 [DB done] t=2.5 [API done] t=1.5 [API done] [Cache starts] t=3 [Cache done] Total: 1.5s Total: 3.0s The event loop interleaves the waiting: while one coroutine is waiting for I/O, the others get to run. Quick recap Blocking calls run one after another, so total time = sum of all waits. With asyncio.gather , waits overlap, so total time = the longest single wait.
docs.title: How It Works Under the Hood

docs.text: # A coroutine function is defined with 'async def' async def my_coroutine (): print ( "Coroutine started" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) # Yield control to the event loop print ( "Coroutine resumed" ) return 42 # Calling it returns a coroutine OBJECT: it does NOT execute yet! coro = my_coroutine () print ( f "Type: { type ( coro ) } " ) print ( f "It hasn't printed anything yet!" ) # 'await' actually executes it result = await coro print ( f "Result: { result } " ) Type: <class 'coroutine'> It hasn't printed anything yet! Coroutine started Coroutine resumed Result: 42 Calling my_coroutine() only creates a coroutine object; none of the code inside runs yet. That's why "Coroutine started" appears after our two print lines. The code runs when we await it.
docs.title: 2.1 Anatomy of a Coroutine

docs.text: You can only await awaitable objects. There are three kinds: # 1. Coroutines (from 'async def') async def get_value (): return "from coroutine" result1 = await get_value () print ( f "1. Coroutine: { result1 } " ) # 2. Tasks (scheduled coroutines) async def delayed_value (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) return "from task" task = asyncio . create_task ( delayed_value ()) result2 = await task print ( f "2. Task: { result2 } " ) # 3. Futures (low-level, rarely used directly) loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () future = loop . create_future () future . set_result ( "from future" ) result3 = await future print ( f "3. Future: { result3 } " ) # NOT awaitable (this would raise TypeError): # await 42 # await "hello" # await [1, 2, 3] 1. Coroutine: from coroutine 2. Task: from task 3. Future: from future In everyday code you'll await coroutines and tasks. Futures are the low-level building block that tasks are built on; libraries use them, but application code rarely creates one directly. Inside async code, get the current loop with asyncio.get_running_loop() . The older asyncio.get_event_loop() is deprecated in many situations.
docs.title: 2.2 What Can You await?

docs.text: Every await is a checkpoint where the event loop may switch to another task. No await means no switching, which means no concurrency. async def cooperative (): """Good: yields control regularly.""" for i in range ( 3 ): print ( f " Cooperative: step { i } " ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) # Yield control, even with 0 delay! async def greedy (): """Bad: hogs the event loop with CPU-bound work.""" total = 0 for i in range ( 3 ): print ( f " Greedy: step { i } " ) # No await here! Other tasks are BLOCKED until this finishes. for _ in range ( 1_000_000 ): # CPU-bound work total += 1 return total async def other_task (): print ( " Other: I want to run!" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) print ( " Other: I finally ran!" ) # With the cooperative coroutine, other_task gets interleaved print ( "=== Cooperative ===" ) await asyncio . gather ( cooperative (), other_task ()) print ( " \n === Greedy ===" ) results = await asyncio . gather ( greedy (), other_task ()) # Notice: other_task only runs AFTER greedy finishes! === Cooperative === Cooperative: step 0 Other: I want to run! Cooperative: step 1 Other: I finally ran! Cooperative: step 2 === Greedy === Greedy: step 0 Greedy: step 1 Greedy: step 2 Other: I want to run! Other: I finally ran! In the cooperative run, other_task gets a turn between the steps. In the greedy run, greedy never reaches an await , so other_task has to wait until it's completely finished. asyncio uses cooperative multitasking : a task only gives up control when it reaches an await . One long block of synchronous code freezes everything else. For heavy blocking work inside async code, use asyncio.to_thread() (Section 7).
docs.title: 2.3 The Golden Rule of await

docs.text: In Jupyter we can await at the top level. In a normal .py script you need asyncio.run() : # This is how you'd write it in a .py file: script_code = ''' import asyncio async def main(): print("Hello from async!") await asyncio.sleep(1) print("Done!") # This creates the event loop, runs main(), and cleans up asyncio.run(main()) ''' print ( "In a .py script, you use asyncio.run():" ) print ( script_code ) # In Jupyter, asyncio.run() won't work because a loop is already running. # Instead, just use 'await' directly: async def main (): print ( "Hello from async!" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( "Done!" ) await main () In a .py script, you use asyncio.run(): import asyncio async def main(): print("Hello from async!") await asyncio.sleep(1) print("Done!") # This creates the event loop, runs main(), and cleans up asyncio.run(main()) Hello from async! Done! If you call asyncio.run() inside Jupyter you get RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop . Jupyter already runs an event loop for you, which is why this notebook uses top-level await instead.
docs.title: 2.4 asyncio.run(): The Entry Point

docs.text: Write a coroutine countdown(name, seconds) that counts down from seconds , printing one number per second, and prints DONE! at the end. Then run two countdowns concurrently . async def countdown ( name , seconds ): """Count down from 'seconds' to 0, printing each second.""" # YOUR CODE HERE pass # Run two countdowns concurrently # YOUR CODE: use asyncio.gather to run countdown("A", 5) and countdown("B", 3) # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # start = time.time() # await asyncio.gather(countdown("A", 2), countdown("B", 1)) # elapsed = time.time() - start # assert 1.8 < elapsed < 2.5, "The two countdowns should run at the same time" # print("✓ Countdown works!") Show solution async def countdown ( name , seconds ): for i in range ( seconds , 0 , - 1 ): print ( f " [ { name } ] { i } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) print ( f " [ { name } ] DONE!" ) await asyncio . gather ( countdown ( "A" , 5 ), countdown ( "B" , 3 )) Quick recap Calling an async def function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited. You can await coroutines, tasks and futures. The event loop can only switch tasks at an await ; long synchronous code blocks everything. In scripts, start async code with asyncio.run(main()) . In Jupyter, use top-level await .
docs.title: Try It: Async Timer

docs.text: async def fetch ( name , delay ): await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) return f " { name } (took { delay } s)" # gather returns results in the SAME ORDER as the arguments results = await asyncio . gather ( fetch ( "Alpha" , 2 ), fetch ( "Beta" , 0.5 ), fetch ( "Gamma" , 1 ), ) # Even though Beta finishes first, results are ordered Alpha, Beta, Gamma for i , r in enumerate ( results ): print ( f " Result { i } : { r } " ) Result 0: Alpha (took 2s) Result 1: Beta (took 0.5s) Result 2: Gamma (took 1s) Beta finishes first, but the results come back in the order of the arguments. The whole cell takes about 2 seconds (the slowest call), not 3.5.
docs.title: 3.1 asyncio.gather: Run Several and Collect the Results

docs.text: async def might_fail ( name , fail = False ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.3 ) if fail : raise ValueError ( f " { name } failed!" ) return f " { name } ok" # Default: one failure crashes ALL tasks print ( "=== Default (crash on first error) ===" ) try : results = await asyncio . gather ( might_fail ( "A" ), might_fail ( "B" , fail = True ), might_fail ( "C" ), ) except ValueError as e : print ( f " Caught: { e } " ) print ( " All results lost!" ) # With return_exceptions=True: failures become return values print ( " \n === return_exceptions=True (resilient) ===" ) results = await asyncio . gather ( might_fail ( "A" ), might_fail ( "B" , fail = True ), might_fail ( "C" ), return_exceptions = True , ) for r in results : if isinstance ( r , Exception ): print ( f " FAILED: { r } " ) else : print ( f " OK: { r } " ) === Default (crash on first error) === Caught: B failed! All results lost! === return_exceptions=True (resilient) === OK: A ok FAILED: B failed! OK: C ok Be careful with the default behaviour. "All results lost!" means you don't get the results back from gather . A and C are not cancelled: they keep running in the background. With return_exceptions=True , exceptions are returned in the results list like normal values, so you can check each one.
docs.title: 3.2 Error Handling with gather

docs.text: async def slow_upload ( filename ): print ( f " Uploading { filename } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 2 ) print ( f " Upload complete: { filename } " ) return f " { filename } uploaded" async def main (): # create_task schedules the coroutine to run in the BACKGROUND task = asyncio . create_task ( slow_upload ( "photo.jpg" )) # We can do other work while it runs! print ( " Doing other work..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) print ( " Still doing work..." ) # When we need the result, we await the task result = await task print ( f " Result: { result } " ) # We can also check state without awaiting task2 = asyncio . create_task ( slow_upload ( "video.mp4" )) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( f " Is task2 done? { task2 . done () } " ) await task2 print ( f " Is task2 done? { task2 . done () } " ) await main () Doing other work... Uploading photo.jpg... Still doing work... Upload complete: photo.jpg Result: photo.jpg uploaded Uploading video.mp4... Is task2 done? False Upload complete: video.mp4 Is task2 done? True Notice that "Doing other work..." is printed before "Uploading photo.jpg...". create_task schedules the upload, but it only starts at the next await , when main hands control back to the event loop. task.done() lets you check on a task without waiting for it.
docs.title: 3.3 asyncio.create_task: Schedule and Continue

docs.text: TaskGroup is the modern way to manage a group of tasks. When the async with block ends, every task in it has finished . If one task fails, the group cancels the others. import sys async def process_item ( item , delay ): await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) return f " { item } : processed" if sys . version_info >= ( 3 , 11 ): # TaskGroup is available in Python 3.11+ async with asyncio . TaskGroup () as tg : task1 = tg . create_task ( process_item ( "A" , 1 )) task2 = tg . create_task ( process_item ( "B" , 0.5 )) task3 = tg . create_task ( process_item ( "C" , 1.5 )) # All tasks guaranteed to be done here print ( f " { task1 . result () } " ) print ( f " { task2 . result () } " ) print ( f " { task3 . result () } " ) else : # Fallback for Python 3.10 and below print ( f " Python { sys . version_info . major } . { sys . version_info . minor } detected." ) print ( " TaskGroup requires Python 3.11+. Using gather instead:" ) results = await asyncio . gather ( process_item ( "A" , 1 ), process_item ( "B" , 0.5 ), process_item ( "C" , 1.5 ), ) for r in results : print ( f " { r } " ) A: processed B: processed C: processed If a task inside a TaskGroup raises an exception, the other tasks are cancelled and the errors are raised together as an ExceptionGroup , which you can catch with except* .
docs.title: 3.4 asyncio.TaskGroup: Structured Concurrency (Python 3.11+)

docs.text: Feature gather create_task TaskGroup (3.11+) Returns results Yes, in argument order Await each task yourself Via task.result() Error handling return_exceptions=True Your own try/except Cancels the other tasks on error Cancellation Manual Manual Automatic Use when You want all results together You want to start now and await later You need cleanup guarantees
docs.title: gather vs create_task vs TaskGroup

docs.text: import random async def api_call ( endpoint ): delay = random . uniform ( 0.5 , 2.5 ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) return { "endpoint" : endpoint , "latency" : round ( delay , 2 )} endpoints = [ "/users" , "/products" , "/orders" , "/reviews" , "/stats" ] # gather waits for ALL to complete, then gives you results # as_completed gives you results ONE AT A TIME as they finish! print ( "Results arriving as they complete:" ) coros = [ api_call ( ep ) for ep in endpoints ] for i , coro in enumerate ( asyncio . as_completed ( coros )): result = await coro print ( f " # { i + 1 } finished: { result [ 'endpoint' ] } ( { result [ 'latency' ] } s)" ) Results arriving as they complete: #1 finished: /orders (1.41s) #2 finished: /products (1.61s) #3 finished: /users (2.03s) #4 finished: /stats (2.19s) #5 finished: /reviews (2.38s) Unlike gather , as_completed hands you results in finishing order , so the fastest endpoint comes first. Use it when you want to show progress or act on each result as soon as it's ready.
docs.title: 3.5 asyncio.as_completed: Process Results As They Arrive

docs.text: Write fetch_all(server_ids) , which queries all servers concurrently and returns two lists: the successful results and the error messages. Use gather with return_exceptions=True . async def query_server ( server_id ): """Simulates querying a server. Some servers will fail.""" delay = random . uniform ( 0.2 , 1.0 ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) if random . random () < 0.3 : # 30% failure rate raise ConnectionError ( f "Server { server_id } is down" ) return { "server" : server_id , "data" : f "response_ { server_id } " , "latency" : round ( delay , 2 )} async def fetch_all ( server_ids ): """ Query all servers concurrently. Return a tuple: (successes, failures) - successes: list of result dicts - failures: list of error strings """ # YOUR CODE HERE pass # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # successes, failures = await fetch_all(range(1, 11)) # print(f"Successes: {len(successes)}") # for s in successes: # print(f" Server {s['server']}: {s['data']} ({s['latency']}s)") # print(f"\nFailures: {len(failures)}") # for f in failures: # print(f" {f}") # assert len(successes) + len(failures) == 10 # assert all(isinstance(s, dict) for s in successes) # assert all("is down" in f for f in failures) # print("✓ fetch_all works!") Show solution async def fetch_all ( server_ids ): results = await asyncio . gather ( * [ query_server ( sid ) for sid in server_ids ], return_exceptions = True , ) successes = [ r for r in results if not isinstance ( r , Exception )] failures = [ str ( r ) for r in results if isinstance ( r , Exception )] return successes , failures successes , failures = await fetch_all ( range ( 1 , 11 )) print ( f "Successes: { len ( successes ) } " ) for s in successes : print ( f " Server { s [ 'server' ] } : { s [ 'data' ] } ( { s [ 'latency' ] } s)" ) print ( f " \n Failures: { len ( failures ) } " ) for f in failures : print ( f " { f } " ) Quick recap gather runs coroutines concurrently and returns results in argument order. By default the first exception propagates out of gather ; return_exceptions=True collects them instead. create_task starts a coroutine in the background. Keep a reference and await it later. TaskGroup (3.11+) waits for all its tasks and cancels the rest if one fails. as_completed gives you results in the order they finish.
docs.title: Try It: Parallel Data Fetcher

docs.text: async def slow_query (): print ( " Query started..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 5 ) # Takes 5 seconds return "query result" # Set a 2-second timeout print ( "=== wait_for timeout ===" ) try : result = await asyncio . wait_for ( slow_query (), timeout = 2.0 ) print ( f " Result: { result } " ) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( " Timed out! Query took too long." ) print ( " The coroutine was automatically CANCELLED." ) === wait_for timeout === Query started... Timed out! Query took too long. The coroutine was automatically CANCELLED. When the timeout runs out, wait_for cancels slow_query and raises a timeout error, so the cell takes about 2 seconds instead of 5. (Since Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is just another name for the built-in TimeoutError .)
docs.title: 4.1 Timeouts with asyncio.wait_for

docs.text: async def long_running_job (): try : print ( " Job: Starting..." ) for i in range ( 10 ): print ( f " Job: Step { i + 1 } /10" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) print ( " Job: Completed!" ) # This won't print except asyncio . CancelledError : # This is where you do cleanup! print ( " Job: CANCELLED! Cleaning up resources..." ) raise # Re-raise to properly cancel async def supervisor (): task = asyncio . create_task ( long_running_job ()) # Let it run for 1.5 seconds, then cancel await asyncio . sleep ( 1.5 ) print ( " Supervisor: Cancelling the job!" ) task . cancel () try : await task except asyncio . CancelledError : print ( " Supervisor: Job was successfully cancelled." ) await supervisor () Job: Starting... Job: Step 1/10 Job: Step 2/10 Job: Step 3/10 Supervisor: Cancelling the job! Job: CANCELLED! Cleaning up resources... Supervisor: Job was successfully cancelled. task.cancel() doesn't stop the task instantly. It raises CancelledError inside the task at its next await . The task can catch it to clean up (close files, release connections), but it should then re-raise it so the cancellation actually completes.
docs.title: 4.2 Task Cancellation

docs.text: Sometimes a piece of work must not be cancelled , for example saving data to a database: async def critical_save ( data ): """This MUST complete even if the parent is cancelled.""" print ( f " Saving ' { data } ' to database..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) print ( f " Save complete!" ) return True async def process_with_save (): print ( " Processing..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) # Shield protects the inner coroutine from cancellation try : result = await asyncio . shield ( critical_save ( "important_data" )) print ( f " Save result: { result } " ) except asyncio . CancelledError : print ( " Process was cancelled, but save continues in background!" ) raise task = asyncio . create_task ( process_with_save ()) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.8 ) # Let it start the save task . cancel () try : await task except asyncio . CancelledError : pass # Give the shielded save time to complete await asyncio . sleep ( 1.5 ) print ( " All done." ) Processing... Saving 'important_data' to database... Process was cancelled, but save continues in background! Save complete! All done. Cancelling task cancels process_with_save , which was waiting on the shield. The inner critical_save is protected, so it keeps running in the background and "Save complete!" still appears. The final asyncio.sleep(1.5) is only there to give it time to finish before the cell ends.
docs.title: 4.3 Shielding Tasks from Cancellation

docs.text: wait gives you more control than gather : you can wait for the first task to complete, the first one to raise an exception, or all of them. async def racer ( name , speed ): await asyncio . sleep ( speed ) return f " { name } finished in { speed } s!" tasks = [ asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Alice" , 2.0 )), asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Bob" , 1.0 )), asyncio . create_task ( racer ( "Charlie" , 1.5 )), ] # FIRST_COMPLETED: returns as soon as ONE task finishes done , pending = await asyncio . wait ( tasks , return_when = asyncio . FIRST_COMPLETED ) print ( "First to finish:" ) for task in done : print ( f " { task . result () } " ) print ( f " \n Still running: { len ( pending ) } tasks" ) # Clean up: wait for the rest remaining_done , _ = await asyncio . wait ( pending ) print ( " \n Remaining results:" ) for task in remaining_done : print ( f " { task . result () } " ) First to finish: Bob finished in 1.0s! Still running: 2 tasks Remaining results: Alice finished in 2.0s! Charlie finished in 1.5s! wait returns two sets of tasks, done and pending , rather than results; call .result() on each finished task. Sets have no order, so the remaining results may print in either order. Quick recap asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout) cancels the coroutine if it takes too long. task.cancel() raises CancelledError inside the task; clean up, then re-raise. asyncio.shield() protects inner work from being cancelled along with its caller. asyncio.wait() returns (done, pending) sets and can stop at the first finished task.
docs.title: 4.4 asyncio.wait: Fine-Grained Control

docs.text: When coroutines share data or resources, they need ways to coordinate. asyncio provides the same tools you'd find in threading, in async form.
docs.title: 5. Coordination: Queues, Locks, Semaphores, Events

docs.text: async def producer ( queue , n_items ): for i in range ( n_items ): item = f "item- { i } " await asyncio . sleep ( random . uniform ( 0.1 , 0.5 )) await queue . put ( item ) print ( f " [Producer] Put: { item } (queue size: { queue . qsize () } )" ) async def consumer ( queue , name ): while True : item = await queue . get () # Blocks until an item is available if item is None : # Poison pill = stop signal print ( f " [ { name } ] Received stop signal. Shutting down." ) break # Process the item process_time = random . uniform ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Processing: { item } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( process_time ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Done: { item } ( { process_time : .1f } s)" ) queue . task_done () # Bounded queue: maxsize prevents producer from getting too far ahead queue = asyncio . Queue ( maxsize = 3 ) # Start 1 producer and 2 consumers prod = asyncio . create_task ( producer ( queue , 6 )) cons1 = asyncio . create_task ( consumer ( queue , "Worker-A" )) cons2 = asyncio . create_task ( consumer ( queue , "Worker-B" )) # Wait for producer to finish await prod # Wait for all items to be processed await queue . join () # Send stop signals await queue . put ( None ) await queue . put ( None ) await asyncio . gather ( cons1 , cons2 ) print ( " \n All work complete!" ) [Producer] Put: item-0 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-0... [Producer] Put: item-1 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Processing: item-1... [Worker-A] Done: item-0 (0.5s) [Producer] Put: item-2 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-2... [Producer] Put: item-3 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Done: item-1 (0.8s) [Worker-B] Processing: item-3... [Worker-A] Done: item-2 (0.6s) [Producer] Put: item-4 (queue size: 1) [Worker-A] Processing: item-4... [Producer] Put: item-5 (queue size: 1) [Worker-B] Done: item-3 (0.8s) [Worker-B] Processing: item-5... [Worker-A] Done: item-4 (0.5s) [Worker-B] Done: item-5 (0.4s) [Worker-A] Received stop signal. Shutting down. [Worker-B] Received stop signal. Shutting down. All work complete! maxsize=3 means put waits when the queue is full, so a fast producer can't run far ahead of the consumers. queue.join() waits until every item has been marked done with task_done() . Only then do we send one None (the stop signal, or poison pill ) per worker.
docs.title: 5.1 asyncio.Queue: Producer/Consumer

docs.text: # Shared counter WITHOUT a lock: race condition! counter_no_lock = 0 async def increment_unsafe ( n ): global counter_no_lock for _ in range ( n ): temp = counter_no_lock await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) # Context switch point! counter_no_lock = temp + 1 counter_no_lock = 0 await asyncio . gather ( increment_unsafe ( 100 ), increment_unsafe ( 100 ), ) print ( f "Without lock: counter = { counter_no_lock } (expected 200)" ) # Shared counter WITH a lock: safe! counter_with_lock = 0 lock = asyncio . Lock () async def increment_safe ( n ): global counter_with_lock for _ in range ( n ): async with lock : # Only one coroutine can enter at a time temp = counter_with_lock await asyncio . sleep ( 0 ) counter_with_lock = temp + 1 counter_with_lock = 0 await asyncio . gather ( increment_safe ( 100 ), increment_safe ( 100 ), ) print ( f "With lock: counter = { counter_with_lock } (expected 200)" ) Without lock: counter = 100 (expected 200) With lock: counter = 200 (expected 200) Without the lock, both coroutines read the same value, pause at await asyncio.sleep(0) , and then both write temp + 1 , so half of the increments are lost. Inside async with lock , only one coroutine at a time can run the read-pause-write steps. So yes, single-threaded async code can still have race conditions, but only at await points.
docs.title: 5.2 asyncio.Lock: Mutual Exclusion

docs.text: A semaphore limits how many coroutines can use a resource at the same time. It's ideal for rate limiting API calls. async def call_api ( endpoint , semaphore ): async with semaphore : # Blocks if too many concurrent calls print ( f " Calling { endpoint } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( random . uniform ( 0.5 , 1.5 )) print ( f " Done: { endpoint } " ) return f " { endpoint } : ok" # Allow at most 3 concurrent API calls sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( 3 ) endpoints = [ f "/api/item/ { i } " for i in range ( 8 )] print ( "Processing 8 endpoints with max 3 concurrent: \n " ) start = time . time () results = await asyncio . gather ( * [ call_api ( ep , sem ) for ep in endpoints ]) print ( f " \n All done in { time . time () - start : .1f } s" ) print ( f "Results: { results } " ) Processing 8 endpoints with max 3 concurrent: Calling /api/item/0... Calling /api/item/1... Calling /api/item/2... Done: /api/item/0 Calling /api/item/3... Done: /api/item/2 Calling /api/item/4... Done: /api/item/1 Calling /api/item/5... Done: /api/item/4 Calling /api/item/6... Done: /api/item/3 Calling /api/item/7... Done: /api/item/5 Done: /api/item/6 Done: /api/item/7 All done in 3.1s Results: ['/api/item/0: ok', '/api/item/1: ok', '/api/item/2: ok', '/api/item/3: ok', '/api/item/4: ok', '/api/item/5: ok', '/api/item/6: ok', '/api/item/7: ok'] There are never more than three calls in progress; a new call starts only when one finishes. Eight calls of about 1 second each, three at a time, take about 3 seconds in total.
docs.title: 5.3 asyncio.Semaphore: Rate Limiting

docs.text: async def waiter ( event , name ): print ( f " [ { name } ] Waiting for the signal..." ) await event . wait () # Blocks until the event is set print ( f " [ { name } ] Got the signal! Proceeding." ) async def trigger ( event ): print ( " [Trigger] Preparing... (1 second)" ) await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) print ( " [Trigger] Setting the event!" ) event . set () # All waiters are released simultaneously! event = asyncio . Event () # Three coroutines wait, one triggers results = await asyncio . gather ( waiter ( event , "Worker-A" ), waiter ( event , "Worker-B" ), waiter ( event , "Worker-C" ), trigger ( event ), ) [Worker-A] Waiting for the signal... [Worker-B] Waiting for the signal... [Worker-C] Waiting for the signal... [Trigger] Preparing... (1 second) [Trigger] Setting the event! [Worker-A] Got the signal! Proceeding. [Worker-B] Got the signal! Proceeding. [Worker-C] Got the signal! Proceeding. All three workers block on event.wait() . A single event.set() releases every one of them at once. Use an Event when several tasks need to wait for one thing to happen (for example "configuration loaded" or "shutdown requested").
docs.title: 5.4 asyncio.Event: Signal Between Coroutines

docs.text: Write download_file(file_id, semaphore) and use it to download 20 "files" concurrently, but never more than 5 at a time . Track the total time and compare it with how long the downloads would take one after another. async def download_file ( file_id , semaphore ): """Simulate downloading a file. Takes 0.5 - 1.5 seconds.""" # YOUR CODE HERE: # 1. Acquire the semaphore # 2. Print that you're starting the download # 3. Sleep for a random time # 4. Return a dict: {"file": file_id, "time": <seconds it took>} pass # YOUR CODE: create a semaphore, download 20 files, print stats # Hint: Track total time, count successes, calculate average latency # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # sem = asyncio.Semaphore(5) # start = time.time() # results = await asyncio.gather(*[download_file(i, sem) for i in range(20)]) # elapsed = time.time() - start # assert len(results) == 20 # assert elapsed < sum(r["time"] for r in results), "Downloads should overlap" # assert elapsed > 1.9, "At most 5 at a time: 20 files need at least 4 rounds of 0.5s" # print(f"✓ Downloaded 20 files in {elapsed:.1f}s") Show solution async def download_file ( file_id , semaphore ): async with semaphore : delay = random . uniform ( 0.5 , 1.5 ) print ( f " Downloading file { file_id } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) return { "file" : file_id , "time" : round ( delay , 2 )} sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( 5 ) start = time . time () results = await asyncio . gather ( * [ download_file ( i , sem ) for i in range ( 20 )] ) total = time . time () - start seq_estimate = sum ( r [ "time" ] for r in results ) print ( f " \n { '=' * 40 } " ) print ( f "Downloaded { len ( results ) } files" ) print ( f "Concurrent time: { total : .1f } s" ) print ( f "Sequential would be: ~ { seq_estimate : .1f } s" ) print ( f "Speedup: { seq_estimate / total : .1f } x" ) Quick recap asyncio.Queue hands work from producers to consumers; task_done() + join() track completion. asyncio.Lock lets only one coroutine at a time into a critical section. asyncio.Semaphore(n) lets at most n coroutines in at once, which is handy for rate limiting. asyncio.Event lets many coroutines wait until one of them signals with set() .

6. Async Iteration: async for and async with

docs.text: async def event_stream ( source , count = 5 ): """Simulates a stream of events arriving over time.""" for i in range ( count ): await asyncio . sleep ( random . uniform ( 0.2 , 0.8 )) event = { "source" : source , "id" : i , "value" : random . randint ( 1 , 100 ), } yield event # 'yield' in an 'async def' = async generator # Consume with 'async for' print ( "Receiving events:" ) async for event in event_stream ( "sensor-1" , count = 5 ): print ( f " Event # { event [ 'id' ] } : value= { event [ 'value' ] } " ) Receiving events: Event #0: value=85 Event #1: value=40 Event #2: value=56 Event #3: value=52 Event #4: value=15 An async def that contains yield is an async generator . async for awaits each item, so while the loop waits for the next event, other tasks can run.
docs.title: 6.1 Async Generators

docs.text: async def get_price ( item ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) prices = { "apple" : 1.50 , "banana" : 0.75 , "cherry" : 3.00 , "date" : 5.50 } return prices . get ( item , 0 ) # Async list comprehension (awaits inside the comprehension!) items = [ "apple" , "banana" , "cherry" , "date" ] prices = [ await get_price ( item ) for item in items ] print ( f "Prices: { dict ( zip ( items , prices )) } " ) # Async generator comprehension with 'async for' async def number_stream ( n ): for i in range ( n ): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.05 ) yield i # Filter even numbers from the async stream evens = [ x async for x in number_stream ( 10 ) if x % 2 == 0 ] print ( f "Even numbers: { evens } " ) Prices: {'apple': 1.5, 'banana': 0.75, 'cherry': 3.0, 'date': 5.5} Even numbers: [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] Careful: [await get_price(item) for item in items] awaits the calls one after another , so it's sequential (4 × 0.1 s). To fetch all the prices at the same time, you'd write await asyncio.gather(*(get_price(item) for item in items)) .
docs.title: 6.2 Async Comprehensions

docs.text: Use async with when setting up or tearing down a resource involves async operations. from contextlib import asynccontextmanager # Method 1: Class-based (implement __aenter__ and __aexit__) class AsyncTimer : """Times an async block.""" def __init__ ( self , label ): self . label = label async def __aenter__ ( self ): self . start = time . time () print ( f " [ { self . label } ] Timer started" ) return self async def __aexit__ ( self , exc_type , exc_val , exc_tb ): elapsed = time . time () - self . start print ( f " [ { self . label } ] Timer stopped: { elapsed : .2f } s" ) async with AsyncTimer ( "fetch" ) as timer : await asyncio . sleep ( 0.7 ) print ( " Doing work..." ) # Method 2: Decorator-based (simpler for most cases) @asynccontextmanager async def managed_connection ( db_name ): print ( f " Connecting to { db_name } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.3 ) conn = { "db" : db_name , "status" : "connected" } try : yield conn # Hand the connection to the caller finally : print ( f " Disconnecting from { db_name } ..." ) await asyncio . sleep ( 0.1 ) print ( f " Disconnected." ) print () async with managed_connection ( "mydb" ) as conn : print ( f " Using connection: { conn } " ) [fetch] Timer started Doing work... [fetch] Timer stopped: 0.70s Connecting to mydb... Using connection: {'db': 'mydb', 'status': 'connected'} Disconnecting from mydb... Disconnected. Two ways to write the same idea: Class-based : write __aenter__ (setup) and __aexit__ (teardown). @asynccontextmanager : write one async generator. The code before yield is the setup, the code after it is the teardown. Putting the teardown in finally makes sure it runs even if the block raises an error. Quick recap An async def with yield is an async generator; consume it with async for . await inside a list comprehension runs the calls sequentially; use gather to run them concurrently. Async context managers handle async setup/teardown; @asynccontextmanager is the short way to write one.
docs.title: 6.3 Async Context Managers (async with)

docs.text: Sometimes you need to call blocking code from async code (for example a library that has no async version), or start async code from normal synchronous code.
docs.title: 7. Bridging Sync and Async: Threads and Processes

docs.text: import hashlib def cpu_heavy_work ( data ): """Simulates CPU-bound work (blocking!).""" result = data for _ in range ( 100_000 ): result = hashlib . sha256 ( result . encode ()) . hexdigest () return result [: 16 ] def blocking_io (): """Simulates blocking I/O (like a non-async database driver).""" time . sleep ( 1 ) return "data from blocking call" # BAD: calling blocking functions directly freezes the event loop # GOOD: run them in a thread with to_thread() print ( "Running blocking + async work concurrently:" ) start = time . time () results = await asyncio . gather ( asyncio . to_thread ( cpu_heavy_work , "hello" ), # Runs in a thread asyncio . to_thread ( blocking_io ), # Runs in a thread asyncio . sleep ( 1 ), # Runs in the event loop ) print ( f " \n Hash result: { results [ 0 ] } " ) print ( f "IO result: { results [ 1 ] } " ) print ( f "Total time: { time . time () - start : .1f } s (all ran concurrently!)" ) Running blocking + async work concurrently: Hash result: 3b2d9ab4b38fe0bc IO result: data from blocking call Total time: 1.0s (all ran concurrently!) The event loop stays free while the two threads work, so the sleep, the blocking I/O and the hashing all overlap. One caveat: because of Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), only one thread runs Python code at a time. Moving cpu_heavy_work to a thread stops it from freezing the loop, but it does not make CPU-heavy Python code faster. For real CPU speed-ups you need separate processes.
docs.title: 7.1 asyncio.to_thread: Run Blocking Code Without Freezing the Loop

docs.text: run_in_executor lets you choose the pool the work runs in. Here's a thread pool: from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor def compute ( n ): """A CPU-bound function.""" return sum ( i * i for i in range ( n )) # Using a custom thread pool loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () with ThreadPoolExecutor ( max_workers = 4 ) as pool : results = await asyncio . gather ( loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 1_000_000 ), loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 2_000_000 ), loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , 3_000_000 ), ) for i , r in enumerate ( results ): print ( f " Result { i } : { r : , } " ) Result 0: 333,332,833,333,500,000 Result 1: 2,666,664,666,667,000,000 Result 2: 8,999,995,500,000,500,000 We print the results with {r:,} . Formatting with {r:,.0f} would first turn these big integers into floats and print slightly wrong digits at the end. For CPU-bound work, swap in a ProcessPoolExecutor so each job runs in its own process, on its own core. Process pools need the worker function to be importable by the child processes, so they don't work reliably with functions defined in a notebook. Use them from a .py script like this: # cpu_jobs.py import asyncio from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def compute ( n ): return sum ( i * i for i in range ( n )) async def main (): loop = asyncio . get_running_loop () with ProcessPoolExecutor () as pool : results = await asyncio . gather ( * ( loop . run_in_executor ( pool , compute , n ) for n in ( 1_000_000 , 2_000_000 , 3_000_000 )) ) print ( results ) if __name__ == "__main__" : asyncio . run ( main ())
docs.title: 7.2 loop.run_in_executor: Thread Pools and Process Pools

docs.text: Situation Solution Blocking I/O (file reads, a non-async database driver) asyncio.to_thread() or a ThreadPoolExecutor CPU-bound computation ProcessPoolExecutor or multiprocessing Async-native I/O ( aiohttp , asyncpg ) Just await it directly Calling async code from sync code asyncio.run() Quick recap Never call blocking functions directly in async code; they freeze the event loop. asyncio.to_thread(func, *args) runs a blocking function in a thread and lets you await the result. Threads keep the loop responsive but don't speed up CPU-bound Python code (GIL). Use processes for that. loop.run_in_executor(pool, func, *args) lets you pick a thread pool or a process pool.
docs.title: When to Use What

docs.text: Let's put everything together. We'll build a simulated web crawler that: starts from a list of seed URLs, fetches pages concurrently, with a semaphore limiting how many fetches run at once, reads the links on each page, uses a queue to keep track of the pages still to visit (the crawl frontier ), stops following links beyond a maximum depth, and stops after a maximum number of pages, retries a failed fetch a couple of times before giving up on that page. Instead of a real network we use FAKE_WEB , a dictionary of pages and their links, so the crawler runs anywhere. import asyncio import random import time # Simulated web: maps each URL to the links on that page FAKE_WEB = { "/" : [ "/about" , "/products" , "/blog" ], "/about" : [ "/about/team" , "/about/history" , "/" ], "/products" : [ "/products/1" , "/products/2" , "/products/3" ], "/blog" : [ "/blog/post-1" , "/blog/post-2" , "/" ], "/about/team" : [ "/about" ], "/about/history" : [ "/about" , "/" ], "/products/1" : [ "/products" , "/" ], "/products/2" : [ "/products" , "/products/1" ], "/products/3" : [ "/products" ], "/blog/post-1" : [ "/blog" , "/blog/post-2" ], "/blog/post-2" : [ "/blog" , "/" ], } async def fetch_page ( url , semaphore ): """Simulate fetching a web page.""" async with semaphore : delay = random . uniform ( 0.1 , 0.5 ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) if random . random () < 0.1 : # 10% chance of failure raise ConnectionError ( f "Failed to fetch { url } " ) links = FAKE_WEB . get ( url , []) size = random . randint ( 500 , 5000 ) return { "url" : url , "links" : links , "size" : size , "latency" : round ( delay , 3 )} async def fetch_with_retry ( url , semaphore , worker_id , attempts = 3 ): """Try a fetch up to `attempts` times before giving up.""" for attempt in range ( 1 , attempts + 1 ): try : return await fetch_page ( url , semaphore ) except ConnectionError as e : print ( f " [W { worker_id } ] ERROR (attempt { attempt } / { attempts } ): { e } " ) return None # every attempt failed async def crawl ( seeds , max_pages = 15 , max_depth = 2 , max_concurrent = 3 ): """Crawl starting from the seed URLs.""" visited = set () results = [] queue = asyncio . Queue () # holds (url, depth) pairs semaphore = asyncio . Semaphore ( max_concurrent ) for url in seeds : queue . put_nowait (( url , 0 )) async def worker ( worker_id ): while True : url , depth = await queue . get () try : if url in visited or len ( visited ) >= max_pages : continue # skip it (the finally block still runs) visited . add ( url ) page = await fetch_with_retry ( url , semaphore , worker_id ) if page is None : continue results . append ( page ) print ( f " [W { worker_id } ] Crawled { url } (depth { depth } , " f " { page [ 'size' ] } B, { page [ 'latency' ] } s, { len ( page [ 'links' ]) } links)" ) # Queue the links we found, unless we're already at max depth if depth < max_depth : for link in page [ "links" ]: if link not in visited : queue . put_nowait (( link , depth + 1 )) finally : queue . task_done () # mark this queue item as handled workers = [ asyncio . create_task ( worker ( i )) for i in range ( max_concurrent )] # join() returns once every queued URL has been handled # (including all the links discovered along the way) await queue . join () # The workers are now idle, waiting on an empty queue, so stop them for w in workers : w . cancel () await asyncio . gather ( * workers , return_exceptions = True ) return results # Run the crawler! print ( "Starting web crawler... \n " ) start = time . time () pages = await crawl ([ "/" ], max_pages = 11 , max_depth = 2 , max_concurrent = 3 ) elapsed = time . time () - start total_bytes = sum ( p [ "size" ] for p in pages ) avg_latency = sum ( p [ "latency" ] for p in pages ) / len ( pages ) if pages else 0 print ( f " \n { '=' * 50 } " ) print ( "CRAWL REPORT" ) print ( f " { '=' * 50 } " ) print ( f " Pages crawled: { len ( pages ) } " ) print ( f " Total data: { total_bytes : , } bytes" ) print ( f " Avg latency: { avg_latency : .3f } s" ) print ( f " Wall clock time: { elapsed : .1f } s" ) print ( f " Sequential est: ~ { sum ( p [ 'latency' ] for p in pages ) : .1f } s" ) Starting web crawler... [W0] Crawled / (depth 0, 1638B, 0.357s, 3 links) [W0] Crawled /about (depth 1, 1862B, 0.209s, 3 links) [W2] Crawled /blog (depth 1, 1888B, 0.346s, 3 links) [W1] ERROR (attempt 1/3): Failed to fetch /products [W2] Crawled /about/history (depth 2, 1348B, 0.145s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /about/team (depth 2, 3923B, 0.474s, 1 links) [W1] Crawled /products (depth 1, 4847B, 0.278s, 3 links) [W2] Crawled /blog/post-1 (depth 2, 800B, 0.255s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /blog/post-2 (depth 2, 3632B, 0.199s, 2 links) [W2] ERROR (attempt 1/3): Failed to fetch /products/2 [W1] Crawled /products/1 (depth 2, 4731B, 0.487s, 2 links) [W0] Crawled /products/3 (depth 2, 4505B, 0.355s, 1 links) [W2] Crawled /products/2 (depth 2, 4574B, 0.227s, 2 links) ================================================== CRAWL REPORT ================================================== Pages crawled: 11 Total data: 33,748 bytes Avg latency: 0.303s Wall clock time: 1.8s Sequential est: ~3.3s How the pieces fit together: The queue holds (url, depth) pairs waiting to be crawled. Three workers take URLs off it. The visited set makes sure no page is crawled twice, even though many pages link back to / . Every queue.get() is matched by a queue.task_done() in a finally block, even when a URL is skipped. That's what lets await queue.join() know when all the work, including newly discovered links, is finished. Once the queue is drained, the workers are just waiting forever on queue.get() , so we cancel them. The semaphore caps how many fetches run at once. Here it matches the number of workers; in a bigger crawler you might have many workers sharing a smaller limit. Your report will differ between runs because of the random delays and failures. Try changing max_depth to 1 and see which pages drop out. Quick recap A queue plus a fixed number of worker tasks is the standard shape for an async crawler or job runner. Pair every queue.get() with queue.task_done() (in finally ) so queue.join() knows when the work is done. Cancel idle workers after join() , then gather them so their cancellation is cleaned up.

docs.text: Build an async job scheduler that: accepts jobs with priorities (higher priority runs first), limits concurrency with a semaphore, supports a timeout per job, collects results and errors separately, and prints some statistics at the end. Store each success as {"name": ..., "result": ...} in self.results and each failure as {"name": ..., "error": ...} in self.errors , using the string "timeout" as the error for jobs that time out. import asyncio import random import time class AsyncJobScheduler : def __init__ ( self , max_concurrent = 3 , default_timeout = 5.0 ): self . max_concurrent = max_concurrent self . default_timeout = default_timeout self . jobs = [] # List of (priority, name, coro_func, timeout) self . results = [] self . errors = [] def add_job ( self , name , coro_func , priority = 0 , timeout = None ): """Add a job. Higher priority = runs first.""" # YOUR CODE HERE pass async def run_all ( self ): """Run all jobs respecting priority, concurrency, and timeouts.""" # YOUR CODE HERE: # 1. Sort jobs by priority (highest first) # 2. Create a semaphore # 3. For each job, create a task that: # a. Acquires the semaphore # b. Runs the coroutine with wait_for (timeout) # c. Stores result or error # 4. Gather all tasks # 5. Return (results, errors) pass # --- Test jobs --- async def fast_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.3 ) return "fast result" async def slow_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 3 ) return "slow result" async def flaky_job (): await asyncio . sleep ( 0.5 ) if random . random () < 0.5 : raise RuntimeError ( "Random failure!" ) return "flaky result" # --- Build and run --- scheduler = AsyncJobScheduler ( max_concurrent = 2 , default_timeout = 2.0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-1" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-2" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Slow-1" , slow_job , priority = 0 ) # Will timeout! scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-1" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) # Highest priority scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-2" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-3" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) # Tests (uncomment after finishing): # results, errors = await scheduler.run_all() # assert len(results) + len(errors) == 6 # assert {"name": "Slow-1", "error": "timeout"} in errors # assert [name for _, name, _, _ in scheduler.jobs][:2] == ["Flaky-1", "Flaky-2"] # highest priority first # print(f"✓ Successes: {len(results)}, Failures: {len(errors)}") Show solution class AsyncJobScheduler : def __init__ ( self , max_concurrent = 3 , default_timeout = 5.0 ): self . max_concurrent = max_concurrent self . default_timeout = default_timeout self . jobs = [] self . results = [] self . errors = [] def add_job ( self , name , coro_func , priority = 0 , timeout = None ): timeout = timeout or self . default_timeout self . jobs . append (( priority , name , coro_func , timeout )) async def _run_job ( self , name , coro_func , timeout , semaphore ): async with semaphore : try : print ( f " [ { name } ] Starting..." ) result = await asyncio . wait_for ( coro_func (), timeout = timeout ) print ( f " [ { name } ] Success: { result } " ) self . results . append ({ "name" : name , "result" : result }) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( f " [ { name } ] TIMEOUT after { timeout } s" ) self . errors . append ({ "name" : name , "error" : "timeout" }) except Exception as e : print ( f " [ { name } ] FAILED: { e } " ) self . errors . append ({ "name" : name , "error" : str ( e )}) async def run_all ( self ): self . results . clear () self . errors . clear () # Sort by priority (highest first) self . jobs . sort ( key = lambda j : j [ 0 ], reverse = True ) sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( self . max_concurrent ) tasks = [ self . _run_job ( name , coro_func , timeout , sem ) for _ , name , coro_func , timeout in self . jobs ] start = time . time () await asyncio . gather ( * tasks ) elapsed = time . time () - start print ( f " \n { '=' * 40 } " ) print ( f "JOB REPORT ( { elapsed : .1f } s total)" ) print ( f " { '=' * 40 } " ) print ( f " Successes: { len ( self . results ) } " ) print ( f " Failures: { len ( self . errors ) } " ) for e in self . errors : print ( f " - { e [ 'name' ] } : { e [ 'error' ] } " ) return self . results , self . errors scheduler = AsyncJobScheduler ( max_concurrent = 2 , default_timeout = 2.0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-1" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-2" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Slow-1" , slow_job , priority = 0 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-1" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Flaky-2" , flaky_job , priority = 2 ) scheduler . add_job ( "Fast-3" , fast_job , priority = 1 ) results , errors = await scheduler . run_all () Quick recap Sorting the jobs before creating the tasks, plus a semaphore, makes higher-priority jobs start first. wait_for gives every job its own timeout; try/except around it keeps one bad job from stopping the rest.

docs.text: async def f ( label , delay ): print ( f "start { label } " ) await asyncio . sleep ( delay ) print ( f "end { label } " ) results = await asyncio . gather ( f ( "X" , 1 ), f ( "Y" , 0.5 ), f ( "Z" , 0.1 )) start X start Y start Z end Z end Y end X Show answer start X start Y start Z end Z (0.1s) end Y (0.5s) end X (1.0s) All three start immediately, because gather runs them concurrently. They finish in order of their sleep time.
docs.title: Q1: What's the output order?

docs.text: To be safe, the cell stops waiting after 2 seconds, so a hang can't freeze your notebook. lock = asyncio . Lock () async def task_a (): async with lock : await task_b () async def task_b (): async with lock : print ( "done" ) try : await asyncio . wait_for ( task_a (), timeout = 2 ) except asyncio . TimeoutError : print ( "Still waiting after 2 seconds..." ) Still waiting after 2 seconds... Show answer No, it deadlocks. task_a holds the lock and then calls task_b , which tries to take the same lock. asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant (the task that holds it can't take it a second time), so task_b waits forever. Without the wait_for timeout, the cell would never finish. Fix: restructure the code so the lock isn't held while calling task_b , or avoid taking the same lock twice.
docs.title: Q2: Will this code finish?

docs.text: Assume fetch(url) is a coroutine that takes about 1 second. async def fetch_all ( urls ): results = [] for url in urls : result = await fetch ( url ) results . append ( result ) return results Show answer It's sequential. The for loop awaits each fetch() one at a time, so 10 URLs take about 10 seconds. To fetch them concurrently: async def fetch_all ( urls ): return await asyncio . gather ( * [ fetch ( url ) for url in urls ]) This is the most common asyncio performance mistake.
docs.title: Q3: What's wrong with this code?

docs.text: Show answer When you need to call a blocking function from async code without freezing the event loop. Common cases: Database drivers that aren't async ( sqlite3 , psycopg2 ) File I/O ( open , read , write ) Third-party libraries that don't support async CPU-heavy work, to keep the loop responsive (it won't run faster, because of the GIL) def read_file ( path ): with open ( path ) as f : return f . read () # Instead of: data = read_file ( "big_file.csv" ) # blocks the event loop # Do: data = await asyncio . to_thread ( read_file , "big_file.csv" ) # runs in a thread Quick recap Coroutines in gather start together and finish in order of how long they wait. asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: taking it twice in the same task deadlocks. Awaiting inside a for loop is sequential; use gather to overlap the waits. asyncio.to_thread is for blocking calls you can't make async.
docs.title: Q4: When should you use asyncio.to_thread()?

docs.text: import asyncio # Define a coroutine async def work (): await asyncio . sleep ( 1 ) return "done" # Run from a .py script (not inside Jupyter) asyncio . run ( work ()) # Run concurrently results = await asyncio . gather ( a (), b (), c ()) # Start in the background, await later (keep the reference!) task = asyncio . create_task ( work ()) result = await task # Structured concurrency (3.11+) async with asyncio . TaskGroup () as tg : t1 = tg . create_task ( a ()) t2 = tg . create_task ( b ()) # Process results as they complete for coro in asyncio . as_completed ([ a (), b (), c ()]): result = await coro

FIRST_COMPLETED )

Queue ( maxsize = 10 ) await queue . put ( item ) item = await queue . get () queue . task_done () # Lock (one at a time): create it ONCE and share it lock = asyncio . Lock () async with lock : ... # critical section # Semaphore (at most 5 at a time): create it ONCE and share it sem = asyncio . Semaphore ( 5 ) async with sem : ... # rate-limited work # Event (signalling) event = asyncio . Event () await event . wait () # block until set event . set () # release all waiters
